category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Chemical messengers that are secreted by cells into the extracellular fluid to affect neighboring target cells of a different type are defined as [___].
back: • Paracrines • These act locally on nearby cells via interstitial fluid rather than the blood. • Examples include somatostatin in the pancreatic islets or various growth factors.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: The rate-limiting step in the synthesis of all adrenocortical hormones is the conversion of cholesterol to [___] by the enzyme cholesterol desmolase.
back:
• Pregnenolone
  • Occurs within the mitochondria
  • Stimulated by ACTH in the zona fasciculata/reticularis
  • Stimulated by Angiotensin II in the zona glomerulosa

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: A 45-year-old female presents with cold intolerance, weight gain, and non-pitting edema (myxedema). Laboratory tests show elevated TSH. Identify the deficient hormones and their specific cellular source.
back:
• Hormones: Thyroxine (T4) and Triiodothyronine (T3)
  • Source: Thyroid follicular epithelial cells
  • Diagnosis: Primary Hypothyroidism (e.g., Hashimoto's disease)

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Explain how the hypothalamus regulates the secretion of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary.
back:
• GHRH: Stimulates GH secretion via somatotropes
  • Somatostatin (GHIH): Inhibits GH secretion
  • Transport: Hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels
  • Feedback: Regulated by IGF-1 and GH levels

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: A child presents with polydipsia and polyuria. Imaging shows a tumor compressing the pituitary stalk. Contrast the physiological mechanism of central diabetes insipidus with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
back:
• Central: Lack of ADH synthesis/secretion from the posterior pituitary
  • Nephrogenic: Renal tubule resistance to ADH (V2 receptor/aquaporin defect)
  • Treatment: Vasopressin analogs (Desmopressin) work only in Central DI

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: List the three primary hormones secreted by the kidney and their high-yield physiological functions.
back:
• Renin: Catalyzes angiotensinogen to angiotensin I
  • 1,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol: Increases intestinal calcium absorption
  • Erythropoietin: Stimulates erythrocyte production in bone marrow

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: In the Islets of Langerhans, the [___] cells secrete insulin to lower blood glucose, while [___] cells secrete glucagon to increase it.
back:
• Beta cells (60%): Secrete Insulin and Amylin
  • Alpha cells (25%): Secrete Glucagon
  • Delta cells (10%): Secrete Somatostatin

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: A 30-year-old male presents with bitemporal hemianopia and milky nipple discharge. Identify the likely hormone-secreting tumor and the inhibitory factor that normally controls this hormone.
back:
• Tumor: Prolactinoma (Lactotrope tumor)
  • Inhibitory Factor: Dopamine (Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone)
  • Source: Hypothalamic arcuate nuclei

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Describe the functional mechanism of the 'Double Bohr Effect' at the placental interface.
back:
• Fetal side: CO2 loss to mother increases fetal hemoglobin's O2 affinity
  • Maternal side: CO2 gain from fetus decreases maternal hemoglobin's O2 affinity
  • Result: Enhanced O2 transfer to fetal blood

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Contrast the chemical nature and transport mechanisms of steroid hormones versus thyroid hormones (T3/T4).
back:
• Steroids: Derived from cholesterol; not stored; lipophilic; cross membranes easily
  • Thyroid Hormones: Derived from tyrosine; stored in follicles as thyroglobulin; lipophilic; require carrier proteins (TBG)

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Identify the primary hormones produced by the placenta and their roles in maintaining pregnancy.
back:
• hCG: Prevents corpus luteum involution
  • Estrogens: Uterine and breast enlargement
  • Progesterone: Decidual cell development; decreases uterine contractility
  • HCS: Decreases maternal insulin sensitivity

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Chemical messengers released by glands or specialized cells into the circulating blood to influence target cells at a distant location are defined as [___].
back:
• Endocrine hormones.
• Transported via the systemic circulation.
• Influence metabolic functions, growth, and reproduction by binding to specific receptors.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: A 25-year-old obese male is found to have a genetic deficiency in a peptide messenger produced by adipocytes that acts on the hypothalamus to regulate satiety. This messenger is classified as a/an [___].
back:
• Leptin (an adipokine).
• A specialized cytokine produced by fat cells.
• Functions as a hormonal signal for energy balance and appetite suppression.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Explain the biological mechanism of paracrine signaling within the extracellular fluid.
back:
• Cells secrete chemicals into the ECF.
• The messenger diffuses to and affects neighboring target cells.
• Crucially, target cells must be of a different type than the secreting cell.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Contrast autocrine signaling with paracrine signaling based on the target cell type.
back:
• Autocrines: Affect the same cells that produced them.
• Paracrines: Affect neighboring cells of a different type.
• Both systems utilize the extracellular fluid for local transport.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Define neuroendocrine hormones and provide an example of their secretion site.
back:
• Chemicals secreted by neurons into the circulating blood.
• Act on distant target cells at another location.
• Example: Hypothalamic neurons secreting ADH or Oxytocin into the blood.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Peptides secreted by cells into the extracellular fluid that can function as autocrines, paracrines, or endocrine hormones are collectively called [___].
back:
• Cytokines.
• Include interleukins and other lymphokines.
• Regulate immune responses and metabolic functions (e.g., leptin).

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: A patient experiences rapid local control of nerve cell function via messengers released at synaptic junctions. This describes the action of [___].
back:
• Neurotransmitters.
• Released by neuronal axon terminals.
• Act locally at the synaptic cleft to alter postsynaptic cell excitability.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Describe how the body ensures that endocrine hormones only affect specific tissues despite systemic circulation.
back:
• Presence of specific protein receptors in target cells.
• Only tissues with high-affinity receptors for a specific hormone respond.
• Receptors are located on the membrane, cytoplasm, or nucleus.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Contrast the mode of delivery between endocrine hormones and neurotransmitters.
back:
• Endocrine: Secreted into the blood to reach distant targets.
• Neurotransmitters: Secreted into synaptic junctions to act locally.
• Both coordinate complex body functions through chemical signaling.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Enlist the six primary types of chemical messenger systems that coordinate body functions.
back:
1. Neurotransmitters.
2. Endocrine hormones.
3. Neuroendocrine hormones.
4. Paracrines.
5. Autocrines.
6. Cytokines.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: The [___] lobe of the pituitary gland (adenohypophysis) secretes six major hormones including GH, ACTH, and TSH, whereas the posterior lobe releases ADH and Oxytocin.
back:
- Anterior
- Hormones: GH, TSH, ACTH, Prolactin, FSH, and LH
- Coordinates growth, metabolism, and thyroid/adrenal/gonadal function
- Regulated by hypothalamic releasing hormones via the portal system

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Hormones released by adipocytes that inhibit appetite and stimulate thermogenesis are known as [___].
back:
• Leptin
• Classified as a peptide hormone
• Acts on the hypothalamus to regulate energy balance

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: A patient is diagnosed with a hyperfunctional tumor of the alpha cells of the pancreatic Islets of Langerhans. The hormone primarily oversecreted in this condition is [___].
back:
• Glucagon
• Increases blood glucose via glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
• Functions as a diametric antagonist to insulin

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Explain the role of the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels in the delivery of hypothalamic factors.
back:
• Conducts releasing and inhibitory hormones from the median eminence
• Transports these factors directly to the anterior pituitary sinuses
• Allows rapid, concentrated regulation of adenohypophyseal secretion

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Contrast the sites of hormone synthesis for the anterior pituitary versus the posterior pituitary glands.
back:
• Anterior: Synthesized locally within glandular cells (e.g., somatotropes, corticotropes)
• Posterior: Synthesized in the hypothalamus (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei)
• Posterior hormones travel via axoplasm to terminal nerve endings

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Enlist the primary hormones produced by the kidneys and their high-yield physiological roles.
back:
• Renin: Catalyzes angiotensinogen conversion to angiotensin I
• 1,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol: Increases intestinal calcium absorption
• Erythropoietin: Stimulates erythrocyte production in bone marrow

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: The enzyme aldosterone synthase, required for mineralocorticoid production, is uniquely localized to the [___] of the adrenal cortex.
back:
• Zona Glomerulosa
• Outermost layer of the cortex
• Regulated primarily by Angiotensin II and extracellular potassium

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: A male fetus presents with ambiguous genitalia due to failed testosterone production in utero. This failure is often linked to insufficient placental secretion of [___].
back:
• Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)
• Stimulates fetal Leydig cells to produce testosterone
• Essential for male sexual organ differentiation during gestation

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Describe the dual inhibitory mechanism of Somatostatin within the endocrine system.
back:
• Anterior Pituitary: Inhibits the release of Growth Hormone (GH)
• Pancreas: Locally depresses secretion of both Insulin and Glucagon
• GI Tract: Decreases motility and secretory activity

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Distinguish between the hormonal products of thyroid follicular cells and parafollicular C-cells.
back:
• Follicular cells: Produce Thyroxine (T4) and Triiodothyronine (T3)
• Parafollicular cells: Produce Calcitonin
• T3/T4 regulate metabolic rate, while Calcitonin lowers plasma calcium

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Name the primary hormones secreted by the human placenta during pregnancy.
back:
• Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)
• Estrogens (Estradiol, Estrone, Estriol)
• Progesterone
• Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS)

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Chemical messengers released by axon terminals into synaptic junctions to act locally to control nerve cell functions are specifically termed [___].
back:
• Neurotransmitters
• Acts locally at the synaptic cleft
• Examples include Acetylcholine and Norepinephrine.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: A 45-year-old female is diagnosed with a thyroid adenoma secreting excessive thyroxine into the blood to affect distant tissues. This signaling system is classified as [___].
back:
• Endocrine signaling
• Hormones are released into the circulating blood
• Influence target cells at distant locations.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Explain the biological pathway of neuroendocrine hormones from secretion to target action.
back:
• Secreted by neurons (e.g., in the hypothalamus)
• Enter the circulating blood
• Influence target cells at distant locations in the body.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Contrast the target cells of paracrine messengers with those of autocrine messengers.
back:
• Paracrines: Affect neighboring cells of a different type.
• Autocrines: Affect the same cells that produced them.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Define the specific group of cytokine messengers produced by adipocytes that regulate appetite and thermogenesis.
back:
• Adipokines
• Primary example: Leptin
• Function as hormones via endocrine or paracrine pathways.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Peptide messengers such as interleukins, secreted by immune cells to act on other immune cells or themselves, are known as [___].
back:
• Cytokines
• Can function as autocrines, paracrines, or endocrine hormones
• Crucial for coordinating immune responses.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: A cell releases a chemical into the extracellular fluid that binds to receptors on the same cell to modulate its own activity. This depicts [___] signaling.
back:
• Autocrine signaling
• Common in immune cells and cancer cell growth
• Acts locally within the immediate microenvironment.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: How do hypothalamic neurons specifically coordinate the function of the anterior pituitary gland?
back:
• Secrete hypothalamic releasing/inhibitory hormones
• Transported via hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels
• Act as neuroendocrine signals to regulate pituitary secretion.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Contrast the transport medium used by endocrine hormones versus neurotransmitters.
back:
• Endocrine: Transported via the circulating blood.
• Neurotransmitters: Transported across the synaptic cleft (local diffusion).

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Enlist the three major chemical classes of hormones found in the human body.
back:
• Proteins and Polypeptides (e.g., Insulin)
• Steroids (e.g., Cortisol)
• Tyrosine derivatives/Amines (e.g., Thyroxine).

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Chemical messengers released by glands or specialized cells into the circulating blood to influence target cells at a distant location are defined as [___].
back:
• Endocrine hormones.
• Transported via the circulatory system.
• Act on specific target tissues possessing appropriate receptors.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: A physiological study observes that somatostatin released from pancreatic delta cells inhibits insulin secretion from adjacent beta cells without entering the systemic circulation. Identify the messenger type.
back:
• Paracrine messenger.
• Secreted into extracellular fluid (ECF).
• Affects neighboring cells of a different type.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Explain the mechanism by which neuroendocrine hormones reach their target tissues compared to standard neurotransmitters.
back:
• Neuroendocrine: Secreted by neurons into blood to reach distant targets (e.g., ADH).
• Neurotransmitters: Released by axon terminals into synapses to act locally.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: In a laboratory experiment, Cell A secretes a peptide that binds to its own surface receptors, while Cell B secretes a factor affecting only the cell immediately next to it. Contrast these two signaling types.
back:
• Cell A: Autocrine (acts on the same cell that produced it).
• Cell B: Paracrine (acts on different neighboring cells).

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Identify the class of peptide messengers that include interleukins and lymphokines, and explain their unique functional flexibility.
back:
• Cytokines.
• Can function as autocrines, paracrines, or endocrine hormones.
• Includes adipokines (e.g., leptin) produced by fat cells.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Chemical messengers released by axon terminals into synaptic junctions to control local nerve cell functions are called [___].
back:
• Neurotransmitters.
• Act locally at the synapse.
• Rapidly control excitable cell functions.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: A patient is diagnosed with a deficiency in Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH). Although ADH is secreted by hypothalamic neurons, it is carried by the blood to the kidneys. What is the classification of this messenger?
back:
• Neuroendocrine hormone.
• Produced by specialized neurons.
• Travels via the general circulation to distant target organs.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: A specific immune cell produces a cytokine that enhances its own phagocytic activity. Explain the biological mechanism involved in this specific response.
back:
• Autocrine signaling.
• Messenger is released into ECF.
• Binds to receptors on the secreting cell to modify its own function.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Contrast endocrine and paracrine messengers regarding the medium of transport and the distance to the target cell.
back:
• Endocrine: Transported via blood to distant targets.
• Paracrine: Diffuses through extracellular fluid (ECF) to neighboring cells.

category: Define different chemical messengers
front: Name the specific term for cytokines produced by adipocytes and provide a high-yield example mentioned in coordination of body functions.
back:
• Adipokines.
• Primary example: Leptin.
• Functions in appetite regulation and thermogenesis.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: The hormone secreted by the [___] cells of the pancreatic islets that functions as the primary 'hyperglycemic' factor by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis is glucagon.
back:
• Alpha cells.
• It increases blood glucose levels within minutes.
• Directly opposes the effects of insulin.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: A 45-year-old male with a history of head trauma presents with extreme thirst and the production of large volumes of highly dilute urine. This presentation suggests a deficiency in which hormone?
back:
• Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) / Vasopressin.
• Secreted by the posterior pituitary.
• Synthesized in the supraoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: How does the hypothalamus communicate with the anterior pituitary gland to regulate hormone secretion compared to its communication with the posterior pituitary?
back:
• Anterior: Via hypothalamic-hypophysial portal blood vessels (releasing/inhibitory hormones).
• Posterior: Via the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract (direct neural axons).
• Anterior cells are epithelioid; posterior tissue is neural.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Distinguish between the cutaneous findings in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) and secondary adrenal insufficiency, and explain the hormonal basis for this difference.
back:
• Primary: Hyperpigmentation due to high ACTH levels (MSH-like activity).
• Secondary: No hyperpigmentation due to low/absent ACTH.
• In Primary, loss of cortisol feedback triggers POMC overproduction.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Enumerate the three distinct layers of the adrenal cortex from the capsule inward and name the primary hormone class each layer secretes.
back:
• Zona Glomerulosa: Mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone).
• Zona Fasciculata: Glucocorticoids (Cortisol).
• Zona Reticularis: Androgens (Dehydroepiandrosterone).
• Memory Aid: GFR (Glomerulosa, Fasciculata, Reticularis).

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: In the thyroid gland, the large glycoprotein stored within follicles that serves as the essential substrate for the synthesis and storage of T3 and T4 is [___].
back:
• Thyroglobulin.
• Contains tyrosine residues that undergo iodination.
• Provides a 2-3 month supply of thyroid hormones.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: A pregnant woman presents with a tendency to retain sodium and water. Beyond placental hormones, which corticosteroid increases twofold by the end of gestation to contribute to this effect?
back:
• Aldosterone.
• Increases due to high metabolic load and placental signals.
• Causes renal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Explain the dual-mechanism role of Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) in early pregnancy regarding the corpus luteum and fetal development.
back:
• Prevents involution of the corpus luteum (maintaining progesterone/estrogen).
• Stimulates male fetal testes to produce testosterone.
• Essential for male sex organ differentiation in utero.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Contrast the effects of Insulin and Growth Hormone (GH) on blood glucose levels and identify their synergistic metabolic role.
back:
• Insulin: Hypoglycemic (promotes glucose uptake).
• Growth Hormone: Diabetogenic (decreases glucose utilization).
• Synergy: Both are required to promote optimal body growth.

category: Enlist endocrine organs and hormones of the body
front: Enlist three non-traditional endocrine hormones secreted by the kidneys and their primary physiological roles.
back:
• Renin: Activates RAAS for blood pressure regulation.
• Erythropoietin: Stimulates RBC production in bone marrow.
• 1,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol: Active Vitamin D for calcium absorption.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Hormones like cortisol and aldosterone, which are synthesized from cholesterol and not stored in secretory vesicles, are chemically categorized as [___].
back:
• Steroids
• Lipid-soluble compounds derived from cholesterol
• Secreted via simple diffusion across cell membranes
• Produced by adrenal cortex, ovaries, testes, and placenta.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: A 14-year-old male presents with polyuria and weight loss due to an inability to produce insulin. The missing hormone belongs to the chemical class of [___].
back:
• Proteins and Polypeptides
• Synthesized as preprohormones on the rough endoplasmic reticulum
• Stored in secretory vesicles until stimulus triggers exocytosis.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Explain the role of the amino acid tyrosine as a precursor for two distinct endocrine gland secretions.
back:
• Forms Thyroid Hormones (T3, T4) in the thyroid gland follicles
• Forms Catecholamines (Epinephrine, Norepinephrine) in the adrenal medulla
• Classified as Amine hormones.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Contrast the storage mechanisms of steroid hormones with those of protein/polypeptide hormones.
back:
• Polypeptides: Synthesized and stored in cytoplasmic secretory vesicles until needed
• Steroids: Not stored; synthesized on demand from large pools of cholesterol esters.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Identify the chemical nature and primary source of Dopamine when it acts as a Prolactin-Inhibiting Factor.
back:
• Amine hormone
• Derived from the amino acid tyrosine
• Secreted by neurons in the hypothalamus into the portal system.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Every hormone secreted by both the anterior and posterior pituitary glands belongs to the chemical class of [___].
back:
• Proteins and Polypeptides
• Includes GH, ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, ADH, and Oxytocin
• All are water-soluble and circulate freely in plasma.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
coreConcept: Thyroid Hormone Storage and Amine Nature
front: A patient with tremors and exophthalmos has high levels of T3 and T4. These hormones are unique amines because they are stored [___].
back:
• Within the thyroid gland follicles as part of the protein thyroglobulin
• Storage can last 2–3 months
• They are lipid-soluble but require protein carriers in blood.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Explain how the chemical nature of hormones determines their mode of transport in the blood.
back:
• Water-soluble (Peptides/Catecholamines): Dissolve in plasma and circulate in free form
• Lipid-soluble (Steroids/Thyroid): Require specific carrier proteins (e.g., albumin or globulins) for transport.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Contrast the solubility and receptor locations of catecholamines versus steroid hormones.
back:
• Catecholamines: Water-soluble; bind to cell membrane receptors
• Steroids: Lipid-soluble; bind to intracellular receptors (cytoplasm or nucleus) to activate gene transcription.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: List the three general classes of hormones based on their chemical structure.
back:
• Proteins and Polypeptides (e.g., Insulin, Pituitary hormones)
• Steroids (e.g., Cortisol, Testosterone)
• Tyrosine-derived Amines (e.g., Thyroxine, Epinephrine).

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: On the basis of chemical nature, hormones such as Insulin and Glucagon are classified as [___], while those derived from cholesterol, like Aldosterone, are known as [___].
back: * Proteins/Polypeptides: Water-soluble; includes pituitary and pancreatic hormones. * Steroids: Lipid-soluble; includes adrenal cortex and gonadal hormones. * Amine Derivatives: Derived from tyrosine (e.g., Thyroxine, Epinephrine).

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: The predominant regulatory mechanism in the endocrine system that prevents the oversecretion of a hormone by using the products of its biological action to suppress its further production is [___].
back:
• Negative feedback
• Maintains homeostasis of hormone activity
• Regulates levels through gene transcription, translation, and release steps

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Hormones derived from cholesterol, such as cortisol and testosterone, belong to the [___] class of chemical messengers.
back:
* **Steroids**
* Synthesized from cholesterol via specific enzymatic pathways.
* Lipid-soluble; they diffuse easily across cell membranes.
* Not stored in secretory vesicles; released upon demand.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: A patient presents with high levels of Growth Hormone and Insulin. Based on their chemical nature, these hormones are classified as [___] and are synthesized in the [___].
back:
* **Proteins and Polypeptides**
* Synthesized on the **Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum**.
* Initially formed as preprohormones, then cleaved to prohormones.
* Water-soluble; travel freely in the blood.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Explain how the chemical nature of steroid hormones determines their storage and release mechanism.
back:
* **Lipid solubility:** Prevents storage in lipid-bilayer vesicles as they would diffuse out.
* **Synthesis-on-demand:** Mobilized from cholesterol esters in cytoplasm vacuoles upon stimulus.
* **Release:** Simple diffusion across the membrane immediately after synthesis.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Contrast the two main sub-groups of amine hormones regarding their solubility and receptor location.
back:
* **Thyroid (T3/T4):** Lipid-soluble; act on nuclear receptors.
* **Catecholamines (Epi/NE):** Water-soluble; act on cell membrane receptors.
* **Precursor:** Both are derived from the amino acid tyrosine.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Enumerate the three primary chemical classes of hormones found in the human body.
back:
* **Proteins and Polypeptides:** e.g., Insulin, Pituitary hormones.
* **Steroids:** e.g., Cortisol, Estrogen, Testosterone.
* **Tyrosine derivatives (Amines):** e.g., Thyroxine, Epinephrine.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Hormones that are water-soluble and circulate freely in the blood without carrier proteins are typically [___] or [___].
back:
* **Peptides/Proteins** and **Catecholamines**.
* They cannot cross cell membranes due to hydrophilicity.
* They interact with surface receptors to initiate second messenger cascades.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: A lab finding shows a hormone requires a carrier protein for plasma transport and binds to a receptor in the cell nucleus. Identify the likely chemical classes.
back:
* **Steroids** or **Thyroid hormones**.
* Both are lipid-soluble and poorly soluble in plasma.
* They primarily influence gene transcription and protein synthesis.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Explain why polypeptide hormones require second messenger systems like cAMP to exert their effects.
back:
* **Hydrophilic barrier:** Cannot penetrate the lipid cell membrane.
* **First Messenger:** Binds to extracellular receptors.
* **Transduction:** Receptor activation triggers intracellular enzymes to carry out functions.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Distinguish between the synthesis sites of protein hormones versus steroid hormones within the endocrine cell.
back:
* **Proteins:** Ribosomes on the **Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum**.
* **Steroids:** **Mitochondria** and **Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum**.
* **Packaging:** Proteins use the Golgi; steroids do not.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Identify the specific amino acid precursor for hormones like Epinephrine and Thyroxine.
back:
* **Tyrosine**.
* Forms the basis of 'Amine' hormones.
* Processed by cytoplasmic enzymes in the thyroid and adrenal medulla.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: The process where a chronic increase in hormone concentration leads to a decrease in the number of active receptors is termed [___], which serves to diminish tissue responsiveness.
back:
- Down-regulation
- Occurs via receptor inactivation, sequestration, or lysosomal destruction
- Up-regulation increases receptor numbers or signaling proteins
- These mechanisms adjust target tissue sensitivity to maintain hormonal homeostasis

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: In the majority of endocrine systems, the primary mechanism used to maintain hormone levels within a narrow physiological range and prevent overactivity is [___] feedback.
back:
Negative feedback.
- Prevents oversecretion of the hormone.
- The biological action or product of the hormone suppresses its further release.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: A 28-year-old female presents with tachycardia, weight loss, and low TSH levels despite high free T3/T4. This clinical finding of suppressed TSH is explained by [___].
back:
Negative feedback inhibition.
- High circulating T3/T4 inhibits the anterior pituitary thyrotropes.
- Prevents additional TSH release despite the primary pathology.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Explain the role of the estrogen threshold in triggering the preovulatory Luteinizing Hormone (LH) surge.
back:
Positive feedback mechanism.
- Estrogen reaches a critical high level for 2-3 days.
- This reverses the normal inhibition, stimulating a massive burst of LH from the pituitary.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Contrast the plasma ACTH levels in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) with secondary adrenal insufficiency regarding feedback loops.
back:
- Primary (Addison’s): High ACTH due to loss of cortisol-mediated negative feedback.
- Secondary: Low ACTH due to hypothalamic/pituitary failure, causing low cortisol.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: In the control of insulin secretion, identify the specific 'controlled variable' monitored by the pancreatic beta cells.
back:
Blood glucose concentration.
- Hyperglycemia stimulates insulin release.
- Insulin-induced glucose uptake lowers blood sugar, subsequently terminating the secretion stimulus.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Cortisol exerts direct negative feedback inhibition on the anterior pituitary gland to specifically decrease the formation of [___].
back:
Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).
- It also inhibits Corticotropin-Releasing Factor (CRF) in the hypothalamus.
- Ensures cortisol levels do not become excessive.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: A patient with suspected Cushing's Disease receives a high dose of Dexamethasone, which results in a suppression of ACTH. This indicate that the [___] is the likely source of the pathology.
back:
Anterior Pituitary.
- Pituitary adenomas (Cushing's Disease) retain partial sensitivity to negative feedback.
- Ectopic tumors (e.g., lung) usually show zero suppression.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: How does the Sertoli cell use Inhibin to regulate the rate of spermatogenesis?
back:
Negative feedback on FSH.
- Inhibin is secreted when sperm production is too rapid.
- It acts directly on the anterior pituitary to inhibit FSH secretion.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Contrast 'short-loop' and 'long-loop' feedback within the hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland hierarchy.
back:
- Long-loop: Target gland hormone (e.g., Cortisol) inhibits Hypothalamus/Pituitary.
- Short-loop: Pituitary hormone (e.g., TSH) inhibits Hypothalamic releasing factor (e.g., TRH).

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: What is the primary stimulus that triggers the parathyroid glands to increase PTH secretion within minutes?
back:
Decreased extracellular calcium ion concentration.
- Sensed by calcium-sensing receptors (CaSR).
- Low calcium removes the inhibitory feedback signal for PTH release.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: To maintain homeostasis and prevent hormone overactivity, the mechanism where a hormone's biological action suppresses its further secretion is termed [___].
back:
• Negative feedback
• Ensures hormone activity at target tissues remains at appropriate levels
• Most common control mechanism in endocrinology.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: A patient with long-term glucocorticoid therapy presents with adrenal insufficiency upon sudden drug withdrawal. Explain the feedback pathophysiology behind the resulting bilateral adrenal atrophy.
back:
• Exogenous cortisol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary.
• Suppresses CRF and ACTH secretion.
• Chronic lack of ACTH results in atrophy of the zona fasciculata and reticularis.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Describe the mechanism of the preovulatory LH surge in the female sexual cycle.
back:
• Sustained high levels of estrogen reach a critical threshold.
• Switch from negative to positive feedback on the anterior pituitary.
• Triggers a 6- to 10-fold surge in LH.
• Induces follicular rupture and ovulation.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Contrast the TSH and T3/T4 profiles in primary hyperthyroidism (Graves' disease) versus a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma.
back:
• Graves' (Primary): High T3/T4 with suppressed (near-zero) TSH due to negative feedback.
• Pituitary Adenoma (Secondary): High T3/T4 with inappropriately high or normal TSH; tumor ignores negative feedback.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Describe the pharmacological basis of the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test in differentiating causes of Cushing's syndrome.
back:
• Dexamethasone provides potent negative feedback to the pituitary.
• Pituitary adenomas (Cushing's Disease) typically suppress ACTH at high doses.
• Ectopic ACTH-producing tumors (e.g., lung cancer) remain non-responsive and do not suppress.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Growth hormone (GH) secretion is suppressed via negative feedback by the liver-derived protein [___].
back:
• Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
• Also known as Somatomedin C
• GH also self-inhibits by acting on the hypothalamus.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: A 40-year-old female presents with hyperpigmentation and hypotension. Labs show low serum cortisol and very high ACTH. Identify the specific feedback failure in this clinical presentation.
back:
• Primary Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's Disease).
• Failure of the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol.
• Loss of negative feedback leads to compensatory overproduction of ACTH/MSH by the pituitary.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Explain the role of the Calcium-Sensing Receptor (CaSR) in the feedback control of Parathyroid Hormone (PTH).
back:
• CaSRs on parathyroid cell membranes detect extracellular Ca2+.
• Increased Ca2+ activates the receptor, inhibiting PTH secretion.
• Decreased Ca2+ removes inhibition, rapidly stimulating PTH release and bone resorption.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Contrast the feedback triggers for Insulin versus Glucagon secretion regarding blood glucose levels.
back:
• Insulin: Stimulated by high blood glucose (negative feedback to lower glucose).
• Glucagon: Inhibited by high blood glucose and stimulated by hypoglycemia (negative feedback to raise glucose).

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Identify the hypothalamic hormone that provides the primary inhibitory feedback control for Prolactin secretion.
back:
• Dopamine
• Also known as Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone (PIH)
• Secreted by the arcuate nuclei into the hypophysial portal system.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Prolonged exposure to high hormone concentrations often leads to [___] of receptors, decreasing the target tissue's responsiveness.
back:
• Down-regulation
  • Involves decreasing the number of active receptors
  • Prevents over-stimulation of the target cell by chronic ligand excess

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: A patient with a chronic hormone-secreting tumor develops resistance to that hormone despite high circulating levels. Describe the likely receptor-level pathophysiology.
back:
• Receptor down-regulation
  • Sequestration or internalization of receptors away from the surface
  • Lysosomal destruction of receptor-ligand complexes
  • Inactivation of intracellular signaling proteins

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: How does up-regulation enhance the sensitivity of a target tissue to a specific hormone?
back:
• Stimulates greater formation of receptor molecules
  • Increases availability of receptors for ligand binding
  • Synthesizes more intracellular signaling proteins
  • Heightens the cell's response to minimal stimuli

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Contrast the receptor-level response seen in 'denervation supersensitivity' versus hormone resistance due to chronic ligand excess.
back:
• Supersensitivity: Up-regulation occurs due to a lack of neurotransmitter release
  • Resistance: Down-regulation occurs due to chronic ligand excess
  • Result: Increased sensitivity vs. decreased responsiveness

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: List the five specific cellular mechanisms responsible for the down-regulation of hormone receptors.
back:
• Inactivation of receptor molecules
  • Inactivation of signaling proteins
  • Temporary sequestration (internalization)
  • Lysosomal destruction of internalized receptors
  • Decreased production of new receptors

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: The phenomenon where the number of receptors increases on the postsynaptic membrane following a chronic lack of neurotransmitter release is known as [___].
back:
• Up-regulation (Denervation Supersensitivity)
  • Increases tissue sensitivity to exogenous ligands
  • Compensates for the absence of normal endogenous stimulation

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: A researcher observes that a cell becomes 'hypersensitive' after being deprived of its usual chemical messenger for several days. Explain the molecular change occurring at the membrane.
back:
• Up-regulation
  • The cell induces greater formation of surface receptors
  • Increased receptor availability ensures minute messenger amounts trigger a full response

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Explain the role of lysosomes in the down-regulation process after a hormone binds to a cell membrane receptor.
back:
• Hormone-receptor complexes are internalized via endocytosis
  • Vesicles fuse with intracellular lysosomes
  • Proteolytic enzymes destroy the internalized receptors
  • Reduces the total receptors available for subsequent binding

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Distinguish between receptor 'sequestration' and 'decreased production' in the context of receptor regulation.
back:
• Sequestration: Temporary movement of receptors to the cell interior (rapid)
  • Decreased production: Reduced genetic synthesis of new receptor proteins (slower, long-term)

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Identify the primary physiological purpose of varying receptor density via up-regulation and down-regulation.
back:
• Homeostatic regulation of cellular responsiveness
  • Prevents toxicity/over-stimulation during excess (down-regulation)
  • Maintains vital signaling during ligand deficiency (up-regulation)

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: In the majority of endocrine systems, the primary mechanism used to maintain hormone activity at a target tissue and prevent oversecretion is [___] feedback.
back:
• Negative feedback
• Ensures homeostasis by suppressing further hormone release once the desired biological effect or concentration is achieved.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: A 35-year-old female presents with palpitations and weight loss. Labs show elevated T3 and T4 but undetectable TSH. This lab pattern demonstrates the physiological principle of [___].
back:
• Negative feedback inhibition
• Elevated thyroid hormones act directly on the anterior pituitary to suppress the secretion of TSH.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Explain the role of estrogen as a positive feedback signal during the late follicular phase of the ovarian cycle.
back:
• High estrogen levels reach a critical threshold for 2–3 days
• Stimulates the preovulatory LH surge
• Triggers ovulation by switching from negative to positive feedback.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Contrast the primary feedback signals that regulate Insulin versus Parathyroid Hormone (PTH).
back:
• Insulin: Regulated by blood glucose levels (metabolic substrate).
• PTH: Regulated by plasma ionized calcium levels (ion concentration).
• Both utilize negative feedback loops to maintain substrate/ion stability.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Identify the specific hypothalamic nucleus that acts as the 'master clock' for cyclical/diurnal hormone variations.
back:
• Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN)
• Controls rhythmic patterns of biological clocks in neuroendocrine cells and peripheral glands (e.g., cortisol and growth hormone).

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Cortisol regulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis by inhibiting the secretion of [___] from the hypothalamus and ACTH from the anterior pituitary.
back:
• Corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF)
• This represents long-loop negative feedback designed to maintain stable glucocorticoid levels.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) has low cortisol levels. Predict the resulting change in ACTH levels and the mechanism involved.
back:
• Elevated ACTH
• Mechanism: Loss of negative feedback inhibition due to low circulating cortisol, leading to disinhibition of the pituitary.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Describe the multi-level feedback mechanism by which Growth Hormone (GH) inhibits its own production.
back:
• Direct: Inhibits pituitary somatotropes
• Indirect: Stimulates hypothalamic Somatostatin (GHIH) release
• IGF-1 (Somatomedin C): Exerts negative feedback on the anterior pituitary and hypothalamus.

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Contrast the feedback effect of hyperglycemia on pancreatic Alpha cells versus Beta cells.
back:
• Beta cells: Stimulated to secrete Insulin (to lower glucose).
• Alpha cells: Inhibited from secreting Glucagon (to prevent further glucose rise).

category: Discuss the feedback control of hormone secretion
front: Which feedback type is characterized by a hormone's biological action causing even more of that hormone to be secreted?
back:
• Positive Feedback
• Examples include the LH surge (estrogen-mediated) and oxytocin release during labor (cervical stretch-mediated).

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: The process by which an increased hormone concentration leads to a decrease in the number of active receptors on a target cell is termed [___].
back:
• Down-regulation
  • It results in decreased target tissue responsiveness and sensitivity to the stimulating hormone.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: A patient with a chronic insulin-secreting tumor (insulinoma) develops significant insulin resistance at the cellular level. Identify the receptor-level adaptation responsible.
back:
• Receptor Down-regulation
  • Continuous high insulin levels trigger receptor internalization or destruction.
  • Reduces the total number of active binding sites on the cell membrane.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Explain the role of lysosomes in the mechanism of receptor down-regulation.
back:
• Hormone-receptor complexes are internalized (sequestered) by endocytosis.
  • Intracellular lysosomes then fuse with these vesicles.
  • Proteolytic enzymes in lysosomes permanently destroy the receptor proteins.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Contrast receptor sequestration with receptor destruction during the down-regulation process.
back:
• Sequestration: Temporary translocation of receptors from the cell membrane to the interior.
  • Destruction: Permanent degradation of receptors by lysosomes.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Explain why the number of hormone receptors on a target cell is not constant but varies over time.
back:
• Cells dynamically regulate receptor counts to maintain homeostasis.
  • Receptors are constantly inactivated/destroyed and synthesized/reactivated.
  • Adaptation depends on the surrounding hormone concentration.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: [___] occurs when a hormone induces greater than normal formation of its receptors or signaling proteins, making the tissue progressively more sensitive.
back:
• Up-regulation
  • Commonly occurs in response to hormone deficiency or receptor blockade.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Following the destruction of a sympathetic nerve, the denervated organ becomes 2 to 10 times more responsive to injected norepinephrine. What is this phenomenon called?
back:
• Denervation Supersensitivity
  • It is caused by receptor up-regulation.
  • The number of receptors in the postsynaptic membrane increases significantly.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Explain how hormone receptors can be down-regulated without altering the physical number of receptors on the surface.
back:
• Inactivation of the receptor molecules themselves.
  • Inactivation of intracellular protein signaling molecules.
  • Decoupling of the receptor from its second messenger cascade (e.g., adenylyl cyclase).

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Contrast the effects of receptor up-regulation and down-regulation on tissue sensitivity.
back:
• Up-regulation: Increases sensitivity to stimulating effects.
  • Down-regulation: Decreases sensitivity and responsiveness.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Enlist four cellular mechanisms responsible for the down-regulation of hormone receptors.
back:
• Inactivation of receptor molecules.
  • Inactivation of intracellular signaling proteins.
  • Temporary sequestration (internalization).
  • Lysosomal destruction or decreased production.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: The common chemical precursor from which all steroid hormones, including aldosterone, cortisol, and testosterone, are synthesized is [___].
back:
*   Substrate: Cholesterol.
*   Source: Primarily from low-density lipoproteins (LDLs) in plasma.
*   Rate-limiting step: Conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone in the mitochondria.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
coreConcept: Chemical nature vs. Onset of action
front: A patient with acute asthma is given an injection of epinephrine (amine) followed by oral prednisone (steroid). Explain the difference in onset of action between these two drugs.
back:
*   Epinephrine: Water-soluble; acts rapidly via cell surface receptors and second messengers (cAMP).
*   Prednisone: Lipid-soluble; requires 45-60 minutes for gene transcription and new protein synthesis.
*   Chemical nature determines receptor location and mechanism speed.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Explain the typical synthesis and processing steps of polypeptide hormones like insulin within endocrine cells.
back:
*   Rough ER: Translated initially as large, inactive preprohormones.
*   ER/Golgi: Cleaved into smaller prohormones and then active hormones.
*   Storage: Packaged into secretory vesicles and stored until exocytosis is triggered.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: In a patient with hypermetabolism, contrast the receptor locations and signaling pathways for Growth Hormone (peptide) versus Thyroid Hormone (amine).
back:
*   Growth Hormone: Water-soluble; binds cell membrane receptors (JAK2 tyrosine kinase pathway).
*   Thyroid Hormone: Lipid-soluble; binds nuclear receptors to modulate DNA transcription.
*   Solubility: GH cannot cross membranes; T3/T4 diffuse directly into the nucleus.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Identify which chemical classes of hormones utilize cell surface receptors and second messenger systems versus those that act on the genome.
back:
*   Surface Receptors: Peptides/proteins and catecholamines (water-soluble).
*   Genomic Action: Steroids and thyroid hormones (lipid-soluble).
*   Exception: Some rapid nongenomic effects exist for steroids/thyroid hormones.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: To assess endogenous insulin production in a diabetic patient receiving exogenous insulin injections, clinicians measure the plasma concentration of [___].
back:
*   C-peptide (Connecting peptide).
*   Rationale: It is cleaved from proinsulin and secreted in equimolar amounts with insulin.
*   Significance: Unlike exogenous insulin, it indicates actual beta-cell secretory function.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: A patient with Addison's disease receives oral hydrocortisone but cannot be treated with oral ACTH. Explain this conceptual application based on chemical nature.
back:
*   Hydrocortisone: A steroid (lipid); small and lipid-soluble enough to be absorbed intact from the GI tract.
*   ACTH: A polypeptide (protein); hydrolyzed/digested by GI proteolytic enzymes before absorption.
*   Clinical rule: Proteins must be injected; many steroids can be oral.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which lipid-soluble steroid hormones initiate their biological response after entering the target cell.
back:
*   Binding: Hormones bind to specific protein receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
*   DNA Interaction: The hormone-receptor complex binds to 'Hormone Response Elements' on DNA.
*   Response: This activates or represses gene transcription, forming mRNA and new functional proteins.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Contrast the transport and blood-solubility characteristics of the two main types of tyrosine-derived hormones: Thyroid hormones and Catecholamines.
back:
*   Thyroid (T3/T4): Lipid-soluble; poorly soluble in water; transported mainly bound to plasma proteins.
*   Catecholamines: Water-soluble; circulate in blood mainly in a free, dissolved form.
*   Half-life: Thyroid hormones have long half-lives; catecholamines are cleared within minutes.

category: Enlist the hormones on the basis of chemical nature
front: Enlist the three general chemical classes of hormones found in the human body.
back:
*   Proteins and Polypeptides: E.g., Insulin, Pituitary hormones.
*   Steroids: E.g., Cortisol, Estrogen (derived from cholesterol).
*   Tyrosine Derivatives (Amines): E.g., Thyroxine, Epinephrine.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Primary receptors for steroid hormones, such as cortisol and aldosterone, are characteristically located in the cell [___].
back:
• Cytoplasm.
• After binding, the hormone-receptor complex migrates to the nucleus to activate or repress gene transcription.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: A patient presents with polyuria and polydipsia; investigations reveal insulin resistance. The receptors for the hormone responsible for this condition are located [___].
back:
• On the surface of the cell membrane.
• Specifically, these are enzyme-linked (tyrosine kinase) receptors composed of alpha and beta subunits.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Explain the receptor location and signaling mechanism used by Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) to stimulate the adrenal cortex.
back:
• Location: Outer surface of the cell membrane.
• Mechanism: Activates G-protein linked adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP, which initiates the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Contrast the receptor locations and immediate genomic effects of Catecholamines versus Thyroid hormones.
back:
• Catecholamines: Cell membrane surface; activate second messengers (cAMP/IP3).
• Thyroid hormones: Cell nucleus; bind directly to chromosomal DNA to induce mRNA formation.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Enlist the three primary cellular locations where hormone receptors are found according to their chemical nature.
back:
• Cell membrane: Proteins, peptides, and catecholamines.
• Cytoplasm: Steroid hormones.
• Nucleus: Thyroid hormones (T3 and T4).

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Receptors for thyroid hormones are found in the [___], specifically in direct association with one or more chromosomes.
back:
• Cell nucleus.
• These receptors typically form a heterodimer with the Retinoid X Receptor (RXR).

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: A 35-year-old female presents with weight gain and striae. If the cause is excessive cortisol, identify the cellular compartment where the hormone initially binds its receptor.
back:
• Cytoplasm.
• The resulting complex then enters the nucleus to bind with Glucocorticoid Response Elements (GRE) on the DNA.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Explain why the physiological response to Aldosterone binding its receptor in the renal tubules is delayed for 45–60 minutes.
back:
• Aldosterone binds to cytoplasmic mineralocorticoid receptors.
• The delay is caused by the time required for DNA transcription, mRNA formation, and translation of new transport proteins.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Contrast the receptor locations of Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH) with those of the Estrogens.
back:
• GHRH: Cell membrane surface (activates cAMP system).
• Estrogens: Intracellular (Cytoplasm/Nucleus), characteristic of lipid-soluble steroid hormones.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Name the specific type of membrane-bound receptor and associated enzyme system used by Leptin to regulate appetite.
back:
• Enzyme-linked receptor.
• It signals through the Janus Kinase 2 (JAK2) family, leading to STAT3 protein phosphorylation.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Receptor down-regulation often involves the temporary [___] of the receptor protein to the interior of the cell, moving it away from the site of hormone action.
back:
* Sequestration
* Removes receptors from the cell membrane surface
* Prevents extracellular hormone binding
* Decreases target tissue responsiveness to high hormone levels

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: A patient with a hormone-secreting tumor initially responds to the hormone, but eventually develops resistance despite increasing serum hormone levels. Explain the likely cellular adaptation.
back:
* Down-regulation of receptors
* Caused by chronic exposure to high hormone concentrations
* Involves receptor inactivation or destruction
* Reduces the tissue's functional sensitivity to the stimulus

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which up-regulation increases the sensitivity of a target tissue to a specific hormone.
back:
* Increased synthesis of new receptor proteins
* Increased availability of existing receptors at the cell membrane
* Enhanced formation of intracellular signaling molecules
* Result: Greater functional response to lower hormone concentrations

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Contrast the fate of receptors during sequestration versus lysosomal destruction in the process of down-regulation.
back:
* Sequestration: Receptors are temporarily stored inside the cell and can be recycled.
* Lysosomal Destruction: Internalized receptors are permanently degraded by enzymes.
* Both reduce active membrane receptor density.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Describe how the concentration of a hormone in the blood typically influences the number of active receptors in a target cell.
back:
* High concentrations induce down-regulation (decreased density).
* Low concentrations/deficiency induce up-regulation (increased density).
* This feedback maintains homeostasis by adjusting tissue sensitivity.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: The phenomenon where a tissue becomes significantly more sensitive to a neurotransmitter after its nerve supply has been destroyed is termed [___] supersensitivity.
back:
* Denervation
* Caused by receptor up-regulation in the postsynaptic membrane
* Results in enhanced reaction to injected or circulating hormones

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: A cell decreases its responsiveness to a peptide hormone by inactivating its intracellular signaling cascade rather than the receptor itself. Identify this type of adaptation.
back:
* Post-receptor down-regulation
* Involves inactivation of signaling molecules (e.g., G-proteins)
* Effectively stops the intracellular response despite hormone-receptor binding

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Explain the role of endocytosis in the regulation of cell surface hormone receptors.
back:
* Triggered by hormone-receptor complex formation
* Internalizes receptors into the cytoplasm via vesicles
* Initiates the down-regulation pathway (sequestration or degradation)
* Rapidly reduces the number of available binding sites

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Contrast the long-term metabolic consequences of receptor down-regulation versus up-regulation in endocrine disorders.
back:
* Down-regulation: Leads to hormone resistance (e.g., Type 2 Diabetes).
* Up-regulation: Leads to hyper-sensitivity or exaggerated responses (e.g., denervated organs).
* Both represent adaptive shifts in the dose-response curve.

category: Explain the up and down regulation of receptors
front: Enlist three specific mechanisms that lead to a decrease in active receptor numbers during down-regulation.
back:
* Inactivation of receptor molecules
* Sequestration or lysosomal destruction of receptors
* Decreased production (synthesis) of new receptors

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
coreConcept: Intracellular and Extracellular Locations of Hormone Receptors
front: Hormone receptors are specifically located in three areas: protein and catecholamine hormones bind to the [___], steroid hormones to the [___], and thyroid hormones to the [___].
back: • Cell membrane: Protein, peptide, and catecholamine hormones. • Cytoplasm: Primary receptors for lipid-soluble steroid hormones. • Nucleus: Thyroid hormone receptors, located in direct association with chromosomes.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
coreConcept: Location of peptide and catecholamine receptors
front: Hormone receptors for proteins, peptides, and catecholamines are primarily located [___].
back: • In or on the surface of the cell membrane.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
coreConcept: Intracellular location of steroid hormone receptors
front: A 45-year-old male with central obesity and hypertension is suspected of having hypercortisolism. The hormone involved in this pathophysiology binds to receptors located in the [___].
back: • Cell cytoplasm (specifically the glucocorticoid receptor).

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Explain the specific binding site and cellular location of thyroid hormone receptors.
back:
• Located in the cell nucleus.
• Bound directly to chromosomes.
• Usually forms a heterodimer with Retinoid X Receptor (RXR).

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
coreConcept: Differential receptor location of metabolic hormones
front: Contrast the receptor locations of Insulin versus Aldosterone.
back:
• Insulin: Transmembrane protein on the cell surface.
• Aldosterone: Specific receptor protein in the cell cytoplasm.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Name the specific intracellular compartment where Vitamin D receptors are predominantly found.
back: • The cell nucleus (associated with target genes).

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Primary receptors for steroid hormones, such as progesterone and testosterone, are typically found in the [___].
back: • Cell cytoplasm.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: A patient presents with excessive growth of the jaw and hands (acromegaly). Growth Hormone, which is elevated in this condition, binds to receptors located on the [___].
back: • Surface of the target cell membrane.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Explain the biological function and physical structure of G protein-linked hormone receptors in terms of cell location.
back:
• Located on the cell membrane.
• Consist of seven transmembrane segments.
• Indirectly regulate enzymes or ion channels via heterotrimeric G proteins.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
coreConcept: Catecholamine vs. Thyroid hormone receptor location
front: Contrast the receptor locations for Adrenaline (epinephrine) and Thyroxine (T4).
back:
• Adrenaline: Cell membrane surface.
• Thyroxine: Within the cell nucleus.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Enlist the three general locations of hormone receptors within target cells.
back:
• 1. In or on the cell membrane surface.
• 2. In the cell cytoplasm.
• 3. In the cell nucleus.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Receptors for protein, peptide, and catecholamine hormones are primarily located [___].
back: • In or on the surface of the cell membrane.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: A 45-year-old female is prescribed Prednisolone (a glucocorticoid) for rheumatoid arthritis. This lipophilic hormone initiates its action by binding to receptors located in the [___].
back:
• Cell cytoplasm.
• These cytoplasmic receptors then migrate to the nucleus once bound.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Describe the anatomical location and association of thyroid hormone receptors within a target cell.
back:
• Located in the cell nucleus.
• Found in direct association with one or more chromosomes.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Contrast the primary intracellular location of steroid hormone receptors with that of thyroid hormone receptors.
back:
• Steroid Receptors: Primarily in the cytoplasm.
• Thyroid Receptors: Exclusively in the nucleus.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Specify the precise location of the alpha and beta subunits of the insulin receptor relative to the cell membrane.
back:
• Alpha subunits: Entirely outside the cell membrane (extracellular).
• Beta subunits: Penetrate through the membrane into the cytoplasm (intracellular).

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Each target cell typically contains between [___] and [___] highly specific hormone receptors.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: A patient with Conn's syndrome has an aldosterone-secreting tumor. To exert its mineralocorticoid effects, aldosterone must bind to MR receptors located in the [___] of renal tubular cells.
back:
• Cytoplasm.
• Specifically within the principal cells of the collecting tubules.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Explain the structural orientation of G-protein linked receptors (GPCRs) within the plasma membrane.
back:
• Seven-transmembrane segments.
• They loop in and out of the membrane seven times.

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Distinguish between the receptor locations for water-soluble (peptide) hormones versus lipid-soluble (steroid) hormones.
back:
• Water-soluble: Cell membrane surface (cannot cross lipid bilayer).
• Lipid-soluble: Intracellular (cross membrane by simple diffusion).

category: Enlist the location of hormone receptors
front: Identify the location of the receptors that the sperm head binds to during the acrosome reaction.
back: • Located on the zona pellucida of the ovum.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: In the inactive state of a G-protein-linked receptor, the alpha subunit of the heterotrimeric G protein is bound to [___].
back:
• Guanosine diphosphate (GDP).
• Activation causes the exchange of GDP for GTP.
• The alpha subunit then dissociates to interact with effector enzymes like adenylyl cyclase.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: A 55-year-old obese male with Type 2 Diabetes shows elevated insulin levels but poor glucose uptake in skeletal muscle. This 'insulin resistance' is primarily caused by defects in the [___] that link receptor activation to cellular effects.
back:
• Intracellular signaling pathways.
• Specifically involves Insulin-Receptor Substrates (IRS-1/2).
• Defects prevent the translocation of GLUT 4 transporters to the cell membrane.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Explain how the adenylyl cyclase-cAMP system achieves significant signal amplification after a single hormone molecule binds a membrane receptor.
back:
• Enzyme cascade: One activated cyclase produces multiple cAMP molecules.
• cAMP activates multiple protein kinases.
• Each kinase phosphorylates many target enzymes, multiplying the response a millionfold.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Contrast the physiological roles of Inositol triphosphate (IP3) and Diacylglycerol (DAG) following the activation of Phospholipase C.
back:
• IP3: Mobilizes calcium ions from the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria into the cytoplasm.
• DAG: Activates protein kinase C (PKC) and provides arachidonic acid for prostaglandin synthesis.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Describe the specific intracellular signaling pathway utilized by the Leptin receptor to regulate appetite and energy balance.
back:
• JAK-STAT pathway.
• Leptin binding triggers phosphorylation of Janus kinase 2 (JAK2).
• JAK2 phosphorylates STAT proteins, which enter the nucleus to initiate gene transcription.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Lipophilic hormones like aldosterone bind to intracellular receptors that then interact with a specific DNA sequence called the [___] to activate transcription.
back:
• Hormone response element (HRE).
• The complex acts as a transcription factor.
• Leads to synthesis of proteins like Na+-K+ ATPase and epithelial sodium channels.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: A patient presents with hyperthyroidism due to Graves' disease. The autoimmune antibodies (TSIs) in this condition stimulate the thyroid gland by mimicking TSH and activating the [___] second messenger system.
back:
• Adenylyl cyclase–cAMP system.
• TSIs bind the TSH receptor on the basal membrane.
• This induces continual activation and chronic hormone overproduction.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Explain the biochemical transition required for the Calcium-Calmodulin system to activate myosin light chain kinase in smooth muscle.
back:
• Intracellular calcium must rise to 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁵ mol/L.
• Calcium binds to four sites on calmodulin.
• Calmodulin changes shape, activating protein kinases to trigger phosphorylation.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Distinguish between the downstream metabolic effects of stimulating a Gs protein versus a Gi protein.
back:
• Gs (Stimulatory): Activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and activating protein kinases.
• Gi (Inhibitory): Inhibits adenylyl cyclase, decreasing cAMP and reducing enzyme phosphorylation.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Identify the primary cellular location of receptors for thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) and their typical binding partner.
back:
• Location: Cell nucleus.
• Binding Partner: Retinoid X Receptor (RXR).
• Function: They form a heterodimer at the thyroid hormone response element.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
coreConcept: Hormone Response Elements in Genomic Signaling
front: Upon entering the target cell, the activated lipophilic hormone-receptor complex binds to a specific regulatory sequence of DNA known as the [___] to initiate or repress gene transcription.
back: • Hormone Response Element (HRE) • Functions as a promoter or repressor on DNA strands • Triggers mRNA formation and subsequent protein synthesis • Mechanism used by steroids and thyroid hormones

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Upon hormone binding to a G protein-linked receptor, the trimeric G protein becomes active by exchanging [___] for [___] on the alpha subunit.
back:
• Guanosine Diphosphate (GDP) for Guanosine Triphosphate (GTP).
• This exchange causes the alpha subunit to dissociate from the beta and gamma subunits to interact with membrane-bound enzymes.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency is administered intravenous cortisol. The physician notes that metabolic effects are not seen for nearly 60 minutes. Explain the pathophysiology of this delay.
back:
• Genomic mechanism: Cortisol must diffuse into cells and bind intracellular receptors.
• Translation/Transcription: The complex binds DNA to initiate mRNA formation and new protein synthesis, a process inherently requiring time.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Explain the step-wise intracellular cascade of the adenylyl cyclase–cAMP second messenger system after Gs protein activation.
back:
• Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP).
• cAMP activates cAMP-dependent protein kinase.
• Protein kinases phosphorylate specific enzymes, triggering the final biochemical response.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Contrast the structural and signaling features of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) with enzyme-linked receptors like the insulin receptor.
back:
• GPCRs: Seven-transmembrane segments; signal via heterotrimeric G proteins and second messengers.
• Enzyme-linked: Single-pass membrane proteins; possess intrinsic enzymatic activity (e.g., tyrosine kinase) or associate directly with enzymes (e.g., JAK).

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Describe the mechanism that terminates the signaling activity of an activated G-protein alpha subunit.
back:
• Self-inactivation: The alpha subunit has intrinsic GTPase activity.
• GTP Hydrolysis: It converts its bound GTP back to GDP, allowing it to re-associate with the beta and gamma subunits.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: In the cell membrane phospholipid second messenger system, the enzyme [___] cleaves PIP2 into the two second messengers [___] and [___].
back:
• Phospholipase C.
• Inositol triphosphate (IP3).
• Diacylglycerol (DAG).

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: A research study identifies a cytokine receptor that functions via JAK2 phosphorylation and subsequent activation of STAT proteins. This mechanism is characteristic of the [___] receptor.
back:
• Leptin receptor.
• Activated STAT (signal transducer and activator of transcription) proteins initiate gene transcription for appetite and energy balance regulation.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Explain the role of the Hormone Response Element (HRE) in the mechanism of action of lipid-soluble hormones.
back:
• It is a specific regulatory DNA sequence in the promoter region.
• The activated hormone-receptor complex binds here to activate or repress gene transcription and mRNA formation.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Contrast the specific roles of IP3 and DAG once they are released into the cytoplasm from membrane phospholipids.
back:
• IP3: Mobilizes calcium ions from mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum.
• DAG: Activates protein kinase C, which phosphorylates proteins to elicit the cell's response.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Distinguish between the primary cellular locations of receptors for Thyroid hormones versus steroid hormones.
back:
• Thyroid hormones: Receptors are located in the nucleus, bound to or associated with chromosomes.
• Steroid hormones: Receptors are primarily located in the cytoplasm.

category: Name the hormones that use enzyme-linked hormone receptors signaling
front: Metabolic and growth-regulating hormones that utilize enzyme-linked receptors (e.g., Receptor Tyrosine Kinases or JAK/STAT pathways) for transmembrane signaling include insulin, growth hormone, and [___].
back:
* Leptin
* Prolactin
* Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1)
* Various growth factors (FGF, HGF, VEGF)

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: The primary receptors for lipid-soluble hormones, such as adrenal and gonadal steroids, are located within the [___].
back:
• Cell cytoplasm (or nucleus).
• They act as ligand-activated transcription factors.
• They bind to specific DNA hormone response elements to modulate gene transcription.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: A patient with a pituitary adenoma shows excessive ACTH levels. Explain the immediate intracellular signaling event that occurs in the adrenal cortex to increase cortisol secretion.
back:
• ACTH binds to Gs-protein coupled receptors.
• Adenylyl cyclase is activated, increasing cAMP levels.
• Protein kinase A activates enzymes to convert cholesterol into pregnenolone.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Describe the activation sequence of a heterotrimeric G protein once a hormone-receptor complex is formed.
back:
• Alpha subunit exchanges GDP for GTP.
• Alpha-GTP subunit dissociates from beta and gamma subunits.
• Active alpha subunit modulates target proteins like adenylyl cyclase or ion channels.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Contrast the intracellular signaling of peptide hormones with that of thyroid hormones regarding speed and primary mechanism.
back:
• Peptides: Rapid (seconds to minutes); utilize membrane-bound receptors and second messengers.
• Thyroid Hormones: Slow (hours to days); bind nuclear receptors to activate gene transcription and protein synthesis.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
front: Identify the signaling cascade utilized by the Leptin receptor to mediate its effects on energy balance.
back:
• Janus Kinase (JAK2) phosphorylation.
• Activation of Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription (STAT) proteins.
• STAT proteins migrate to the nucleus to initiate target gene transcription.

category: Explain the mechanism of intracellular signaling after hormone receptor activation
