front: Specify why the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system is essential for maintaining high local concentrations of neurohormones.
back:
• It provides a direct, low-volume route to target cells.
• It bypasses the systemic circulation.
• Allows minute quantities of hypothalamic hormones to avoid degradation and trigger immediate responses.

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: The lowermost portion of the hypothalamus that serves as the functional link to the anterior pituitary by containing the primary capillary plexus is the [___].
back:
• Median eminence.
• Site where neurosecretory neurons discharge releasing/inhibitory factors.
• Coalesces to form the portal blood vessels.

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
coreConcept: Secondary Endocrine Failure via Portal Obstruction
front: A 35-year-old female suffers from severe postpartum hemorrhage leading to Sheehan’s syndrome. If the pathology involves portal vessel thrombosis, how does this affect the delivery of TRH?
back:
• TRH cannot reach the thyrotropes in the anterior pituitary.
• Leads to secondary hypothyroidism.
• Results from loss of the vascular link between the hypothalamus and adenohypophysis.

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: Explain how the portal circulation regulates the secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH).
back:
• Hypothalamic GnRH is released into the primary capillary plexus.
• It travels via portal vessels to anterior pituitary gonadotropes.
• Binds to G-protein receptors to stimulate cAMP/phospholipase C pathways.

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: Distinguish between the 'Primary' and 'Secondary' capillary plexuses in the context of the hypophysial portal system.
back:
• Primary: Located in the median eminence; site of neurohormone absorption.
• Secondary: Located in the adenohypophysis sinuses; site of hormone action on glandular cells.

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: Identify the primary amine transported through the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels that exerts tonic inhibition on lactation.
back:
• Dopamine (Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone).
• Secreted by arcuate nucleus neurons into the median eminence.
• Continuously suppresses prolactin secretion in non-lactating states.

category: Name the hormones/ factors of hypothalamus
front: Growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) is primarily synthesized by neurons located in the arcuate and [___] nuclei of the hypothalamus.
back:
• Ventromedial nuclei.
• These same areas are sensitive to blood glucose, linking nutritional status to growth signals.

category: Name the hormones/ factors of hypothalamus
front: A 25-year-old male with a hypothalamic lesion is found to have normal ACTH and TSH but lacks pulsatile LH and FSH secretion. This suggests a deficiency in which hypothalamic decapeptide?
back:
• Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).
• It is synthesized in the arcuate nuclei and preoptic area to control the pituitary-gonadal axis.

category: Name the hormones/ factors of hypothalamus
front: Describe the intracellular signaling mechanism utilized by Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH) to trigger growth hormone release from somatotropes.
back:
• Activates the adenylyl cyclase-cAMP system.
• Increases intracellular cAMP.
• Stimulates calcium ion transport into the cell.
• Triggers fusion and exocytosis of GH secretory vesicles.

category: Name the hormones/ factors of hypothalamus
front: Contrast the primary hypothalamic nuclei responsible for synthesizing Vasopressin (ADH) versus Oxytocin, including the degree of cross-synthesis.
back:
• ADH: Primarily synthesized in the Supraoptic nuclei.
• Oxytocin: Primarily synthesized in the Paraventricular nuclei.
• Cross-synthesis: Each nucleus produces approximately 1/6th of the other's primary hormone.

category: Name the hormones/ factors of hypothalamus
front: Identify the hypothalamic hormone that, when administered continuously instead of pulsatily, is used pharmacologically to suppress the pituitary-gonadal axis.
back:
• Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).
• Continuous infusion causes down-regulation/desensitization of GnRH receptors on anterior pituitary gonadotropes, halting LH/FSH secretion.

category: Name the hormones/ factors of hypothalamus
front: The hypothalamic neurons responsible for synthesizing both Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone (TRH) and Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone (CRH) are located primarily in the [___] nucleus.
back:
• Paraventricular nucleus (PVN).
• TRH is a tripeptide, while CRH is a larger 41-amino acid polypeptide.

category: Name the hormones/ factors of hypothalamus
front: An arctic explorer experiences a 50-100% increase in thyroid hormone output. Identify the specific hypothalamic releasing factor and the physiological stimulus responsible for this adaptation.
back:
• Factor: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH).
• Stimulus: Exposure to severe cold.
• Rationale: Excitation of hypothalamic temperature control centers increases BMR to maintain core heat.

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Hypophysial Portal Vessels
front: The functional vascular link between the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary gland, which transports hypophysiotropic hormones to their target cells, is the [___] system.
back: • Hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system • Connects the median eminence to the adenohypophysis • Allows high local concentrations of releasing/inhibiting hormones without systemic dilution

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: A patient suffers a traumatic head injury resulting in the total transection of the pituitary stalk. Predict the effect on serum Prolactin levels compared to other anterior pituitary hormones.
back: • Prolactin levels rise significantly (loss of hypothalamic dopamine inhibition) • Other hormones (GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH/LH) decrease to low levels • Occurs because the portal link for releasing factors is severed

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: Describe the physiological sequence of neurohormone transport from the hypothalamic neurons to the glandular cells of the adenohypophysis.
back: • Neurons release factors into the median eminence tissue fluid • Hormones enter the primary capillary plexus • Transport occurs via portal veins to the secondary capillary plexus (sinuses) • Releasing/inhibiting factors bind specific pituitary cells

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: Contrast the delivery route of hypothalamic hormones to the anterior pituitary with the delivery route to the posterior pituitary.
back: • Anterior: Vascular transport via hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels • Posterior: Neural transport (axoplasmic flow) via the hypothalamic-hypophysial nerve tract • Anterior uses blood; Posterior uses neuronal axons

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: Identify the primary physiological benefit of a portal system over systemic blood delivery for hypothalamic-pituitary signaling.
back: • Prevents dilution of releasing hormones in large systemic blood volume • Allows extremely small quantities of neurohormones to act effectively • Ensures rapid, direct, and high-concentration delivery to target cells

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: Hypophysiotropic hormones are initially secreted into the [___] of the hypothalamus before entering the primary capillary plexus of the portal system.
back: • Median eminence • Functional interface between the brain and the anterior pituitary • Site where hypothalamic nerve endings release neurohormones into interstitial fluid

category: Explain the significance of hypothalamic- hypophysial portal circulation
front: A female patient has a pituitary tumor compressing the hypophysial portal vessels. Explain the pathophysiology behind her subsequent development of lethargy and cold intolerance.
back: • Secondary hypothyroidism • Portal compression prevents hypothalamic TRH from reaching the anterior pituitary • Results in decreased TSH and subsequent low Thyroxine (T4) levels • Leads to slowed basal metabolism

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: Magnocellular Neurons of the Hypothalamic-Hypophysial Tract
front: The hypothalamic-hypophysial tract originates from large neurons known as [___] neurons, located within the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei.
back:
• Magnocellular neurons.
• Their axons form the neural tract passing through the pituitary stalk.
• They terminate in the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: Functional Resilience of the Hypothalamic-Hypophysial Tract
front: A patient suffers a traumatic injury that severs the pituitary stalk while leaving the hypothalamus intact. Explain the long-term status of ADH and Oxytocin secretion.
back:
• Secretion continue after a transient decrease.
• Hormones are released from the cut ends of fibers within the hypothalamus.
• Hypothalamic cell bodies remain functional.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: Axonal Transport in the Hypothalamic-Hypophysial Tract
front: Describe the physiological process of hormone transport from the hypothalamus to the posterior pituitary.
back:
• Hormones are synthesized in hypothalamic cell bodies.
• Bound to carrier proteins called neurophysins.
• Transported via axoplasm (axonal transport) down the tract to nerve endings.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Contrast the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract with the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system regarding their target pituitary lobes.
back:
• Tract: Neural connection to the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).
• Portal System: Vascular connection to the anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis).

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: Storage and Release at Hypophysial Nerve Endings
front: Identify the primary storage site for hormones conducted by the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract prior to their release into the circulation.
back:
• Secretory granules within bulbous nerve endings.
• Located on the surfaces of capillaries in the neurohypophysis.
• Release occurs via exocytosis upon stimulation.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: The [___] nucleus of the hypothalamus is the primary site of synthesis for Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) before it is transported via the neural tract.
back:
• Supraoptic nucleus (primarily ADH).
• Paraventricular nucleus (primarily Oxytocin).
• Both nuclei can synthesize small amounts of either hormone.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: A patient presents with massive polyuria and dilute urine following a lesion in the median eminence. Identify the clinical condition resulting from this tract interruption.
back:
• Central Diabetes Insipidus.
• Caused by failure of ADH transport and release.
• Results in inability of renal collecting ducts to reabsorb water.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: Stimulus-Secretion Coupling in the Hypophysial Tract
front: Explain the role of action potentials in the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract in the eventual release of Oxytocin.
back:
• Impulses travel down axons to the posterior pituitary.
• Triggers membrane depolarization and Calcium influx.
• Calcium induces exocytosis of Oxytocin into adjacent blood vessels.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Distinguish the roles of the two distinct layers of the theca in the developing ovarian follicle.
back:
• Theca interna: Secretes steroid hormones (Estrogen/Progesterone).
• Theca externa: Highly vascular connective tissue capsule.
• Forms the outer structure of the follicle.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Identify the embryological origin of the posterior pituitary gland, which differentiates it from the anterior lobe.
back:
• Neural tissue outgrowth from the hypothalamus.
• Explains the presence of glial-type cells (pituicytes).
• Explains the direct neural connection to the hypothalamus.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: The posterior pituitary hormones are synthesized in the hypothalamus and transported down the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract in combination with carrier proteins called [___].
back:
• Neurophysins
  • Act as carrier proteins for ADH and oxytocin during axonal transport.
  • The hormone separates from the neurophysin immediately upon secretion into capillaries.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: Pituitary Stalk Transection and Compensatory Secretion
front: A patient survives a traumatic brain injury that completely severs the pituitary stalk. Post-injury, ADH levels initially plummet but eventually stabilize because the hormone is then secreted by the [___].
back:
• Cut ends of hypothalamic nerve fibers
  • The supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei remain intact.
  • Hormones continue to be synthesized and are released directly from the hypothalamus into the blood.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Explain the step-wise vascular route hypothalamic releasing hormones take to reach the secretory cells of the adenohypophysis.
back:
• Secreted into the median eminence and tuber cinereum.
  • Absorbed into the primary capillary plexus.
  • Transported via hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels to the anterior pituitary sinuses.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: Embryology and Anatomy of the Hypophysis
front: Contrast the embryological origins and structural composition of the two lobes connected by the hypothalamic-pituitary tracts.
back:
• Anterior Pituitary: Derived from Rathke's pouch (pharyngeal epithelium); epithelioid/glandular cells.
  • Posterior Pituitary: Derived from neural tissue outgrowth (hypothalamus); contains glial-type pituicytes and axons.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: The Median Eminence as a Functional Interface
front: Identify the functional link between the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary gland where hypophysiotropic hormones are first released into the portal circulation.
back:
• Median Eminence
  • Contains the primary capillary plexus.
  • It is the site where hypothalamic neurons terminate to release releasing/inhibitory factors.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: In the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract, ADH is primarily synthesized in the [___] nuclei, whereas oxytocin is primarily synthesized in the [___] nuclei.
back:
• Supraoptic (ADH)
  • Paraventricular (Oxytocin)
  • Each nucleus can synthesize about 1/6th of the second hormone as well.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
coreConcept: Pituitary Stalk Effect on Prolactin vs. Trophic Hormones
front: A large pituitary adenoma compresses the pituitary stalk, disrupting all vascular and neural connections. Predict the effect on Prolactin levels compared to Growth Hormone levels.
back:
• Prolactin increases: Normal tonic inhibition by dopamine (PIH) is removed.
  • Growth Hormone decreases: The mandatory stimulus from GHRH is lost.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Describe the cellular mechanism by which an action potential in the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract triggers hormone release at the posterior pituitary bulbous knobs.
back:
• Depolarization opens Voltage-gated Calcium channels.
  • Calcium influx occurs into the nerve endings.
  • Triggers exocytosis of secretory granules into adjacent capillaries.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Distinguish between the anatomical nature of the 'Hypothalamic-Hypophysial Tract' and the 'Hypothalamic-Hypophysial Portal Vessels'.
back:
• Tract: A neural pathway of axons connecting the hypothalamus to the posterior pituitary.
  • Portal Vessels: A vascular system of blood vessels connecting the median eminence to the anterior pituitary.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Name the two hypothalamic nuclei containing GHRH-secreting neurons that are specifically sensitive to blood glucose concentrations.
back:
• Arcuate and Ventromedial nuclei
  • Same areas that control satiety and hunger.
  • Directly link nutritional status to Growth Hormone regulation.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Growth hormone (GH) initiates intracellular signaling by binding to a transmembrane receptor that recruits and activates the [___] kinase family.
back:
• JAK2 (Janus Kinase 2).
• This activation leads to phosphorylation of STAT proteins.
• STAT proteins then translocate to the nucleus to initiate gene transcription.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: A patient with a GH-secreting tumor presents with heavy ketonuria and a 'fatty liver' appearance on ultrasound. Explain the metabolic mechanism causing this presentation.
back:
• Excessive mobilization of free fatty acids from adipose tissue.
• High liver conversion of fatty acids into acetoacetic acid.
• Results in ketosis and fat accumulation in hepatocytes.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Explain the sequence of events by which Growth Hormone stimulates longitudinal bone growth at the epiphyseal plates.
back:
• Stimulation of liver production of IGF-1 (Somatomedin C).
• Proliferation of chondrocytes in epiphyseal cartilage.
• Conversion of chondrocytes into osteogenic cells to form new bone.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Contrast the effects of Growth Hormone and Insulin on the transport of glucose into skeletal muscle cells.
back:
• Insulin: Increases glucose uptake by translocating GLUT-4 transporters.
• GH: Decreases glucose uptake (anti-insulin effect).
• Result: GH leads to 'adrenal diabetes' and compensatory hyperinsulinemia.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Describe the specific intracellular changes GH induces to increase total body protein deposition.
back:
• Direct enhancement of amino acid transport through cell membranes.
• Increased RNA translation by ribosomes.
• Accelerated nuclear transcription of DNA to form messenger RNA.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: GH fails to promote physiological growth in the absence of [___] and adequate carbohydrate intake.
back:
• Insulin.
• Insulin is required for the transport of certain amino acids into cells.
• Carbohydrates provide the necessary energy for growth-related metabolism.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: A child presents with severe growth retardation but possesses high plasma GH levels and low IGF-1. Based on the mechanism of action, identify the molecular defect.
back:
• Laron Syndrome.
• Mutation in the Growth Hormone receptor.
• Failure of GH to stimulate IGF-1 production in the liver.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Explain the role of 'Protein Sparing' as a secondary mechanism of Growth Hormone action during starvation.
back:
• GH shifts metabolism from carbohydrate to fat utilization.
• Massive fatty acid mobilization provides alternative fuel (Acetyl-CoA).
• This prevents the catabolism of structural and functional cellular proteins.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Contrast the duration of action between Growth Hormone and its mediator, Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1).
back:
• GH: Short half-life (<20 minutes) due to weak plasma protein binding.
• IGF-1: Prolonged half-life (~20 hours) due to strong carrier protein binding.
• Result: IGF-1 prolongs the growth-promoting effects of pulsatile GH bursts.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: List the three primary cellular effects of GH that lead to overall tissue hyperplasia and hypertrophy.
back:
• Increased rate of mitosis (cell multiplication).
• Increased cell size (increased protein synthesis).
• Specific differentiation of cells (e.g., muscle and bone stem cells).

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: The metabolic effect of growth hormone that leads to a decrease in glucose utilization and a subsequent rise in blood glucose concentration is termed its [___] effect.
back:
• Diabetogenic effect
• It results from induced insulin resistance
• Attenuates insulin's ability to stimulate glucose uptake in peripheral tissues.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: A 35-year-old male with an acidophilic pituitary tumor presents with hyperglycemia and high serum insulin levels. The underlying pathophysiology for his elevated glucose is growth hormone-induced [___].
back:
• Insulin resistance
• GH reduces tissue sensitivity to insulin
• Leads to decreased glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Explain how growth hormone (GH) influences the liver to contribute to elevated blood glucose levels.
back:
• Stimulates gluconeogenesis (glucose production)
• Antagonizes insulin's inhibitory effect on liver glucose output
• Increases glycogen storage to provide substrate for glycolytic hormones.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Contrast the physical appearance of a patient with acromegaly-induced hyperglycemia with that of a typical patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
back:
• Acromegaly: Patients are usually lean with little visceral fat
• Type 2 Diabetes: Patients are frequently overweight with excessive visceral fat.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Identify the primary metabolic substrate that, when elevated by growth hormone-induced lipolysis, rapidly decreases insulin sensitivity in the liver and muscle.
back:
• Free Fatty Acids (FFAs)
• GH increases blood concentration of fatty acids
• High FFA levels impair insulin's action on tissue glucose utilization.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Growth hormone fails to promote growth in animals lacking a [___] or those whose diets are devoid of carbohydrates.
back:
• Pancreas
• Insulin and carbohydrates are required to provide the energy for growth metabolism
• Insulin also enhances amino acid transport into cells.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: A patient with acromegaly exhibits high blood glucose despite having a normal to high rate of insulin secretion. Describe the expected response of this 'adrenal diabetes' to exogenous insulin administration.
back:
• Poorly responsive (Insulin-resistant)
• Blood glucose lowers only moderately
• Sensitivity is diminished due to growth hormone's antagonistic effects.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Describe the relationship between growth hormone’s 'protein-sparing' action and its effect on carbohydrate utilization.
back:
• GH increases fat mobilization for energy
• This shifts the body's fuel source from glucose to fatty acids
• Consequently, carbohydrates and proteins are conserved for growth and repair.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Contrast the effects of growth hormone on peripheral tissues versus the pancreatic beta cells.
back:
• Peripheral tissues (Muscle/Fat): GH decreases insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake
• Pancreas: GH stimulates compensatory increases in insulin secretion to counteract hyperglycemia.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Specify the approximate percentage of giants/acromegalics that eventually develop full-blown clinical diabetes mellitus due to beta-cell exhaustion.
back:
• Approximately 10%
• Result of chronic hyperglycemia overstimulating beta cells
• Leads to eventual degeneration of the islets of Langerhans.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Posterior pituitary hormones travel from the hypothalamus to the neurohypophysis along the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract in combination with carrier proteins called [___].
back:
- Neurophysins.
- They bind hormones loosely during axonal transport.
- Hormones and neurophysins are secreted together via exocytosis but separate immediately in the blood.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: A patient experiences a traumatic pituitary stalk transection. While anterior pituitary function is lost, posterior pituitary hormones are still secreted after a few days. Explain the physiological mechanism.
back:
- ADH and Oxytocin are synthesized in hypothalamic cell bodies, not the pituitary.
- The severed nerve endings in the hypothalamus reorganize and resume hormone secretion.
- Hormones enter the general circulation directly from the hypothalamus.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which hormones are delivered through the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract to reach the circulation.
back:
- Synthesis occurs in the cell bodies of magnocellular neurons.
- Hormones are transported via axoplasm along the pituitary stalk.
- Terminal bulbous knobs on capillaries release hormones via exocytosis into the blood.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: A patient presents with polyuria and panhypopituitarism following a tumor in the sella turcica. Contrast the two distinct communication pathways between the hypothalamus and pituitary that are likely compromised.
back:
- Hypothalamic-hypophysial tract: A neural pathway carrying ADH/Oxytocin to the posterior pituitary.
- Hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels: A vascular pathway carrying releasing/inhibitory factors to the anterior pituitary.
- Disruption causes ADH deficiency (polyuria) and loss of anterior tropic hormones.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: Identify the specific anatomical structure in the lowermost hypothalamus that serves as the functional link for both the portal system and the hypophysial tract.
back:
- Median eminence.
- It contains the primary capillary plexus for the portal system.
- It serves as the point of entry for axons forming the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: The hypothalamic-hypophysial tract is composed of large axons originating primarily from the [___] and [___] nuclei of the hypothalamus.
back:
- Supraoptic nucleus.
- Paraventricular nucleus.
- These nuclei contain magnocellular neurons that synthesize ADH and Oxytocin.

category: Explain the hypothalamic pituitary tract
front: A histological section of the posterior pituitary reveals numerous glial-like cells but no secretory glandular cells. Identify these cells and their role in the hypothalamic-hypophysial tract.
back:
- Pituicytes.
- They act solely as supporting structures for the terminal nerve fibers.
- They do not synthesize hormones; ADH and Oxytocin are produced in the hypothalamus.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Growth hormone (GH) exerts its long-term growth-promoting effects on bone and cartilage primarily by stimulating the liver to produce [___].
back:
• Somatomedins (primarily Insulin-like Growth Factor-1/IGF-1).
  • IGF-1 has a much longer half-life (~20 hours) than GH (~20 minutes), providing a prolonged growth stimulus.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: A 40-year-old male with acromegaly presents with hyperglycemia and elevated insulin levels. This 'diabetogenic' effect of growth hormone is primarily caused by [___].
back:
• GH-induced insulin resistance.
  • It decreases glucose uptake in skeletal muscle/fat and increases hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis).

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Describe the triple-mechanism by which Growth Hormone promotes protein deposition in body tissues.
back:
• Directly enhances amino acid transport across cell membranes.
  • Increases RNA translation and nuclear transcription of DNA.
  • Reduces protein catabolism by mobilizing fatty acids as an alternative energy source.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Contrast the effects of Growth Hormone on bone growth before versus after the fusion of epiphyseal cartilages.
back:
• Before fusion: Stimulates lengthening of long bones by promoting chondrocyte proliferation.
  • After fusion: Stimulates osteoblasts to increase bone thickness (membranous bones), leading to features like a protruding lower jaw.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Specify the metabolic 'switching' role of Growth Hormone during periods of fasting or starvation.
back:
• GH promotes lipolysis, increasing plasma free fatty acids for energy utilization.
  • This 'spares' proteins and carbohydrates, ensuring vital tissues can utilize limited glucose.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: At the pituitary level, Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH) triggers GH secretion by activating the [___] second messenger system.
back:
• Adenylyl cyclase–cAMP system.
  • This increases intracellular calcium, which facilitates the fusion of GH secretory vesicles with the cell membrane for exocytosis.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: A child with severe protein deficiency (Kwashiorkor) is found to have paradoxically high plasma Growth Hormone levels but ceases to grow. Explain this finding.
back:
• Protein malnutrition prevents the liver from synthesizing Somatomedins (IGF-1).
  • Growth fails due to lack of IGF-1, and GH remains high due to loss of negative feedback.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: The characteristic elevation of blood glucose and decreased glucose utilization caused by Growth Hormone (GH) is clinically referred to as the [___] effect.
back:
• Diabetogenic effect
• This results from GH-induced insulin resistance
• It involves decreased peripheral glucose uptake and increased hepatic output.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly presents with fasting hyperglycemia and high plasma insulin. Explain why his insulin levels are elevated despite his high blood sugar.
back:
• GH causes "insulin resistance" in skeletal muscle and fat
• Rising blood glucose triggers compensatory insulin secretion
• Chronic overstimulation can eventually lead to pancreatic beta-cell exhaustion.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Explain the role of free fatty acids (FFAs) in the mechanism of Growth Hormone-induced carbohydrate intolerance.
back:
• GH stimulates lipolysis, raising plasma FFA levels
• Elevated FFAs decrease the sensitivity of the liver and muscles to insulin
• This leads to impaired glucose uptake and utilization.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Contrast the physical body composition of a patient with acromegaly-induced diabetes versus a typical patient with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Acromegaly: Patients are usually lean with minimal visceral fat
• Type 2 DM: Patients are frequently overweight with excessive visceral fat which drives resistance.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Specify the two primary hepatic actions of Growth Hormone (GH) that contribute to elevated blood glucose.
back:
• Stimulates gluconeogenesis (glucose production from amino acids)
• Antagonizes insulin's ability to inhibit hepatic glucose output.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Growth hormone significantly decreases carbohydrate utilization by specifically reducing glucose uptake in [___] and [___] tissues.
back:
• Skeletal muscle
• Adipose tissue
• These effects are mediated by a reduction in insulin sensitivity.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: An animal study shows that Growth Hormone (GH) fails to promote growth if the subject is pancreatectomized. Identify the metabolic reason for this failure.
back:
• GH requires insulin to provide necessary energy for growth metabolism
• Insulin is essential for GH-mediated transport of amino acids into cells.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Describe the cellular transport mechanism that is impaired by Growth Hormone to result in carbohydrate conservation.
back:
• GH decreases the translocation of glucose transporters (GLUT 4) to cell membranes
• This is part of the overall "insulin resistance" syndrome observed in GH excess.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Contrast the immediate versus long-term effects of Growth Hormone (GH) on insulin secretion levels.
back:
• Immediate: Increases insulin secretion (compensatory to rising glucose)
• Long-term: May lead to beta-cell degeneration and decreased insulin production.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: State the relationship between a high-carbohydrate meal and the immediate secretion rate of Growth Hormone (GH).
back:
• Hyperglycemia inhibits GH secretion
• GH levels fall rapidly following carbohydrate ingestion due to hypothalamic feedback.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Growth hormone (GH) exerts a 'protein-sparing' effect on tissues primarily by enhancing the mobilization and utilization of [___] as the preferred energy source for cells.
back:
• Free fatty acids (FFAs).
• GH shifts metabolism to utilize fats for energy instead of proteins or carbohydrates.
• This action preserves cellular protein stores for tissue growth and repair.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: A patient with protein malnutrition (kwashiorkor) is found to have significantly elevated plasma growth hormone levels. Justify this pathophysiological finding in the context of GH regulation.
back:
• Chronic cellular protein depletion is a more potent stimulator of GH than glucose insufficiency.
• The body attempts to compensate by increasing GH to stimulate protein synthesis.
• High GH levels persist until dietary protein deficiency is corrected.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Explain the immediate versus long-term intracellular mechanisms by which growth hormone facilitates cellular protein deposition.
back:
• Immediate (minutes): Increases ribosomal RNA translation to synthesize new proteins.
• Short-term: Enhances amino acid transport through cell membranes.
• Long-term (24-48 hours): Stimulates nuclear transcription of DNA to form increased quantities of mRNA.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Contrast the effects of Growth Hormone and Cortisol on amino acid transport and protein synthesis in skeletal muscle tissue.
back:
• GH: Increases amino acid transport into cells and enhances protein synthesis (anabolic).
• Cortisol: Depresses amino acid transport and increases protein catabolism (catabolic).
• Outcome: GH increases lean body mass; Cortisol leads to muscle wasting.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Identify the mandatory dietary and hormonal requirements that must be present for Growth Hormone to effectively promote tissue growth.
back:
• Insulin availability.
• Adequate carbohydrate intake.
• Insulin is necessary for amino acid transport into cells and providing energy for the anabolic process.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: In the liver, growth hormone stimulates the formation of small proteins called [___] that mediate the hormone's growth-promoting effects on bone and peripheral tissues.
back:
• Insulin-like growth factors (IGFs) or Somatomedins.
• IGF-1 (Somatomedin C) is the most clinically significant.
• These mediators have a longer half-life (20 hours) compared to GH (20 minutes).

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: An elderly patient experiences progressive muscle weakness and wrinkling of the skin. Relate these clinical findings to the specific effects of declining growth hormone on protein metabolism during aging.
back:
• Reduced protein deposition in muscles and subcutaneous tissues.
• Decreased amino acid uptake leads to diminished muscle mass and strength.
• Increased fat deposition often replaces lost lean protein mass.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Human Growth Hormone is a small protein molecule consisting of a single chain of [___] amino acids.
back: - 191 amino acids- Molecular weight of 22,005- Formed in the somatotropes of the anterior pituitary

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: A 40-year-old male with an acidophilic pituitary tumor presents with hyperglycemia and insulin resistance. The "diabetogenic" effect of excess growth hormone is primarily due to [___].
back: - Increased hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis)- Decreased glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue- Impairment of insulin's intracellular actions (insulin resistance)

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Explain the mechanism by which Growth Hormone increases total body protein deposition.
back: - Direct enhancement of amino acid transport through cell membranes- Increased RNA translation at the ribosomes- Stimulation of nuclear DNA transcription to form increased mRNA

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Contrast the direct metabolic actions of Growth Hormone on adipose tissue with its indirect actions on skeletal cartilage.
back: - Direct (Adipose): Stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase to increase lipolysis and FFA release.- Indirect (Cartilage): Mediated by IGF-1 to stimulate chondrocyte mitosis and extracellular matrix deposition.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Identify the second messenger system used by Growth Hormone-Releasing Hormone (GHRH) to trigger GH secretion from somatotropes.
back: - Binding to G-protein coupled receptors activates adenylyl cyclase- Increased cAMP levels open membrane calcium channels- Elevated intracellular calcium triggers exocytosis of GH-containing vesicles

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: In the anterior pituitary, Growth Hormone is synthesized and secreted by acidophilic cells known as [___].
back: - Somatotropes- Represent 30% to 40% of all anterior pituitary cells- Stain strongly with acid dyes

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: A patient in a state of severe protein malnutrition (kwashiorkor) shows paradoxically high Growth Hormone levels. Identify the primary nutritional stimulus for this elevation.
back: - Intracellular protein depletion- GH rises to promote amino acid mobilization and new protein synthesis- Note: Calories alone do not lower GH; protein must be added to the diet

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Describe how Growth Hormone stimulates the lengthening of long bones before adolescence.
back: - Stimulates chondrocytic and osteogenic cells at the epiphyseal cartilages- Causes rapid deposition of new cartilage- Converts new cartilage into bone, pushing the epiphyses apart

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Contrast the effects of Insulin and Growth Hormone on the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) in adipose tissue.
back: - Insulin: Potently inhibits HSL, preventing triglyceride breakdown.- Growth Hormone: Activates HSL, promoting the mobilization of fatty acids into the blood.

category: Explain the mechanism of action of growth hormone
front: Name the specific cell conversion stimulated by Growth Hormone that leads to the deposition of new bone in the growth plates.
back: - Conversion of chondrocytes into osteogenic cells- This results in the mineralization of the cartilaginous matrix to form new bone

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Growth hormone promotes the mobilization of [___] from adipose tissue into the blood to be used for energy.
back:
• Free fatty acids (FFAs)
• Enhances fat utilization over carbohydrates
• Increases concentration of FFAs in body fluids

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: A patient with an acidophilic pituitary tumor presents with elevated plasma acetoacetic acid and a fatty liver. Explain the metabolic pathophysiology behind these findings.
back:
• Excess GH causes extreme mobilization of fats from adipose tissue
• The liver converts surplus fatty acids into acetoacetic acid
• Leads to ketosis and hepatic fat accumulation

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Describe the mechanism by which Growth Hormone promotes the utilization of fat for energy at the cellular level.
back:
• Stimulates triglyceride breakdown in adipocytes
• Enhances conversion of fatty acids into Acetyl-CoA
• Promotes beta-oxidation in tissues throughout the body

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Contrast the effects of Growth Hormone and Insulin on the enzyme hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) in adipose tissue.
back:
• Growth Hormone: Activates HSL to increase lipolysis and FFA release
• Insulin: Inhibits HSL to promote fat storage and prevent triglyceride hydrolysis

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Explain how the effects of Growth Hormone on fat metabolism contribute to its 'protein sparer' function.
back:
• GH shifts metabolism to use FFAs as the primary energy source
• Spares proteins and carbohydrates from being catabolized for energy
• Results in increased lean body mass

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Under the influence of Growth Hormone, fatty acids are converted into [___], which serves as the primary substrate for the citric acid cycle.
back:
• Acetyl coenzyme A (Acetyl-CoA)
• Increases energy production via fat oxidation
• Reduces cellular reliance on glucose

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: A patient using recombinant Growth Hormone for its anabolic effects is found to have decreased insulin sensitivity. Identify the link between GH’s lipid effects and this change.
back:
• GH increases blood levels of fatty acids via lipolysis
• High FFAs rapidly decrease liver and muscle sensitivity to insulin
• Contributes to the 'diabetogenic' effect of GH

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Compare the timeline of Growth Hormone-induced fat mobilization with its effect on protein synthesis.
back:
• Protein synthesis: Enhancement begins within minutes
• Fat mobilization: Requires several hours to develop fully
• Delayed fat mobilization results in long-term conservation of glucose

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Contrast the metabolic state of an individual with Acromegaly versus Type 2 Diabetes regarding visceral fat and insulin resistance.
back:
• Acromegaly: High FFAs and insulin resistance, but usually lean with little visceral fat
• Type 2 Diabetes: High FFAs and insulin resistance, but usually associated with excess visceral fat

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Identify the three primary consequences of Growth Hormone's 'metabolic switching' between fat and carbohydrate usage.
back:
• Increased mobilization and utilization of fat
• Conservation of carbohydrates (decreased utilization)
• Enhanced body protein and increased lean mass

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Growth hormone promotes the mobilization of fatty acids from [___], leading to a significant increase in their concentration in the circulating blood.
back:
• Adipose tissue.
• Increases plasma free fatty acids (FFAs).
• Occurs several hours after GH secretion.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: A laboratory animal administered excessive Growth Hormone develops high levels of acetoacetic acid and a fatty liver. This metabolic complication is termed the [___] effect of GH.
back:
• Ketogenic effect.
• Caused by massive fat mobilization from adipose stores.
• Results in excess ketone body formation in the liver.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Explain the intracellular mechanism by which Growth Hormone facilitates the utilization of fat for energy.
back:
• Enhances conversion of fatty acids to Acetyl-CoA.
• Activates beta-oxidation in tissues.
• Promotes fat as the primary energy substrate over carbohydrates.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Contrast the time of onset for Growth Hormone's effect on protein synthesis versus its effect on fat mobilization.
back:
• Protein synthesis: Begins within minutes.
• Fat mobilization: Requires several hours to initiate.
• Reflects differences in rapid anabolic vs. delayed metabolic pathways.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: How does Growth Hormone affect total body composition in terms of fat and muscle mass?
back:
• Decreases total fat stores (lipolysis).
• Increases lean body mass.
• Synergistic effect of lipolytic and protein anabolic actions.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Under the influence of Growth Hormone, the specific substrate used preferentially by most body tissues for metabolic energy is [___].
back:
• Free fatty acids (FFAs).
• Used in preference to glucose and proteins.
• Conserves blood glucose for brain tissue.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: An acromegalic patient exhibits hyperglycemia and high blood fatty acids. Explain how fat metabolism contributes to this 'diabetogenic' state.
back:
• Excessive lipolysis raises free fatty acids.
• High fatty acids rapidly decrease insulin sensitivity in liver and muscle.
• This leads to 'insulin resistance' and impaired glucose uptake.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Describe the sequence of events leading to ketosis during extreme Growth Hormone excess.
back:
• Massive fatty acid release from adipocytes.
• Rapid transport to the liver.
• Liver forms extreme quantities of acetoacetic acid, exceeding peripheral tissue capacity.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Contrast the action of Growth Hormone on adipose fat stores versus its action on liver glycogen stores.
back:
• Adipose fat: Depletes stores (increases mobilization).
• Liver glycogen: Increases stores (due to enhanced gluconeogenesis and decreased glucose utilization).

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Growth hormone is classically described as a 'protein sparer.' How is this achieved via fat metabolism?
back:
• Promotes massive mobilization and oxidation of fats.
• Fat becomes the main energy source.
• Prevents the breakdown of cellular proteins for energy.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Growth hormone acts as a potent [___] by mobilizing free fatty acids from adipose tissue to provide energy, thereby reducing the breakdown of cellular proteins.
back:
• Protein sparer
• Mobilizes FFAs for energy use
• Conserves existing protein stores
• Enhances lean body mass

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: A child with pituitary dwarfism presents with stunted growth and poorly developed musculature. This condition is primarily caused by a failure of Growth Hormone to enhance the transport of [___] into cells.
back:
• Amino acids
• Increases intracellular concentration
• Essential for rapid protein synthesis
• Directly stimulates tissue growth

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Describe the immediate mechanism by which Growth Hormone stimulates protein synthesis at the ribosomal level.
back:
• Enhances RNA translation
• Increases protein production by existing ribosomes
• Occurs independently of increased amino acid levels
• Results in rapid protein deposition

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Contrast the effects of Growth Hormone and Cortisol on protein metabolism in extrahepatic tissues like skeletal muscle.
back:
• GH: Anabolic; increases amino acid uptake and protein synthesis
• Cortisol: Catabolic; decreases protein stores and synthesis
• GH increases muscle mass; Cortisol causes muscle wasting

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Specify the timing and nature of Growth Hormone's long-term effect on the genetic machinery of the cell.
back:
• Occurs over 24–48 hours
• Stimulates nuclear transcription of DNA
• Increases total quantities of RNA
• Promotes sustained synthesis and growth

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Growth hormone is ineffective at promoting growth and protein synthesis in the absence of [___] or adequate dietary carbohydrates.
back:
• Insulin
• Required for energy during metabolism
• Aids transport of specific amino acids
• Acts synergistically with GH

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: A 60-year-old male exhibits wrinkled skin, decreased muscle mass, and increased body fat. Pathophysiologically, this is linked to a decline in Growth Hormone's role in [___].
back:
• Protein deposition
• Reduced amino acid transport
• Increased protein catabolism with age
• Results in diminished organ function

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: How does the mobilization of fatty acids by Growth Hormone contribute to its anabolic protein effects?
back:
• Converts fatty acids to Acetyl-CoA
• Provides alternative energy substrate
• Spares proteins from being used for energy
• Maximizes amino acid availability for synthesis

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Contrast the synergy between Growth Hormone and Insulin regarding their specific roles in amino acid uptake.
back:
• Both hormones increase cellular uptake
• They target different selections of amino acids
• Both are required for maximal growth
• One cannot substitute for the other

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Identify the four key steps in the overall action of Growth Hormone that lead to enhanced protein deposition.
back:
1. Increased amino acid transport
2. Enhanced RNA translation
3. Increased DNA transcription
4. Decreased protein/amino acid catabolism

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Growth hormone (GH) promotes the mobilization of [___] from adipose tissue to increase their concentration in body fluids for energy usage.
back:
• Free fatty acids.
• Mobilization increases plasma fatty acid levels.
• Promotes conversion of fats into acetyl-CoA for energy.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: A patient with an acidophilic pituitary tumor presents with elevated plasma levels of acetoacetic acid and lipid accumulation in the liver. This metabolic state describes the [___] effect of growth hormone.
back:
• Ketogenic effect.
• Caused by excessive fatty acid mobilization from adipocytes.
• Results in high acetoacetic acid production by the liver.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Explain the role of Growth Hormone (GH) as a 'protein sparer' in the context of fat metabolism.
back:
• GH increases the mobilization and utilization of fat for energy.
• This provides an alternative fuel source to glucose and protein.
• Consequently, it prevents the breakdown of cellular proteins for fuel.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
coreConcept: Metabolic Timing of Growth Hormone Action
front: Contrast the induction time required for Growth Hormone to enhance protein synthesis versus its effect on fat mobilization.
back:
• Protein synthesis: Enhancement begins within minutes.
• Fat mobilization: Requires several hours to fully develop.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: Identify the primary substance produced by the liver when fat mobilization under Growth Hormone influence exceeds the tissues' ability to oxidize it.
back:
• Acetoacetic acid.
• Formed from excess acetyl-CoA condensed in the liver.
• Can lead to clinical ketosis and fatty liver.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: The combined effect of Growth Hormone-induced fat utilization and its anabolic protein effect results in a net increase in [___].
back:
• Lean body mass.
• Achieved through simultaneous fat depletion and protein deposition.

category: Describe the actions of Growth hormone on fat metabolism
front: A patient with acromegaly develops secondary insulin resistance. Beyond direct glucose effects, how does GH-stimulated fat metabolism contribute to this 'diabetogenic' state?
back:
• GH-induced lipolysis increases blood free fatty acid levels.
• High fatty acids rapidly decrease the sensitivity of liver and muscle to insulin.
• This impairs insulin-mediated glucose uptake and utilization.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
coreConcept: Protein Sparing Action of Growth Hormone
front: Growth hormone (GH) reduces the breakdown of existing cellular proteins by mobilizing large quantities of free fatty acids for energy, a process known as the [___] effect.
back:
• Protein-sparing effect.
  • Shifts cellular metabolism from using proteins to using fats.
  • Conserves amino acids for structural growth and repair.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: A 35-year-old male with an acidophilic pituitary tumor (acromegaly) exhibits significant muscle hypertrophy and organomegaly. What specific action of Growth Hormone on amino acid kinetics facilitates this protein deposition?
back:
• Directly enhances amino acid transport through cell membranes.
  • Increases intracellular amino acid concentrations.
  • Provides necessary substrates for rapid protein synthesis in target tissues.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Explain the immediate mechanism by which Growth Hormone (GH) enhances protein synthesis at the ribosomal level.
back:
• Accelerates RNA translation.
  • Increases the rate of protein assembly by ribosomes in the cytoplasm.
  • Occurs independently of changes in intracellular amino acid levels.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
coreConcept: Temporal Dynamics of GH Protein Synthesis
front: Contrast the short-term (minutes) versus long-term (24-48 hours) mechanisms by which Growth Hormone (GH) promotes protein synthesis in cells.
back:
• Short-term: Enhanced amino acid transport and immediate acceleration of RNA translation.
  • Long-term: Increased nuclear transcription of DNA to form new mRNA.
  • Net Result: Sustained increase in tissue and skeletal growth.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Why is the presence of insulin and adequate carbohydrate intake essential for Growth Hormone to exert its protein-anabolic effects?
back:
• Provides the energy required for the high metabolic cost of growth.
  • Insulin facilitates the transport of specific amino acids into cells.
  • GH is ineffective in pancreatectomized or carbohydrate-deficient states.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: In the liver, Growth Hormone (GH) stimulates the production of [___], which mediates the hormone's prolonged protein-synthetic effects on bone and cartilage matrix.
back:
• Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1) or Somatomedin C.
  • Attaches strongly to carrier proteins, extending its half-life to 20 hours.
  • Crucial for long-term skeletal protein deposition.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: A child with Kwashiorkor (extreme protein deficiency) has very high plasma GH levels. Apply your knowledge of GH regulation to explain why high carbohydrate feeding alone fails to lower these levels.
back:
• GH secretion is primarily controlled by the long-term state of protein nutrition.
  • Carbohydrates do not correct the cellular protein depletion.
  • Levels only normalize once the protein deficit is specifically addressed.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Detail the metabolic link between GH-induced lipolysis and its role in conserving body proteins during periods of fasting.
back:
• GH increases blood free fatty acids (FFAs).
  • FFAs are converted to acetyl-CoA for cellular energy.
  • This prevents the liver from using amino acids for gluconeogenesis, preserving muscle mass.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: Contrast the functional effects of Growth Hormone versus Cortisol on protein stores in extrahepatic tissues like skeletal muscle.
back:
• Growth Hormone: Anabolic; increases amino acid uptake and protein stores.
  • Cortisol: Catabolic; decreases protein stores and increases amino acid release.
  • Both hormones mobilize fats, but their protein outcomes are opposite.

category: Discuss the actions of Growth hormone on protein metabolism
front: List three specific alterations in body composition that result from the protein-anabolic and lipolytic actions of Growth Hormone.
back:
• Increased lean body mass (protein deposition).
  • Decreased total body fat (mobilization and oxidation).
  • Increased organ size and skeletal thickness (mitosis and matrix formation).

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: The metabolic effect of Growth Hormone that leads to blood glucose elevations similar to those in non-insulin-dependent diabetes is termed its [___] effect.
back:
- Diabetogenic effect.
- It is characterized by insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly presents with impaired glucose tolerance. Despite elevated plasma insulin, he remains hyperglycemic because GH [___].
back:
- Attenuates insulin's action to stimulate glucose uptake in skeletal muscle and fat.
- Increases hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis).

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Explain why Growth Hormone (GH) leads to a compensatory increase in insulin secretion.
back:
- GH reduces peripheral glucose utilization and increases hepatic glucose output.
- The resulting hyperglycemia stimulates pancreatic beta cells to secrete more insulin.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Contrast the body composition of a patient with insulin resistance caused by acromegaly versus typical Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Acromegaly: Lean body mass with minimal visceral fat (due to GH's lipolytic effects).
- Type 2 Diabetes: Typically overweight with excessive visceral fat that drives resistance.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: Identify the role of dietary carbohydrates and insulin in facilitating the growth-promoting action of Growth Hormone.
back:
- Provide necessary energy for the metabolism of growth.
- Insulin is required to enhance the transport of amino acids into the cells.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
coreConcept: GH and Fatty Acid Induced Insulin Resistance
front: Growth hormone-induced stimulation of [___] raises blood fatty acid levels, which contributes significantly to its anti-insulin effect.
back:
- Lipolysis.
- Elevated free fatty acids rapidly decrease the sensitivity of the liver and muscle to insulin.

category: Explain the actions of Growth hormone on Carbohydrate
front: A child with Type 1 Diabetes and concurrent GH deficiency is treated with recombinant GH but shows no growth. Growth remains stunted because [___].
back:
- GH is ineffective without adequate insulin.
- Insulin is essential to transport amino acids into cells to initiate protein synthesis and growth.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Growth hormone-induced skeletal growth is primarily mediated by the liver-derived protein known as [___].
back:
• Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1)
• Also called Somatomedin C

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: An 8-year-old boy presents with extreme height for his age and hyperglycemia. Radiographs show open epiphyseal plates. The most likely diagnosis is [___].
back:
• Gigantism
• Results from Growth Hormone excess before the fusion of long bone epiphyses with shafts

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Explain the two specific physiological processes by which Growth Hormone increases bone size.
back:
• Linear growth: Increases at epiphyseal cartilages via chondrocyte proliferation
• Appositional growth: Stimulates periosteal osteoblasts to deposit new bone on older surfaces

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Contrast the physical development of a child with panhypopituitary dwarfism with that of a child with cretinism.
back:
• Panhypopituitary: Proportional development; normal intelligence; lack of puberty
• Cretinism: Disproportional (short/stocky); mental retardation; sluggish movements

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Describe the typical decline in Growth Hormone secretion from adolescence to old age.
back:
• Secretion falls progressively throughout adult life
• In old age (40-70 years), levels drop to approximately 25% of the adolescent level

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Further lengthening of long bones is terminated when Growth Hormone can no longer act on the [___] due to their fusion with the bone shafts.
back:
• Epiphyses (or Epiphyseal cartilages)
• Occurs by late adolescence

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: A 45-year-old male notices his shoe size has increased and his jaw is protruding forward. This pathological thickening of membranous bones is characteristic of [___].
back:
• Acromegaly
• Caused by GH excess occurring after epiphyseal fusion

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Why do the growth-promoting effects of Growth Hormone bursts persist for many hours despite the hormone's short 20-minute plasma half-life?
back:
• GH stimulates production of Somatomedin C (IGF-1)
• IGF-1 binds strongly to plasma carrier proteins
• IGF-1 has a prolonged half-life of ~20 hours

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Contrast the effect of Growth Hormone on long bones versus membranous bones in an adult.
back:
• Long bones: No further elongation possible due to fused epiphyses
• Membranous bones: Can continue to thicken via osteoblast stimulation (e.g., jaw, cranium)

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: List two physical changes associated with aging that are linked to the natural decrease in Growth Hormone secretion.
back:
• Increased skin wrinkling
• Decreased muscle mass and strength
• Increased fat deposition replacing lean body mass

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: The primary peptide mediator synthesized in the liver that executes the skeletal growth-promoting actions of Growth Hormone (GH) is [___].
back:
• Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1), also known as Somatomedin C.
• Its concentration in plasma follows the rate of GH secretion.
• It possesses a long half-life (20 hours), prolonging GH's growth effects.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: A 35-year-old male presents with a protruding lower jaw (prognathism) and thickened fingers. He has not increased in height for fifteen years. Identify the underlying skeletal pathophysiology.
back:
• Diagnosis: Acromegaly.
• Pathophysiology: Post-pubertal GH excess after epiphyseal fusion.
• Bones cannot lengthen but undergo appositional growth (thickening).
• Marked enlargement occurs in membranous bones (jaw, cranium, vertebrae).

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Explain the role of chondrocytes and osteoblasts in the mechanism of long bone lengthening under Growth Hormone influence.
back:
• GH stimulates rapid reproduction of chondrocytes and osteogenic cells.
• Chondrocytes are converted into osteogenic cells, depositing new bone.
• New cartilage is deposited at epiphyseal plates, followed by its conversion to bone, elongating the shaft.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Contrast the skeletal manifestations of Growth Hormone hypersecretion occurring before versus after the completion of adolescence.
back:
• Pre-adolescent (Gigantism): Occurs before epiphyseal fusion; results in extreme height (up to 8 feet).
• Post-adolescent (Acromegaly): Occurs after fusion; no height increase, but bones thicken.
• Both involve soft tissue overgrowth and potential hyperglycemia.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Identify the specific event in late adolescence that permanently terminates the ability of Growth Hormone to increase a person's height.
back:
• Bony fusion of the epiphyses with the shafts of long bones.
• This process consumes all available epiphyseal cartilage.
• Once fused, no further lengthening of long bones is physiologically possible.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Growth hormone levels decrease significantly with age; by age 70, the average plasma concentration falls to approximately [___] of the adolescent level.
back:
• 25 percent.
• This decline contributes to features of aging.
• Manifests as decreased protein deposition, increased fat deposition, and diminished muscle mass/strength.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: A child presents with severe short stature, high plasma GH levels, but exceptionally low IGF-1. Identify the likely diagnosis and receptor status.
back:
• Diagnosis: Laron Dwarfism.
• Pathophysiology: Mutation of the GH receptor.
• Skeletal growth fails because GH cannot stimulate the production of Somatomedin C/IGF-1 despite high hormone levels.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Describe how Growth Hormone alters the balance between osteoblastic and osteoclastic activity in the bone periosteum throughout life.
back:
• GH strongly stimulates osteoblastic activity.
• When osteoblasts deposit bone faster than osteoclasts remove it, bone thickness increases.
• This allows membranous bones (like the jaw) to continue thickening even after height growth ceases.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Contrast the effect of Growth Hormone on long bones versus its effect on membranous bones in an adult with a GH-secreting tumor.
back:
• Long Bones: No change in length due to closed epiphyseal plates.
• Membranous Bones: Continued growth and thickening.
• Clinical result: Enlarged hands, feet, nose, and supraorbital ridges (Acromegaly).

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Name the hormone and the specific nutrient required for Growth Hormone to effectively promote skeletal development.
back:
• Hormone: Insulin.
• Nutrient: Carbohydrates.
• Insulin enhances amino acid transport into cells; carbohydrates provide the energy required for the high metabolic cost of growth.

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Growth hormone promotes bone elongation by stimulating the proliferation and conversion of [___] into osteogenic cells, leading to new bone deposition at the growth plates.
back:
• Chondrocytes
• GH increases chondrocytic mitosis
• Stimulates deposition of new cartilage
• Subsequent conversion of cartilage to new bone elongates the shaft

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: A 10-year-old child presents with extreme tall stature and open epiphyseal plates. The growth-promoting effects of the hormone involved are primarily mediated by the hepatic production of [___].
back:
• IGF-1 (Somatomedin C)
• Mediates most GH skeletal effects
• Prolonged half-life (20 hours) compared to GH
• Essential for linear bone growth

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Explain the role of osteoblasts and osteoclasts in the GH-mediated increase of bone thickness.
back:
• GH strongly stimulates osteoblasts in the periosteum
• New bone is deposited on the surface of old bone
• Osteoclasts simultaneously remove old bone
• Thickness increases when deposition exceeds resorption

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Contrast the effects of excessive GH secretion on the skeleton when it occurs before versus after the completion of adolescence.
back:
• Before (Gigantism): Excessive linear growth and height due to open epiphyseal plates
• After (Acromegaly): Bones thicken (membranous growth) but cannot lengthen due to epiphyseal fusion

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Identify the two essential metabolic prerequisites that must be available for growth hormone to successfully promote skeletal growth.
back:
• Insulin and Carbohydrates
• Insulin enhances amino acid transport into cells
• Carbohydrates provide the high energy required for the metabolism of growth

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: Linear growth of the skeletal frame ceases during late adolescence when the [___] becomes entirely used up and undergoes bony fusion with the shaft.
back:
• Epiphyseal cartilage
• Fusion occurs at the ends of long bones
• Stimulated by sex hormones (estrogen/testosterone)
• Prevents further increase in body height

category: Explain the effect of growth hormone on skeletal growth and age
front: A 55-year-old male with a history of a pituitary tumor presents with a protruding lower jaw and thickened fingers. Describe the specific skeletal mechanism occurring in his membranous bones.
back:
• Appositional growth
• Continued osteoblastic stimulation by GH
• New bone deposition on the cranium, nose, and jaw
• Leads to forward protrusion (prognathism) and kyphosis

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Most of the growth-promoting effects of Growth Hormone (GH) are not direct but are instead mediated by intermediate proteins produced primarily in the liver called [___].
back:
• Somatomedins (also known as Insulin-like Growth Factors or IGFs).
• Somatomedin C (IGF-1) is the most clinically significant of these mediators.
• They bridge the gap between GH secretion and peripheral tissue growth.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: A 10-year-old child presents with significantly stunted growth. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated plasma Growth Hormone (GH) levels but extremely low Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1). This presentation is characteristic of [___].
back:
• Laron Syndrome (GH insensitivity).
• Pathophysiology involves a mutation in the GH receptor.
• The liver cannot synthesize somatomedins despite high circulating GH levels.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Explain the mechanism by which somatomedins (specifically IGF-1) maintain stable growth stimulation compared to the pulsatile nature of Growth Hormone (GH) secretion.
back:
• IGF-1 binds strongly to carrier proteins, prolonging its half-life to ~20 hours.
• GH binds weakly to proteins and has a short half-life (<20 minutes).
• This provides continuous growth promotion despite intermittent GH pulses.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Contrast Growth Hormone (GH) and Somatomedin C (IGF-1) regarding their relationship with plasma proteins and their resultant duration of action.
back:
• GH: Weak protein binding; very short duration of action (~20 mins).
• Somatomedin C: Strong protein binding; long duration of action (~20 hours).
• Result: Somatomedin levels remain constant while GH levels fluctuate wildly.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Identify the primary target cells and specific actions triggered by Somatomedin C (IGF-1) to facilitate longitudinal bone growth.
back:
• Targets: Chondrocytes and Osteogenic cells at the epiphyseal plates.
• Actions: Increases mitosis (reproduction) and cell differentiation.
• Mechanism: Enhances protein deposition and DNA/RNA synthesis to form new bone.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: While the liver provides the majority of systemic somatomedins, GH also triggers the local production of [___] directly within cartilaginous tissues to promote autocrine growth.
back:
• Local Somatomedin C (IGF-1).
• This local production allows for specific, localized growth at the epiphyseal cartilages.
• It supplements the endocrine somatomedins delivered via the blood.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
coreConcept: Clinical Utility of IGF-1 in Diagnosis
front: A clinician managing a patient with suspected Acromegaly prefers measuring serum Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 (IGF-1) levels over a single random Growth Hormone (GH) measurement. State the physiological rationale.
back:
• GH is secreted pulsatically (peaks during sleep/stress), making single readings misleading.
• IGF-1 plasma levels are stable and constant due to carrier protein binding.
• IGF-1 provides an integrated measurement of overall daily GH activity.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: The primary insulin-like growth factor produced by the liver that mediates the chondrocytic and osteogenic actions of growth hormone is [___].
back:
• Somatomedin C (also called IGF-1).
• Its plasma concentration follows the rate of GH secretion.
• It is the most important of the four isolated somatomedins.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: A child presents with proportionate short stature despite having elevated plasma growth hormone levels. This failure to grow due to an inability to form somatomedins is characteristic of [___].
back:
• Laron dwarfism (or African Pygmies).
• Pathophysiology involves GH receptor mutations or congenital inability to synthesize IGF-1.
• Results in failure of skeletal growth despite normal/high GH.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Explain the biological mechanism that allows Somatomedin C to prolong the growth-promoting effects of growth hormone bursts.
back:
• Somatomedin C binds strongly to carrier proteins in the blood.
• This increases its half-life to 20 hours, compared to GH's 20-minute half-life.
• It ensures a steady growth stimulus between pulsatile GH secretions.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Contrast the anatomical origin and primary function of Somatostatin with those of Somatomedin C.
back:
• Somatostatin: Hypothalamus (periventricular nuclei); inhibits GH secretion.
• Somatomedin C: Liver (and peripheral tissues); stimulates skeletal and tissue growth.
• They represent opposite ends of the GH regulatory axis.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Describe the specific intracellular signaling pathway triggered by GHRH to initiate the eventual release of somatomedins.
back:
• GHRH activates the adenylyl cyclase-cAMP system in somatotropes.
• This increases intracellular calcium, causing GH vesicle exocytosis.
• Circulating GH then travels to the liver to induce somatomedin synthesis.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: The growth-promoting effects of GH on the [___] of long bones are primarily mediated by the local and systemic production of somatomedins.
back:
• Epiphyseal cartilages.
• Somatomedins stimulate chondrocytic and osteogenic cell proliferation.
• This results in increased deposition of new cartilage and conversion to bone.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: A researcher discovers that injecting growth hormone directly into a bone's epiphyseal cartilage causes growth, even in the absence of circulating somatomedins. This suggests [___].
back:
• Local Somatomedin C production.
• GH can induce local tissues to form their own IGF-1.
• This indicates both autocrine/paracrine and endocrine roles for somatomedins.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: How does Somatomedin C participate in the negative feedback regulation of Growth Hormone secretion?
back:
• Directly inhibits GH release from the anterior pituitary.
• Stimulates hypothalamic secretion of somatostatin (GHIH).
• This dual action maintains stable plasma concentrations of IGF-1 and GH.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Contrast the metabolic effects of Growth Hormone with its growth-promoting effects mediated by somatomedins.
back:
• GH Direct: Metabolic effects (lipolysis, insulin resistance, protein sparing).
• Somatomedins: Growth effects (skeletal frame enlargement, chondrocyte mitosis, organomegaly).
• Metabolic shifts occur rapidly; growth effects require protein synthesis.

category: Explain the significance of somatomedins in mediating the actions of growth hormone
front: Identify the chemical nature of somatomedins and their approximate molecular weight.
back:
• Small proteins (polypeptides).
• Molecular weight of Somatomedin C is approximately 7,500.
• They are structurally and functionally similar to proinsulin.

category: Describe the causes and features and treatment of panhypopituitarism in adults and childhood
