front: Thyroid hormone is essential for the metamorphic change of the [___] into the adult frog, illustrating its critical non-metabolic role in growth and tissue differentiation.
back:
• Tadpole
• Triggers complex developmental transitions
• Demonstrates necessity for organogenesis and morphological changes.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: A neonate presents with sluggish movements and retarded physical growth. Failure to provide thyroid therapy within weeks of birth results in permanent [___] due to impaired neuronal branching and myelination.
back:
• Mental deficiency (Retardation)
• Brain development depends on T3/T4 for first few postnatal years
• Retardation is irreversible after the critical window.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Explain the mechanism by which thyroid hormone increases heart rate significantly more than expected from the increase in cardiac output.
back:
• Direct effect on cardiac excitability
• Increases sensitivity of the heart to adrenergic stimuli
• Enhances force of contraction (initially).

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Contrast the characteristic fine muscle tremor of hyperthyroidism with the tremor typical of Parkinson’s disease.
back:
• Hyperthyroid: Fine, rapid (10–15 times/sec); due to increased neuronal synapse reactivity in spinal cord.
• Parkinson: Coarse, resting tremor; different neurological origin.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Identify the two specific alterations in breathing pattern stimulated by the increased oxygen utilization and carbon dioxide formation associated with thyroid hormone action.
back:
• Increased rate of respiration
• Increased depth of respiration (Minute ventilation increases).

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: In the gastrointestinal tract, excessive thyroid hormone typically results in [___], whereas a deficiency is a common cause of constipation.
back:
• Diarrhea
• Due to increased secretion of digestive juices
• Enhanced GI motility (peristalsis).

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: A 10-year-old child with hyperthyroidism is significantly taller than his peers. Predict the likely adult height of this patient and the underlying mechanism.
back:
• Shortened adult height
• Mechanism: Rapid bone maturation and early epiphyseal closure/fusion.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
coreConcept: Thyroid Influence on Sleep and Synaptic Excitability
front: Explain the discrepancy between the physical tiredness and the sleep patterns seen in a patient with thyrotoxicosis.
back:
• Patient feels exhausted but cannot sleep (Insomnia)
• Due to excitatory effects of thyroid hormone on neuronal synapses
• Contrasts with extreme somnolence in hypothyroidism.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
coreConcept: Thyroid Influence on Female Sexual Function
front: Contrast the typical menstrual abnormalities seen in hypothyroidism versus hyperthyroidism.
back:
• Hypothyroidism: Menorrhagia (excessive flow) and polymenorrhea (frequent flow).
• Hyperthyroidism: Oligomenorrhea (reduced flow) or amenorrhea.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Thyroid hormone increases the rate of hepatic inactivation of [___], leading to a feedback-induced increase in ACTH production.
back:
• Adrenal glucocorticoids (Cortisol)
• Results in compensatory increase in adrenal gland secretion.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Thyroid hormone is critical for central nervous system development; specifically, it promotes the [___] and myelination of neuronal cells during fetal and early postnatal life.
back:
• Branching (and growth) of neuronal cells.
• Lack of these processes leads to permanent mental deficiency (Cretinism).

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: A 35-year-old female presents with palpitations and weight loss. On examination, she exhibits a fine vibration (10–15 times/sec) when her fingers are extended. This specific non-metabolic effect is caused by [___].
back:
• Increased reactivity of neuronal synapses in the spinal cord.
• Specifically affects regions controlling muscle tone.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Explain the direct mechanism by which thyroid hormone causes a disproportionate increase in heart rate compared to cardiac output.
back:
• Direct effect on the heart's excitability.
• Up-regulation of beta-adrenergic receptors.
• Increased sensitivity to circulating catecholamines.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Contrast the sleep disturbances typically observed in hyperthyroidism versus severe hypothyroidism (myxedema).
back:
• Hyperthyroidism: Constant tiredness but difficulty sleeping due to excitable synaptic effects.
• Hypothyroidism: Extreme somnolence, with sleep often lasting 12 to 14 hours per day.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Describe the physiological effect of thyroid hormone on gastrointestinal function and its resulting clinical presentation in thyrotoxicosis.
back:
• Increases secretion of digestive juices.
• Increases gastrointestinal motility.
• Clinical result: Frequent bowel movements or diarrhea.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: In women, the specific menstrual abnormality characterized by excessive and frequent bleeding (menorrhagia and polymenorrhea) is most commonly associated with [___].
back:
• Hypothyroidism (Lack of thyroid hormone).
• (Note: Hyperthyroidism usually causes oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea).

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Thyroid hormone is critical for the development of the fetal brain; a deficiency during this period leads to permanent mental retardation, a condition known as [___].
back:
• Cretinism
• Characterized by failure of body growth and severe mental retardation
• Requires thyroid therapy within weeks of birth to prevent permanent neurological damage.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: A 35-year-old female with Graves' disease holds a sheet of paper on her extended fingers, which exhibits a high-frequency vibration. Characterize this sign and its underlying cause.
back:
• Fine muscle tremor (10-15 times/sec)
• Caused by increased reactivity of neuronal synapses
• Specifically affects the spinal cord areas controlling muscle tone.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
coreConcept: Hormonal Interplay: Thyroid and Adrenal Cortex
front: Explain the mechanism by which hyperthyroidism leads to a compensatory increase in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion.
back:
• Thyroid hormone increases hepatic inactivation of glucocorticoids
• Low plasma cortisol triggers the negative feedback loop
• Results in increased hypothalamic CRF and anterior pituitary ACTH release.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Contrast the effects of excessive thyroid hormone on skeletal development in a growing child regarding immediate height versus final adult stature.
back:
• Immediate: Accelerated skeletal growth makes the child taller at an early age
• Final: Adult stature is often shortened
• Mechanism: Excessive hormone causes premature closure of the epiphyses.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
coreConcept: Thyroid Effects on Sleep and Vigor
front: Identify the characteristic sleep-related disturbances seen in hypothyroidism versus hyperthyroidism.
back:
• Hypothyroidism: Extreme somnolence (sleeping 12-14 hours per day)
• Hyperthyroidism: Constant tiredness combined with insomnia
• Mechanism: Results from altered synaptic excitability levels.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: A classic clinical sign of hypothyroidism is the sluggishness of the [___] phase during deep tendon reflex testing, particularly at the Achilles tendon.
back:
• Relaxation
• Hypothyroidism causes muscles to contract and relax more slowly
• Contrast: Hyperthyroidism causes muscles to react with excessive vigor.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
coreConcept: Thyroid Influence on Female Sexual Function
front: A 28-year-old female presents with frequent and excessive menstrual bleeding (polymenorrhea and menorrhagia). If this is due to a thyroid disorder, name the likely underlying state.
back:
• Hypothyroidism
• Characterized by frequent/heavy bleeding and decreased libido
• Results from altered metabolic effects on gonads and pituitary feedback.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
coreConcept: CNS Excitatory Effects of Thyroid Hormone
front: Describe how excessive thyroid hormone alters Central Nervous System (CNS) function, specifically regarding thought processes and behavior.
back:
• Increases the rapidity of cerebration
• Promotes psychoneurotic tendencies (anxiety, extreme worry, or paranoia)
• Enhances overall synaptic excitability in the brain.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Distinguish between the physiological effect of slight thyroid hormone excess versus marked thyroid hormone excess on skeletal muscle performance.
back:
• Slight excess: Muscles react with increased vigor
• Marked excess: Muscles become weakened and catabolized
• Mechanism: Long-term excess causes severe protein catabolism.

category: Explain the non-metabolic functions of thyroid hormone
front: Beyond its metabolic actions, describe the direct effect of thyroid hormone on the heart's rhythmicity and excitability.
back:
• Direct effect on heart excitability increases heart rate (tachycardia)
• This sign is used clinically to assess thyroid hormone levels
• Often accompanied by increased pulse pressure.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: Thyroid hormones enhance fat metabolism by rapidly mobilizing [___] from adipose tissue, significantly decreasing total body fat stores.
back:
• Lipids (fats)
• This increases free fatty acid (FFA) concentration in the plasma
• Oxidation of FFAs in cells is greatly accelerated for energy production.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: A 45-year-old female presents with cold intolerance, weight gain, and sluggishness. Lab reports show significantly elevated plasma cholesterol and triglycerides. Explain the underlying lipid pathophysiology.
back:
• Thyroid hormone deficiency reduces hepatic LDL receptor expression
• This leads to decreased cholesterol clearance from the blood
• Sluggish lipid mobilization results in systemic fat accumulation and fatty liver.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: Explain the specific hepatic mechanism by which thyroid hormones reduce circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels.
back:
• T3/T4 induce increased numbers of LDL receptors on liver cells
• This facilitates rapid removal of LDL from the plasma
• Cholesterol is subsequently secreted into bile and excreted in feces.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: Contrast the lipid profiles of a patient with Myxedema versus one with Toxic Goiter, specifically regarding plasma cholesterol and free fatty acid (FFA) levels.
back:
• Myxedema (Hypothyroid): Elevated plasma cholesterol/triglycerides due to poor clearance; low FFA mobilization
• Toxic Goiter (Hyperthyroid): Decreased plasma cholesterol; elevated plasma FFAs due to intense adipose mobilization.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: Identify the primary physiological route through which thyroid hormones facilitate the permanent removal of cholesterol from the body.
back:
• Increased secretion into bile
• Consequent loss via feces
• Driven by enhanced hepatic uptake via LDL receptors.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: While hyperthyroidism depletes fat stores, a clinical lack of thyroid hormone results in excessive deposition of fat specifically in the [___].
back:
• Liver
• Contributes to significantly increased plasma concentrations of cholesterol and phospholipids
• Strongly associated with the development of severe atherosclerosis.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: A patient with Graves' disease reports profound weight loss despite a 'voracious appetite.' Detail the metabolic logic regarding their lipid stores.
back:
• Excess T3/T4 accelerates the Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)
• Adipose mobilization and FFA oxidation exceed caloric intake
• Fat stores are decreased to a greater extent than any other tissue.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: Beyond simple mobilization, detail how thyroid hormones influence the utilization of free fatty acids (FFAs) once they enter the plasma.
back:
• Greatly accelerates the rate of FFA oxidation within almost all body cells
• Increases cellular metabolic enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle
• Shifts energy preference toward fat utilization to support high BMR.

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: Contrast the effect of increased thyroid hormone on plasma free fatty acid (FFA) concentration versus plasma phospholipid concentration.
back:
• Plasma FFAs: Increased (due to rapid mobilization from adipose tissue)
• Plasma Phospholoids: Decreased (due to increased hepatic clearance and biliary excretion).

category: Explain the actions of thyroid hormones on fat metabolism
front: List the three specific lipid types whose plasma concentrations are characteristically decreased by the action of thyroid hormones.
back:
• Cholesterol
• Phospholipids
• Triglycerides
• (Note: FFAs are the exception, as they increase in plasma).

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: The secretion of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) by the anterior pituitary gland is primarily regulated by the hypothalamic tripeptide known as [___].
back:
• Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH)
• Synthesized in the paraventricular nuclei (PVN)
• Transported to the pituitary via the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: A patient presents with a pituitary adenoma secreting excessive TSH. Predict the resulting levels of plasma T3/T4 and hypothalamic TRH.
back:
• T3 and T4: Elevated (due to direct TSH stimulation)
• TRH: Decreased (due to negative feedback from high T3/T4)
• This represents secondary hyperthyroidism

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Explain the role of the cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) system in the thyroid's response to TSH.
back:
• TSH binds basal follicular membrane receptors
• Activates adenylyl cyclase to form cAMP
• cAMP activates protein kinase
• Triggers immediate proteolysis of thyroglobulin and hormone release

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Contrast the effects of acute environmental cold exposure with acute emotional anxiety on the regulation of TSH.
back:
• Cold: Excites hypothalamic temperature centers, significantly increasing TRH and TSH secretion
• Anxiety: Stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to an acute decrease in TSH secretion

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Identify the specific intracellular second messenger system used by TRH to stimulate TSH-secreting cells in the anterior pituitary.
back:
• Phospholipase C mechanism
• TRH binds receptors activating phospholipase C
• Produces inositol triphosphate and diacylglycerol
• Increases intracellular calcium to trigger TSH release

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: In the autoregulation of thyroid hormone, the primary site where T3 and T4 exert negative feedback to suppress TSH is the [___].
back:
• Anterior pituitary gland
• Occurs even if the pituitary is separated from the hypothalamus
• Ensures constant concentrations of free thyroid hormones

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: A woman with Graves' disease has high Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI). Explain why her endogenous TSH levels are often near zero.
back:
• TSI binds and chronically activates TSH receptors
• Induces massive T3/T4 secretion
• Elevated T3/T4 exerts powerful negative feedback inhibition on the pituitary
• Result: Suppressed endogenous TSH

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: How does leptin participation in the arcuate nucleus influence thyroid hormone regulation during prolonged fasting?
back:
• Fasting reduces plasma leptin
• Low leptin inhibits TRH neurons in the PVN
• Reduces TSH and thyroid hormone levels
• Mechanism: Conserves energy by reducing the basal metabolic rate

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Contrast the 'immediate' versus 'delayed' morphological changes in the thyroid gland caused by chronic TSH stimulation.
back:
• Immediate: Increased proteolysis of thyroglobulin and follicular cell secretion
• Delayed: Increase in cell size (cuboidal to columnar) and cell number (hyperplasia)
• Results in increased infolding of epithelium into follicles

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Identify the primaryエンド end-product of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis that maintains the steady-state concentrations of free hormone.
back:
• Free Triiodothyronine (T3) and Thyroxine (T4)
• T3 is the more active feedback inhibitor
• Functions primarily by direct inhibition of thyrotropes

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: The most common cause of hyperthyroidism is [___], an autoimmune disorder involving antibodies that activate TSH receptors.
back:
• Graves' disease
• Triggered by Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSIs)
• TSIs induce continual activation of the cAMP system in thyroid cells

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: A 35-year-old female presents with heat intolerance, a fine hand tremor (10-15 times/sec), and protruding eyes. The pathophysiology behind her ocular symptoms is [___].
back:
• Exophthalmos (Autoimmune process)
• Edematous swelling of retro-orbital tissues
• Degenerative changes in extraocular muscles triggered by immunoglobulins

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Explain the mechanism by which a localized thyroid adenoma results in hyperthyroidism and total suppression of the remaining healthy thyroid tissue.
back:
• The adenoma autonomously secretes large quantities of T3/T4
• High hormone levels provide potent negative feedback to the anterior pituitary
• TSH secretion is inhibited, causing non-tumorous thyroid tissue to become inactive

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: A clinician compares two patients with high BMR (+40). Contrast the expected TSI and TSH levels if Patient A has Graves' disease and Patient B has a toxic thyroid adenoma.
back:
• Graves' Disease: TSI is high; TSH is suppressed (near zero)
• Toxic Adenoma: TSI is low/absent; TSH is suppressed (near zero)
• Only Graves' involves autoimmune receptor stimulation

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Enumerate the primary steps by which Propylthiouracil treats hyperthyroidism.
back:
• Blocks the peroxidase enzyme system
• Inhibits iodination of tyrosine
• Prevents coupling of iodinated tyrosines to form T3 and T4

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: In the clinical investigation of thyrotoxicosis, the most accurate diagnostic test is the direct measurement of plasma [___] concentration.
back:
• "Free" Thyroxine (T4)
• Free Triiodothyronine (T3) is also measured
• Results are typically 5 to 15 times normal in hyperplastic glands

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Antithyroid substances like thiocyanate and perchlorate ions suppress thyroid hormone production by competitively inhibiting [___].
back:
• The sodium-iodide symporter (iodide trapping mechanism).
• Decreases intracellular iodide availability.
• Prevents the subsequent iodination of thyroglobulin tyrosine residues.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: A 40-year-old female is scheduled for a subtotal thyroidectomy. The surgeon prescribes high-dose inorganic iodides for two weeks preoperatively to [___].
back:
• Paralyze colloid endocytosis, immediately stopping hormone release.
• Reduce the size and vascularity of the gland.
• Minimize operative time and surgical bleeding risks.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain the dual mechanism of action of Propylthiouracil (PTU) in suppressing thyroid hormone synthesis within the gland.
back:
• Blocks the peroxidase enzyme, preventing tyrosine iodination.
• Inhibits the coupling of iodinated tyrosines (MIT and DIT).
• Prevents the formation of T3 and T4 within the thyroglobulin molecule.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the effect of thiocyanate ions with high-concentration inorganic iodides on thyroid gland morphology.
back:
• Thiocyanate: Causes gland enlargement (goiter) by stimulating TSH via negative feedback loops.
• High Iodides: Causes gland shrinkage and decreased blood supply by suppressing all functional phases.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Identify the primary mechanism by which high concentrations of plasma iodides achieve an almost immediate 'shutdown' of thyroid hormone secretion.
back:
• Paralysis of colloid endocytosis from the follicles.
• This blocks the initial step of releasing stored hormone into the blood.
• Note: This effect is usually transient, lasting only a few weeks.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Propylthiouracil does not prevent the formation of thyroglobulin, but the resulting lack of T3 and T4 leads to feedback enhancement of [___], causing a goiter.
back:
• Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).
• Secreted by the anterior pituitary.
• Promotes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the thyroid glandular tissue despite lack of hormone output.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Most of the stimulatory effects of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) on thyroid follicular cells are mediated by the intracellular second messenger [___].
back:
• Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP).
• TSH binds to G-protein coupled receptors, activating adenylyl cyclase.
• This triggers protein kinase activation and phosphorylation of key synthetic enzymes.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: A 40-year-old female presents with heat intolerance, weight loss, and tremors. Lab results show elevated free T4 and nearly undetectable TSH. Identify the regulatory mechanism responsible for the suppressed TSH.
back:
• Negative feedback loop.
• High circulating T3/T4 directly inhibits the anterior pituitary thyrotropes.
• This suppresses TSH secretion to nearly zero in primary hyperthyroidism.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone (TRH) stimulates the thyrotropes of the anterior pituitary.
back:
• TRH binds to membrane receptors on thyrotropes.
• Activates the phospholipase C second messenger system.
• Increases IP3, diacylglycerol, and calcium, leading to TSH release.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Contrast the effects of chronic cold exposure versus acute emotional excitement/anxiety on the secretion of TSH.
back:
• Cold exposure: Stimulates TRH neurons in the hypothalamus to increase TSH and BMR.
• Excitement/Anxiety: Causes an acute decrease in TSH secretion via sympathetic activation.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Identify the specific histological changes in thyroid follicular cells induced by prolonged TSH stimulation.
back:
• Transformation from cuboidal to columnar cells.
• Increased cell number (hyperplasia).
• Increased infolding of the thyroid epithelium into the follicles.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: The earliest effect of TSH, occurring within 30 minutes of administration, is the stimulation of [___] to release T3 and T4 into the blood.
back:
• Proteolysis of thyroglobulin.
• Lysosomes fuse with pinocytic vesicles containing stored colloid.
• Proteases digest thyroglobulin, freeing T3 and T4 for diffusion.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: The active pump responsible for iodide trapping in thyroid glandular cells is competitively inhibited by anions such as [___] and perchlorate.
back:
• Thiocyanate.
• These ions utilize the same sodium-iodide symporter (NIS).
• By occupying the transporter, they prevent iodine from entering the follicular cells for hormone synthesis.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: A 35-year-old female is diagnosed with Graves' disease. Her physician prescribes Propylthiouracil (PTU). Describe the primary enzymatic step targeted by this medication.
back:
• Inhibition of thyroid peroxidase enzyme.
• Prevents the iodination of tyrosine residues on the thyroglobulin molecule.
• Effectively blocks the coupling of iodinated tyrosines to form T3 and T4.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain how high concentrations of inorganic iodides (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) reduce the secretion of thyroid hormones.
back:
• Reduces the rate of iodide trapping.
• Paralyzes the endocytosis of colloid from the follicles.
• This causes an almost immediate shutdown of thyroid hormone secretion into the blood.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the effects of Propylthiouracil and Thiocyanate on the morphological appearance of the thyroid gland versus the effects of high-dose inorganic iodides.
back:
• PTU/Thiocyanate: Induce goiter (enlargement) via feedback-mediated TSH elevation.
• Inorganic Iodides: Decrease gland size and vascularity.
• Iodides are used pre-operatively to reduce surgical bleeding risk.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Identify the group of antithyroid substances that includes methimazole and carbimazole, and name their two-fold action on thyroid synthesis.
back:
• Thionamides (Thiourea derivatives).
• Action 1: Block the peroxidase enzyme required for tyrosine iodination.
• Action 2: Block the coupling of two iodinated tyrosines.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Administration of antithyroid drugs that do not prevent the formation of thyroglobulin, but do inhibit iodination, leads to the development of a [___].
back:
• Goiter.
• Low T3/T4 levels remove feedback inhibition on the pituitary.
• Increased TSH secretion causes overgrowth (hypertrophy) of the thyroid glandular tissue.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: A patient with hyperthyroidism is scheduled for a subtotal thyroidectomy in two weeks. Why does the surgeon prescribe a course of inorganic iodides instead of PTU alone?
back:
• Iodides decrease the blood supply to the thyroid gland.
• They reduce the physical size of the hyperplastic gland.
• This minimizes the technical difficulty and the risk of intraoperative hemorrhage.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Describe the specific cellular transport protein targeted by thiocyanate ions and the resulting effect on "organification."
back:
• Targets the Sodium-Iodide Symporter (NIS) on the basolateral membrane.
• Causes competitive inhibition of iodide uptake.
• Prevents organification (binding of iodine to thyroglobulin) due to substrate deficiency.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Distinguish between "iodide trapping" and "organification" of thyroglobulin in the context of thyroid hormone synthesis and antithyroid drug action.
back:
• Iodide Trapping: Active transport of iodide into cells (inhibited by Thiocyanate).
• Organification: Binding of oxidized iodine to tyrosine (inhibited by Propylthiouracil).
• Both steps are required to form the thyroglobulin-stored hormones.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Name two common dietary goitrogenic substances that exhibit antithyroid activity similar to propylthiouracil.
back:
• Turnips and Cabbages.
• These contain substances that inhibit the synthesis of thyroid hormones.
• Prolonged ingestion leads to TSH-stimulated enlargement of the thyroid gland.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: TRH stimulates the anterior pituitary thyrotropes by binding to membrane receptors that activate the [___] second messenger system.
back:
* Phospholipase C
* Leads to production of inositol triphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG)
* Resultant increase in intracellular calcium triggers TSH release.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: A 30-year-old female presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, and high serum T4. Despite thyrotoxicosis, her TSH is nearly zero. Identify the regulator being bypassed.
back:
* TSH Receptor (activated by Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins/TSI)
* TSI mimics TSH but is not subject to negative feedback
* High T4 levels directly inhibit endogenous TSH production.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Explain the immediate mechanism by which TSH increases thyroid hormone availability within 30 minutes of administration.
back:
* Stimulation of thyroglobulin proteolysis
* Activates proteinases to cleave T3/T4 from stored colloid
* This "early effect" occurs long before iodine trapping or cell growth increases.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Contrast the inhibitory sensitivity of the anterior pituitary versus the hypothalamus to rising levels of free thyroid hormones.
back:
* Anterior Pituitary: Primary site of feedback; TSH secretion falls to zero at ~1.75x normal T4
* Hypothalamus: Secondary site; inhibits TRH synthesis to a lesser degree.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Describe the neurogenic regulation of the thyroid axis in response to chronic exposure to arctic temperatures.
back:
* Excitation of hypothalamic heat control centers
* Increased TRH secretion from the paraventricular nucleus
* Elevated TSH and T4 levels increase BMR by 15-20%.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: The varied secretory and growth-promoting effects of TSH on thyroid follicular cells are primarily mediated by the [___] second messenger system.
back:
* Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP)
* Binding to TSH receptors activates adenylyl cyclase
* cAMP-dependent protein kinases trigger immediate hormone release and delayed follicular hypertrophy.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: A patient undergoing prolonged fasting shows a decreased metabolic rate and low TSH. Explain the metabolic link between fat stores and TRH secretion.
back:
* Reduced Leptin levels during fasting
* Low leptin inhibits TRH neurons in the paraventricular nucleus
* This suppresses the thyroid axis to conserve energy during starvation.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: How does the administration of high concentrations of inorganic iodides (100x normal) paradoxically regulate thyroid gland activity?
back:
* Paralyzes endocytosis of colloid from follicles
* Causes immediate shutdown of thyroid hormone secretion into blood
* Reduces gland size and blood supply (pre-operative utility).

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Contrast the mechanisms by which Thiocyanate and Propylthiouracil (PTU) lead to the formation of a goiter.
back:
* Thiocyanate: Competitively inhibits the sodium-iodide symporter (iodide trapping)
* PTU: Blocks peroxidase enzyme and coupling of iodinated tyrosines
* Both: Lower T3/T4, causing compensatory TSH-driven overgrowth.

category: Explain the regulation of thyroid hormone
front: Identify the primary hypothalamic nucleus responsible for synthesizing and secreting the hormone that regulates pituitary TSH production.
back:
* Paraventricular Nucleus (PVN)
* Synthesizes Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone (TRH)
* TRH is a tripeptide amide (pyroglutamyl-histidyl-proline-amide) carried via hypophysial portal vessels.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: The antithyroid substance [___] suppresses thyroid hormone production by competitively inhibiting the active transport of iodide ions into thyroid glandular cells.
back:
Thiocyanate (or Perchlorate/Nitrate).
- Inhibits the sodium-iodide symporter (iodide trapping).
- Prevents iodination of thyroglobulin by reducing available intracellular iodide.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: A 35-year-old female with Graves' disease is prescribed Propylthiouracil (PTU). The primary enzymatic target inhibited by this drug is [___].
back:
Thyroid Peroxidase.
- Blocks oxidation of iodide to nascent iodine.
- Prevents iodination (organification) of tyrosine.
- Inhibits coupling of iodinated tyrosines (MIT/DIT).

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which high concentrations of inorganic iodides (100x normal) achieve a rapid shutdown of thyroid hormone secretion.
back:
Paralysis of Colloid Endocytosis.
- Paralyzes the first step of release: swallowing colloid from follicles.
- Decreases the rate of iodide trapping and iodination.
- Effectively stops hormone entry into blood.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the feedback-mediated morphological changes in the thyroid gland when using thiocyanate versus high-dose inorganic iodides.
back:
Thiocyanate vs. Iodides:
- Thiocyanate: Decreased hormone leads to high TSH, causing goiter (enlarged, vascular gland).
- Iodides: Directly decrease all activities, resulting in a smaller, less vascular gland.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Name the specific step in thyroid hormone synthesis inhibited by Propylthiouracil but NOT by thiocyanate ions.
back:
The Coupling Reaction.
- PTU blocks the coupling of monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT) to form T3/T4.
- Thiocyanate only limits the raw material (iodide) for synthesis.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Propylthiouracil and methimazole belong to a class of drugs that prevent the [___] of thyroglobulin, thereby stopping hormone formation.
back:
Organification (or Iodination).
- They prevent the binding of oxidized iodine to tyrosine residues on the thyroglobulin molecule.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: A surgeon prepares a hyperthyroid patient for thyroidectomy by administering Lugol's iodine for two weeks. Describe the intended hemodynamic effect on the gland.
back:
Reduced Vascularity and Bleeding.
- High-dose iodides decrease the blood supply to the thyroid.
- Makes surgical removal safer with significantly less operative hemorrhage.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Describe how the administration of thiocyanate can lead to the clinical development of a goiter despite reducing thyroid hormone levels.
back:
TSH Feedback Hypertrophy.
- Reduced T3/T4 removes negativeph feedback.
- Anterior pituitary secretes excessive TSH.
- TSH stimulates massive growth of non-functional follicular cells.

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the inhibitory mechanisms of Perchlorate ions and Carbimazole on the thyroid follicle.
back:
Symporter vs. Enzyme:
- Perchlorate: Competitive inhibitor of the Sodium-Iodide Symporter (I- Trapping).
- Carbimazole: Inhibitor of Thyroid Peroxidase (Iodination and Coupling).

category: Enumerate antithyroid substances and explain their mechanism of action
front: Identify the common dietary source known to contain 'goitrogens' that mimic the antithyroid activity of Propylthiouracil.
back:
Turnips and Cabbages.
- Contain substances that inhibit peroxidase-mediated iodination and coupling.
- Can cause TSH-stimulated thyroid enlargement (goiter).

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: The most common form of hyperthyroidism, characterized by an autoimmune etiology, is known as [___].
back:
• Graves' disease
• Also known as toxic goiter or thyrotoxicosis

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: A 35-year-old female presents with tremors, heat intolerance, weight loss, and bulging eyes (exophthalmos). The circulating markers responsible for this condition are [___].
back:
• Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSIs)
• These are antibodies against the TSH receptor

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSIs) induce excessive thyroid hormone secretion.
back:
• Bind to TSH receptors in the thyroid gland
• Induce continual activation of the cAMP second messenger system
• Results in follicular hyperplasia and hypersecretion

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Contrast the expected plasma levels of Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI) in Graves' disease versus a localized toxic thyroid adenoma.
back:
• Graves' Disease: TSI concentration is high
• Thyroid Adenoma: TSI concentration is low (non-autoimmune)

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Describe the physiological status of anterior pituitary TSH secretion in a patient with a hyperfunctioning thyroid adenoma.
back:
• TSH secretion is almost totally inhibited
• Caused by excessive T3/T4 feedback suppression of the pituitary

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Hyperthyroidism resulting from a localized tumor in the thyroid tissue that is independent of autoimmune markers is termed a [___].
back:
• Thyroid Adenoma
• Operates autonomously from the rest of the thyroid tissue

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: A patient presents with tachycardia and high basal metabolic rate. Lab results show high free T4 but TSH levels are nearly zero. Identify the two most likely causes for this presentation.
back:
• 1. Graves' Disease (Toxic Goiter)
• 2. Toxic Thyroid Adenoma

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Compare the duration of the stimulatory effect of Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSIs) on the thyroid gland with that of natural TSH.
back:
• TSIs: Prolonged effect, lasting up to 12 hours
• TSH: Short duration, lasting a little over 1 hour

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Contrast the occurrence of exophthalmos (protruding eyes) in autoimmune hyperthyroidism versus its occurrence in hyperthyroidism caused by a functional adenoma.
back:
• Autoimmune (Graves'): Occurs in 1/3 of patients due to extraocular muscle edema
• Adenoma: Usually absent as it lacks the autoimmune component

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Enumerate the three primary pathological triggers for hyperthyroidism (Toxic Goiter).
back:
• 1. Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (Autoimmunity)
• 2. Localized Thyroid Adenoma (Tumor)
• 3. Excessive thyroid antigens release leading to TSI formation

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: The most common cause of hypothyroidism, characterized by autoimmune-mediated inflammation and progressive fibrosis of the thyroid gland, is [___].
back:
• Hashimoto's disease (Autoimmune thyroiditis)
• Autoantibodies cause progressive gland destruction
• Results in diminished or absent secretion of T3 and T4

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: A patient from a mountainous region presents with a massive neck swelling and lethargy. Labs reveal low serum T4 and significantly elevated TSH. Identify the most likely cause of this specific goiter.
back:
• Endemic Colloid Goiter
• Caused by dietary iodide deficiency
• Low iodine prevents T3/T4 production, removing negative feedback on TSH
• High TSH stimulates massive thyroglobulin production

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Explain the mechanism by which dietary goitrogens found in turnips and cabbages induce a hypothyroid state.
back:
• They contain propylthiouracil-type antithyroid activity
• This blocks the peroxidase enzyme and the coupling of iodinated tyrosines
• Leads to TSH-stimulated gland enlargement despite low hormone output

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Contrast the diagnostic laboratory findings of Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) in primary hypothyroidism versus secondary hypothyroidism.
back:
• Primary: High TSH (due to lack of negative feedback from the failing thyroid)
• Secondary: Low or undetectable TSH (due to pituitary gland failure or TRH deficiency)

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Enlist four specific enzyme or transport defects that can cause idiopathic nontoxic colloid goiter.
back:
• Deficient iodide-trapping pump
• Deficient peroxidase system (oxidation failure)
• Deficient coupling of iodinated tyrosines
• Deiodinase enzyme deficiency (recycling failure)

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Hypothyroidism resulting from therapeutic interventions, specifically surgical [___] or the administration of [___] iodine, are common iatrogenic causes.
back:
• Thyroidectomy (Surgical removal)
• Radioactive iodine (I-131) therapy
• Both cause permanent loss of functional thyroid follicular cells

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: In Graves' disease, the specific autoimmune antibodies that bind to and chronically activate TSH receptors are known as [___].
back:
* Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs).
* These mimic TSH action but have a longer duration of effect (up to 12 hours).
* They induce continual activation of the cAMP second messenger system.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: A 32-year-old female presents with heat intolerance, fine hand tremors, and proptosis. Labs reveal suppressed TSH and elevated Free T4. Identify the diagnosis and the underlying cause of her eye findings.
back:
* Diagnosis: Graves' disease (Thyrotoxicosis).
* Cause of Exophthalmos: Autoimmune-mediated edematous swelling of retro-orbital tissues.
* Associated with degenerative changes and immunoglobulin reactions in extraocular muscles.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Explain the intracellular signaling mechanism by which Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSIs) induce the hyperplastic changes seen in Graves' disease.
back:
* TSIs bind to TSH receptors on the basal membrane.
* This activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP.
* cAMP-dependent protein kinases trigger follicular cell proliferation and excessive thyroid hormone synthesis.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Contrast Graves’ disease from a toxic thyroid adenoma regarding their immune etiology and plasma levels of Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulin (TSI).
back:
* Graves' Disease: Autoimmune etiology; high plasma TSI levels.
* Toxic Adenoma: Localized tumorous growth (non-autoimmune); low or absent TSI levels.
* Both conditions result in suppressed TSH due to excessive T3/T4 feedback.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Identify the primary physiological goals of administering high concentrations of inorganic iodides to a thyrotoxic patient 1-2 weeks before a thyroidectomy.
back:
* Paralyzes endocytosis of colloid to immediately shut down hormone secretion.
* Reduces the total blood supply to the thyroid gland.
* Decreases the physical size and vascularity of the gland to minimize surgical bleeding.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
coreConcept: Mechanism of Fine Tremor in Hyperthyroidism
front: The characteristic 'fine' muscle tremor observed in thyrotoxicosis is attributed to the increased reactivity of neuronal synapses in the [___].
back:
* Areas of the spinal cord that control muscle tone.
* It occurs at a rapid frequency of 10 to 15 times per second.
* Differs from the coarse tremors seen in Parkinson’s or shivering.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: The primary autoimmune markers responsible for chronic, unregulated stimulation of the thyroid gland in Graves' disease are [___].
back:
• Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs).
• These antibodies bind to TSH receptors.
• They induce continual activation of the intracellular cAMP second messenger system.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: A 32-year-old female presents with heat intolerance, weight loss, and protruding eyeballs. The ocular condition, known as [___], results from [___].
back:
• Exophthalmos.
• Pathophysiology: Edematous swelling of retro-orbital tissues and autoimmune-mediated degenerative changes in extraocular muscles.
• Strongly associated with high concentrations of TSIs.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs) trigger thyrotoxicosis.
back:
• TSIs mimic Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).
• They bind TSH receptors on the basal membrane.
• This leads to sustained cAMP production, causing cellular hypertrophy and hormone secretion rates 5–15 times normal.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Contrast Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) with physiological TSH regarding their duration of action and feedback on the pituitary.
back:
• Duration: TSI lasts up to 12 hours; TSH lasts ~1 hour.
• Pituitary Effect: TSI-induced high T3/T4 levels suppress pituitary TSH to near zero.
• Source: TSI is an autoantibody; TSH is a pituitary hormone.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: List the clinical objectives for administering high concentrations of inorganic iodides for 1–2 weeks prior to surgical thyroidectomy.
back:
• Reduces the physical size of the thyroid gland.
• Diminishes the gland’s blood supply.
• Minimizes intraoperative bleeding and surgical mortality.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: The characteristic hyperthyroid tremor is a fine vibration occurring at [___] times per second and is believed to be caused by [___].
back:
• 10 to 15 times per second.
• Mechanism: Increased reactivity of neuronal synapses in the spinal cord regions that regulate muscle tone.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: A patient with thyrotoxicosis presents with a BMR of +45%. Predict the likely laboratory findings for Free T4 and plasma TSH.
back:
• Free T4: Greatly increased.
• Plasma TSH: Extremely low or undetectable (suppressed).
• This pattern distinguishes Graves' from TSH-secreting tumors.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Explain the pharmacological mechanism of Propylthiouracil in the management of Graves’ disease.
back:
• Blocks the peroxidase enzyme responsible for iodinating tyrosine.
• Prevents the coupling of iodinated tyrosines (MIT/DIT).
• Inhibits the formation of T3 and T4 within the thyroglobulin molecule.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Contrast the pathophysiology of Toxic Goiter (Graves') with Endemic Colloid Goiter regarding TSH levels and hormone status.
back:
• Toxic: Hyperthyroid state, suppressed TSH, autoimmune TSI stimulation.
• Endemic: Hypothyroid/Euthyroid state, highly elevated TSH, dietary iodine deficiency.
• Gland Size: Both show enlargement, but mechanisms are opposite.

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Describe the effects of excessive thyroid hormone on the cardiovascular system during thyrotoxicosis.
back:
• Increased heart rate (tachycardia) and excitability.
• Increased cardiac output (often 60% above normal).
• Increased pulse pressure (elevated systolic, reduced diastolic).

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: The most common primary cause of hypothyroidism is an autoimmune condition known as [___], which results in progressive gland inflammation and fibrosis.
back:
- Hashimoto’s disease (Autoimmune thyroiditis).
- It is characterized by antibodies that destroy thyroid tissue rather than stimulate it.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: A 48-year-old female presents with fatigue, cold intolerance, and non-pitting edema (myxedema). Lab results show very low free T4 and significantly elevated TSH. Identify the most likely underlying pathophysiology.
back:
- Primary hypothyroidism (likely Hashimoto’s disease).
- Destruction of thyroid tissue leads to loss of negative feedback, causing the pituitary to oversecrete TSH.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Explain the mechanism by which dietary iodide deficiency leads to the development of an endemic colloid goiter.
back:
- Lack of iodine prevents T3/T4 production.
- Low thyroid hormones remove negative feedback on the pituitary.
- Excess TSH stimulates massive thyroglobulin secretion into follicles, enlarging the gland.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Contrast the etiology of endemic colloid goiter with that of idiopathic nontoxic colloid goiter regarding iodine availability.
back:
- Endemic: Caused by external lack of dietary iodine in specific geographical regions.
- Idiopathic: Occurs despite normal iodine intake, often due to mild thyroiditis or subtle enzyme defects.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Enlist three specific enzymatic abnormalities in the thyroid follicle that can result in goitrous hypothyroidism.
back:
- Deficient iodide-trapping mechanism.
- Deficient peroxidase system (prevents iodide oxidation).
- Deficient coupling of iodinated tyrosines to form T3 or T4.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: The development of goiter in individuals consuming large quantities of turnips or cabbages is attributed to the presence of [___] substances.
back:
- Goitrogenic substances.
- These possess propylthiouracil-type antithyroid activity that blocks hormone formation.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: A patient previously treated for Grave’s disease now presents with weight gain, sluggishness, and constipation. Identify the two most common iatrogenic causes for this transition.
back:
- Surgical removal of the thyroid gland (Thyroidectomy).
- Radioactive iodine irradiation (Ablation of secretory cells).

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Describe how a deficiency in the deiodinase enzyme contributes to the development of hypothyroidism.
back:
- Prevents the recovery of iodine from uncoupled MIT and DIT.
- Iodine is lost from the gland instead of recycled.
- Results in a state of functional iodine deficiency despite adequate intake.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Contrast primary hypothyroidism with secondary hypothyroidism based on TSH levels and pituitary function.
back:
- Primary: High TSH; problem is in the thyroid gland (e.g., Hashimoto’s).
- Secondary: Low/Inappropriate TSH; problem is in the pituitary (e.g., panhypopituitarism).

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Enlist the three primary causes of cretinism occurring during fetal life or infancy.
back:
- Congenital lack of the thyroid gland (Agenesis).
- Genetic defects in hormone-synthesizing enzymes.
- Endemic iodine deficiency (Endemic cretinism).

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: In Graves’ disease, autoimmune antibodies called [———] bind to TSH receptors and induce continual activation of the thyroid gland's intracellular signaling.
back:
• Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs)
• Act as TSH receptor agonists
• Mimic TSH action with a significantly longer duration of effect

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: A 35-year-old female presents with rapid weight loss despite increased food intake, fine hand tremors, and proptosis. Laboratory tests reveal elevated free T4 and suppressed TSH. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Graves' disease (Toxic Goiter)
• Characterized by hyperthyroidism and exophthalmos
• Driven by autoimmune TSI production

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Explain why plasma TSH levels are typically undetectable in a patient suffering from Graves' thyrotoxicosis.
back:
• High levels of free T3 and T4 exert powerful negative feedback
• Feedback occurs primarily at the anterior pituitary
• This shuts down the production and secretion of TSH

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Contrast the autoimmune nature of Graves’ disease with the etiology of a localized thyroid adenoma in the context of hyperthyroidism.
back:
• Graves': Autoimmune; involves Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI)
• Thyroid Adenoma: Non-autoimmune; results from a localized tumor secreting excess hormones independently of TSH or TSI

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Describe the physiological goal of administering high concentrations of inorganic iodides to a hyperthyroid patient for two weeks prior to a surgical thyroidectomy.
back:
• Reduces the size of the thyroid gland
• Decreases the blood supply to the tissue
• Minimizes intraoperative bleeding risk

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: The characteristic protrusion of the eyeballs seen in Graves' disease, resulting from edematous swelling of retro-orbital tissues and extraocular muscle degeneration, is known as [———].
back:
• Exophthalmos
• An autoimmune process distinct from metabolic hyperthyroidism
• Can lead to optic nerve damage or corneal ulceration

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: A patient with severe Graves' disease undergoes a Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) assessment. Describe the typical finding and its underlying metabolic cause.
back:
• Marked increase in BMR (often doubling normal)
• Caused by T3/T4 increasing mitochondria size/activity
• Results in rapid utilization of nutrients and oxygen

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Explain the specific enzymatic targets of propylthiouracil (PTU) during the treatment of hyperthyroidism.
back:
• Blocks the peroxidase enzyme in the apical membrane
• Prevents the iodination of tyrosine residues
• Inhibits the coupling of iodinated tyrosines to form T3/T4

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Contrast the fine muscle tremor observed in thyrotoxicosis with the coarse tremor of Parkinson's disease regarding its physiological origin.
back:
• Hyperthyroid Tremor: High frequency; caused by increased neuronal synapse reactivity in the spinal cord
• Parkinson’s Tremor: Coarse; results from basal ganglia pathology

category: Explain the features, pathophysiology and treatment of thyrotoxicosis/ grave’s disease
front: Identify the primary second messenger system activated within thyroid cells when Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins bind to the TSH receptor.
back:
• Adenylyl cyclase–cAMP system
• Activates protein kinases causing multiple phosphorylations
• Leads to rapid proteolysis of thyroglobulin and hormone release

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: The most common cause of hyperthyroidism, Graves' disease, is an autoimmune condition characterized by the production of antibodies known as [___] that mimic the action of TSH.
back:
• Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs)
• These antibodies bind to TSH receptors
• Induce continual activation of the cAMP system

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: A 32-year-old female presents with tremors, heat intolerance, and a 15-pound weight loss despite high caloric intake. Physical exam reveals a diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid. Identify the most likely diagnosis and the specific antibody responsible.
back:
• Diagnosis: Graves' disease (Toxic goiter)
• Responsible Antibody: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI)
• Pathophysiology: Antibody-mediated hyperplasia of the thyroid gland

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Contrast the duration of cellular stimulation provided by Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) with that of Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSIs) in Graves' disease.
back:
• TSH: Short-acting, with effects lasting approximately 1 hour
• TSIs: Prolonged action, stimulating the gland for up to 12 hours
• Result: Unregulated, excessive hormone secretion

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
coreConcept: Thyroid Adenoma vs. Graves' Disease Palpation
front: A patient presents with a palpable solitary nodule in the right thyroid lobe, while the left lobe appears atrophied. Contrast this with the typical glandular palpation findings in Graves' disease.
back:
• Solitary Nodule: Indicates a thyroid adenoma secreting localized hormone
• Graves' Disease: Typically presents with diffuse, symmetrical enlargement (2-3x normal)
• Adenoma atrophy: Excess T3/T4 suppresses TSH, causing non-tumor tissue to involute

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Describe the physiological step involving the anterior pituitary that results in suppressed TSH levels during primary hyperthyroidism.
back:
• Step: Negative feedback
• Mechanism: High circulating levels of free T3 and T4 inhibit the secretion of TSH from the anterior pituitary
• Result: Plasma TSH is often reduced to near zero

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: In patients with hyperthyroidism caused by a [___], the remainder of the thyroid gland is often inhibited because the localized tumor suppresses TSH production through negative feedback.
back:
• Thyroid Adenoma
• The tumor secretes high quantities of T3/T4
• Inhibits TSH, leaving non-neoplastic tissue non-functional

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: A hyperthyroid patient presents with significant protrusion of the eyeballs and retro-orbital edema. Explain the conceptual link between this finding and the underlying cause of Graves' disease.
back:
• Condition: Exophthalmos
• Cause: Autoimmune process involving immunoglobulins that react with extraocular muscles
• Pathophysiology: Edematous swelling of tissues and degenerative changes in muscles

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Explain the specific intracellular mechanism by which Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSIs) induce hyperthyroidism and how this impacts the diagnosis when compared to a TSH-secreting tumor.
back:
• Mechanism: TSIs bind TSH receptors, activating the adenylyl cyclase-cAMP system
• Graves': TSI is high, TSH is suppressed
• Pituitary Tumor: TSI is low/absent, TSH is inappropriately high

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Contrast the typical findings of Radioactive Iodine (RAI) uptake in a thyroid suffering from Graves' disease versus the remaining normal tissue in a patient with a toxic adenoma.
back:
• Graves': High, diffuse uptake throughout the hyperplastic gland
• Toxic Adenoma: High uptake localized to the nodule; zero/low uptake in the suppressed normal tissue
• Rationale: TSH suppression inhibits iodine trapping in normal follicles

category: Enumerate the causes of hyperthyroidism
front: Enlist the microscopic changes occurring within the thyroid follicles during the development of a toxic goiter.
back:
• Follicular cell hyperplasia and hypertrophy
• Infolding of the follicular lining into the follicles
• Change in epithelial cells from cuboidal to columnar
• Increased number of cells several-fold

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: The most accurate diagnostic test for the usual case of hyperthyroidism involves the direct measurement of plasma [___] concentration using immunoassay.
back:
• Free Thyroxine (T4)
• Free Triiodothyronine (T3) is also measured
• These represent the metabolically active, unbound forms of the hormones.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: A 35-year-old female presents with heat intolerance, weight loss, and exophthalmos. Labs reveal suppressed TSH and elevated Free T4. Identify the likely diagnosis and the specific immunoglobulin causing these findings.
back:
• Diagnosis: Graves' Disease (Hyperthyroidism)
• Pathophysiology: Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSIs)
• Mechanism: TSIs bind to TSH receptors and induce continual cAMP activation.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
coreConcept: Negative Feedback Loop in Thyroid Testing
front: Explain the physiological mechanism behind the finding of suppressed TSH levels in patients with primary hyperthyroidism.
back:
• High levels of circulating Free T3 and T4 exert powerful negative feedback
• Acts directly on the anterior pituitary gland
• Inhibits the secretion of TSH, often reducing it to nearly zero.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: Contrast the diagnostic findings of Thyroid-Stimulating Immunoglobulin (TSI) levels in patients with Graves' disease versus those with a toxic thyroid adenoma.
back:
• Graves' Disease: TSI levels are high (autoimmune etiology)
• Thyroid Adenoma: TSI levels are low or absent
• Adenomas secrete hormone independently of autoimmune stimulation.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: State the typical findings for serum TSH and Free T4 in a patient with Myxedema (severe primary hypothyroidism).
back:
• TSH: Greatly increased (due to lack of negative feedback)
• Free T4: Markedly low
• BMR: Typically reduced by 30% to 50%.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: The [___] test is used to assess thyroid status by measuring the percentage of a tracer dose that is concentrated by the gland within 24 hours.
back:
• Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Uptake
• High Uptake: Suggests hyperplastic glands (e.g., Graves')
• Low/Localized Uptake: Helps differentiate between types of goiter.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: A patient presents with extreme somnolence and a slowed heart rate. A TRH (Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone) test dose is administered, resulting in a massive rise in TSH. Locate the site of the pathology.
back:
• Pathology: Thyroid Gland (Primary Hypothyroidism)
• Reasoning: The pituitary is responsive to TRH, but the thyroid fails to produce T4 to close the feedback loop.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
coreConcept: Basal Metabolic Rate in Thyroid Disorders
front: Explain how measurement of the Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) serves as a functional thyroid test.
back:
• Thyroid hormones increase metabolic activity and O2 consumption
• Hyperthyroidism: BMR increases to +30 or +60
• Hypothyroidism: BMR decreases to -30 or -50.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: Contrast the diagnostic utility of measuring Total T4 versus Free T4 in a pregnant patient.
back:
• Total T4: Elevated due to increased Thyroxine-Binding Globulin (TBG) from estrogen
• Free T4: Remains the more accurate indicator of true thyroid status
• Free T4 is not affected by changes in transport proteins.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: Identify the screening test of choice for detecting early or subclinical thyroid dysfunction.
back:
• Serum TSH measurement
• It is highly sensitive to the slightest changes in Free T4 levels due to the logarithmic relationship in the feedback loop.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: In the routine screening for thyroid dysfunction, the single most sensitive initial laboratory parameter to measure is [___].
back:
* Serum Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
* It detects subtle changes in pituitary feedback
* Reflects the status of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: A 35-year-old female presents with weight loss, heat intolerance, and fine tremors. Laboratory results reveal elevated free T4 and suppressed TSH. Identify the most likely clinical state and its primary biochemical signature.
back:
* Primary Hyperthyroidism
* Characterized by excessive thyroid hormone production
* Suppressed TSH due to negative feedback on the anterior pituitary.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: Explain the biochemical basis for using serum Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulins (TSI) as a specific diagnostic tool for Graves' disease.
back:
* TSI are antibodies that bind/activate TSH receptors
* They mimic TSH action but last longer (12 hours)
* Leads to continuous cAMP activation and thyroid hypersecretion.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: A patient presents with low free T4. Contrast the expected TSH findings in primary hypothyroidism versus secondary (central) hypothyroidism.
back:
* Primary: High TSH (loss of negative feedback)
* Secondary: Low or inappropriately 'normal' TSH (pituitary failure)
* Localizes the site of pathology to the gland or brain.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: Discuss the utility of the TRH stimulation test in differentiating between pituitary and hypothalamic causes of hypothyroidism.
back:
* Pituitary failure: TSH fails to rise after TRH
* Hypothalamic failure: Delayed or normal TSH rise
* Distinguishes the anatomical level of secondary thyroid defects.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: The laboratory finding of a decreased Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) between -30 to -60 is most characteristic of [___].
back:
* Severe Hypothyroidism (Myxedema)
* Reflects decreased cellular metabolic activity
* Accompanied by low serum free thyroxine (T4) levels.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: A patient with a suspected thyroid adenoma shows elevated free T4 and low TSH. On a radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scan, the tracer concentrates only in a single nodule. Define the expected result of the TSI immunoassay in this case.
back:
* TSI is low or absent
* Differentiates localized autonomous nodules from autoimmune Graves' disease
* Suppresses the remainder of the gland via negative feedback.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
coreConcept: Free vs Total Thyroid Hormone Measurement
front: Describe the physiological reason why measuring 'Free' T4 is diagnostically superior to measuring 'Total' T4 in patients with chronic liver disease.
back:
* Total T4 includes protein-bound (inactive) hormone
* Liver disease alters Thyroid-Binding Globulin (TBG) levels
* Free T4 measures the metabolically active fraction unaffected by carriers.

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: Contrast the diagnostic utility of Radioactive Iodine Uptake (RAIU) in a patient with toxic goiter versus a patient with surreptitious ingestion of exogenous thyroxine.
back:
* Toxic Goiter: High RAIU (increased active synthesis)
* Exogenous Thyroxine: Low RAIU (synthesis is suppressed)
* Identifies the source of thyrotoxicosis (endogenous vs exogenous).

category: Explain the thyroid function test to investigate hypo and hyperthyroidism
front: List the classical triad of lab findings required to confirm a diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism.
back:
* Low Serum Free T4
* Elevated Serum TSH
* Decreased Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)
* Reflects direct thyroid gland failure.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: The most common autoimmune cause of hypothyroidism, characterized by progressive deterioration and fibrosis of the thyroid gland, is [___].
back:
• Hashimoto's disease (Autoimmune thyroiditis).
• Characterized by antibodies that destroy the gland rather than stimulating it.
• Results in diminished or absent thyroid hormone secretion.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: A 40-year-old female from a mountainous region presents with a massive neck mass and extreme somnolence. Soil in her area is known to be iodine-deficient. State the hormonal mechanism behind her goiter.
back:
• Lack of iodine prevents T3/T4 production.
• Absence of negative feedback leads to excessive TSH secretion.
• TSH stimulates follicles to secrete massive amounts of thyroglobulin colloid, enlarging the gland.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Explain the mechanism by which goitrogenic substances found in turnips and cabbages induce a state of hypothyroidism.
back:
• These foods contain substances with propylthiouracil-type activity.
• They block the peroxidase enzyme and coupling of iodinated tyrosines.
• This leads to TSH-stimulated enlargement of the gland despite low hormone output.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Contrast the effect of high-concentration inorganic iodides on thyroid gland size versus the effect of thiocyanate administration.
back:
• High Iodides: Paralyze colloid endocytosis and shutdown hormone release, leading to a decrease in gland size and blood supply.
• Thiocyanate: Inhibits iodide trapping, leading to high TSH and compensatory glandular overgrowth (goiter).

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Enlist four specific enzymatic or transport defects in the thyroid follicle that lead to idiopathic nontoxic colloid goiter.
back:
• Deficient iodide-trapping mechanism.
• Deficient peroxidase system (oxidation failure).
• Deficient coupling of iodinated tyrosines.
• Deiodinase enzyme deficiency (prevents iodine recycling).

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Hypothyroidism occurring during fetal life, infancy, or childhood that results in permanent mental retardation and failure of skeletal growth is known as [___].
back:
• Cretinism.
• Causes include congenital lack of the gland, genetic defects in hormone synthesis, or endemic iodine deficiency.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: A patient with a history of chromophobe pituitary tumors presents with lethargy and weight gain. Explain why the thyroid gland in this patient is usually small and inactive.
back:
• Secondary Hypothyroidism.
• Pituitary tumor destroys thyrotropes, causing TSH deficiency.
• Without TSH, the thyroid lacks the trophic signal for size maintenance and hormone synthesis.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Explain the role of the deiodinase enzyme in maintaining thyroid status and how its congenital absence causes iodine deficiency.
back:
• Deiodinase cleaves iodine from MIT and DIT during thyroglobulin digestion.
• This recycles iodine within the gland for new hormone synthesis.
• Absence causes failure of recycling, leading to a functional iodine deficiency and hypothyroidism.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Contrast the biochemical targets of Propylthiouracil (PTU) and Thiocyanate in the induction of hypothyroidism.
back:
• Thiocyanate: Competitively inhibits the sodium-iodide symporter (iodide-trapping pump).
• PTU: Blocks the peroxidase enzyme and prevents the coupling of diiodotyrosines to form T4.

category: Enlist the causes of hypothyroidism
front: Identify two common medical/physical interventions that result in the permanent destruction or loss of functional thyroid tissue.
back:
• Irradiation (e.g., treatment with radioactive iodine or external beam).
• Surgical removal (total or subtotal thyroidectomy).

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: The specific autoimmune condition where the immune system destroys thyroid tissue, leading to progressive fibrosis and reduced hormone secretion, is [___].
back:
• Hashimoto’s disease (Hashimoto’s thyroiditis)
• It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism
• Characterized by autoimmune-mediated gland destruction.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: A 45-year-old female presents with cold intolerance, fatigue, and a firm, non-tender goiter. Labs show low Free T4 and high TSH. The primary pathophysiology involves [___].
back:
• Autoimmune thyroiditis
• Immune-mediated inflammation leading to follicular cell deterioration
• Eventual replacement of functional tissue with fibrous tissue.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Explain the role of Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH) in the formation of a goiter in Hashimoto’s patients with low T4 levels.
back:
• Low T4 reduces negative feedback on the anterior pituitary
• Increased TSH secretion stimulates remaining thyroid tissue
• Causes hypertrophy and overgrowth (goiter) despite failing hormone production.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Contrast the autoimmune mechanism of Graves’ disease with that of Hashimoto’s disease regarding their effect on the TSH receptor.
back:
• Graves’: Antibodies (TSI) bind and stimulate the TSH receptor (agonism)
• Hashimoto’s: Autoimmunity leads to gland inflammation, tissue destruction, and fibrosis (antagonism/destruction).

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Identify the primary histological consequence of chronic, untreated Hashimoto’s thyroiditis on the thyroid gland architecture.
back:
• Progressive deterioration of follicles
• Infiltration by immune cells (inflammation)
• Extensive fibrosis (scarring) of the gland.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: In the progression of Hashimoto's disease, the gland initially demonstrates autoimmune [___], which precedes complete glandular fibrosis.
back:
• Thyroiditis
• This inflammation causes functional tissue loss
• Leads to diminished secretion of T3 and T4.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: A patient with Hashimoto’s disease presents with extreme somnolence and a husky voice. These clinical features are collectively referred to as [___] when hypothyroidism is severe.
back:
• Myxedema
• Result of total lack of thyroid hormone function
• Involves non-pitting edema from interstitial hyaluronic acid accumulation.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Describe the physiological feedback loop response to the thyroid tissue destruction seen in Hashimoto’s hypothyroidism.
back:
• Gland destruction → Decreased serum T3/T4
• Hypothalamus increases TRH release
• Anterior pituitary increases TSH release to compensate.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Contrast the mechanism of goiter development in Endemic Colloid Goiter versus Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.
back:
• Endemic: Lack of iodine prevents T3/T4 synthesis → High TSH → Colloid accumulation
• Hashimoto’s: Autoimmune destruction/inflammation → High TSH → Hyperplasia of remaining tissue.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Which laboratory finding is the most sensitive indicator of primary hypothyroidism caused by Hashimoto's disease?
back:
• Elevated serum TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone)
• Often paired with low Free T4 levels
• Presence of antithyroid antibodies (e.g., TPO).

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Hashimoto’s disease, a leading cause of hypothyroidism, is pathophysiologically characterized by autoimmune [___], which results in the progressive deterioration and fibrosis of the thyroid gland.
back:
• Thyroiditis (autoimmune inflammation)
• Triggered by immune-mediated attack against thyroid tissue
• Leads to diminished or absent secretion of T3 and T4 hormones.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation and Histology of Hashimoto’s
front: A 40-year-old female presents with weight gain, cold intolerance, and extreme somnolence. Laboratory tests show low free thyroxine and high TSH. A biopsy reveals lymphocytic infiltration and fibrotic replacement of secretory tissue. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
• Hashimoto Hypothyroidism (Autoimmune Thyroiditis)
• Characterized by progressive deterioration of the gland
• Most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in non-endemic areas.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Explain the role of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis feedback loop in the pathogenesis of Hashimoto-related goiter.
back:
• Glandular destruction reduces T3 and T4 levels
• Low levels remove the negative feedback on the anterior pituitary
• Excess TSH secretion occurs, which overstimulates non-inflamed thyroid portions, causing enlargement (goiter).

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: Contrast the functional effect of autoantibodies in Graves’ disease versus Hashimoto’s disease.
back:
• Graves: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) activate TSH receptors, causing hyperthyroidism/hypertrophy.
• Hashimoto: Autoantibodies mediate destruction and inflammation, causing fibrosis and hypothyroidism.

category: Explain the pathophysiology of Hashimoto hypothyroidism
front: List the physiological consequences of the total lack of thyroid hormone function seen in end-stage Hashimoto’s disease.
back:
• Fatigue and extreme somnolence (12–14 hours sleep)
• Muscular sluggishness and slowed heart rate
