• Cortisol: Lacks the carbon-18 oxygen.
• This structural difference determines mineralocorticoid vs. glucocorticoid dominance.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Identify the primary embryological and functional distinction between the adrenal cortex and the adrenal medulla.
back:
• Cortex: Mesodermal origin; secretes steroids (Corticosteroids).
• Medulla: Neural crest (ectodermal) origin; secretes catecholamines (Epinephrine/Norepinephrine).
• Functional relationship: Medulla is part of the sympathetic nervous system.

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: The zona glomerulosa is the only layer of the adrenal cortex capable of secreting significant amounts of aldosterone because it contains the enzyme [___].
back:
• Aldosterone synthase
• This layer constitutes approximately 15% of the cortex
• Regulated primarily by extracellular potassium and Angiotensin II.

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: A 35-year-old male presents with hypotension, hyperkalemia, and bronze-like skin pigmentation in the palmar creases. Identify the likely diagnosis and the hormone responsible for the skin changes.
back:
• Diagnosis: Addison’s Disease (Hypoadrenalism)
• Hormone: Excess ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic hormone)
• Mechanism: ACTH contains a melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) sequence, stimulating melanin production.

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: Describe the cellular mechanism by which Cortisol inhibits the early stages of the inflammatory process.
back:
• Stabilizes lysosomal membranes to prevent the release of proteolytic enzymes
• Decreases capillary permeability to prevent plasma leakage
• Suppresses T-lymphocyte reproduction and immune system reactivity.

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: Contrast the effects of chronic glucocorticoid excess on protein metabolism in the liver versus skeletal muscle tissue.
back:
• Liver: Increases protein synthesis and raises circulating plasma protein levels
• Skeletal Muscle: Causes significant protein catabolism and decreased transport of amino acids into cells
• Result: Severe muscle weakness and thin extremities.

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: Identify the two primary androgens secreted by the zona reticularis and their specific function in females.
back:
• Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and Androstenedione
• Promote growth of pubic and axillary hair
• Serve as precursors that are converted to testosterone or estrogens in extra-adrenal tissues.

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: In the circulation, approximately 90–95% of cortisol is transported bound to an alpha-globulin called [___], which slows its metabolic clearance.
back:
• Cortisol-binding globulin (CBG) or Transcortin
• Serves as a reservoir to prevent rapid fluctuations in free cortisol
• Leads to a long half-life of 60 to 90 minutes.

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: A patient presents with hypertension, muscle paralysis due to hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis with suppressed plasma renin. Identify the likely diagnosis.
back:
• Conn’s Syndrome (Primary Aldosteronism)
• Usually caused by a small tumor of the zona glomerulosa cells
• Treated with spironolactone (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist).

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: Detail the genomic mechanism of action for Aldosterone once it enters the principal cells of the renal collecting tubules.
back:
• Binds to cytoplasmic mineralocorticoid receptors (MR)
• Complex enters the nucleus to initiate mRNA transcription
• Synthesizes ENaC (sodium channels) and Na+/K+ ATPase pumps to increase sodium reabsorption.

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: Distinguish between the roles of the two 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) isoforms in modulating tissue glucocorticoid activity.
back:
• 11β-HSD1: Converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol (amplifies effect in liver/adipose)
• 11β-HSD2: Converts cortisol to inactive cortisone (protects mineralocorticoid receptors in kidneys/colon).

category: Name the hormones of adrenal cortex
front: Name the common precursor for all adrenocortical steroids and the rate-limiting enzyme that initiates its conversion.
back:
• Precursor: Cholesterol (mostly from LDLs)
• Enzyme: Cholesterol desmolase (P450scc)
• Result: Conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone within the mitochondria.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
coreConcept: Enzymatic Zonation of the Adrenal Cortex
front: The adrenal cortex is histologically divided into three layers, of which the [___] is the only layer capable of synthesizing aldosterone due to the presence of the enzyme aldosterone synthase.
back:
• Zona glomerulosa
• Constitutes about 15% of the cortex
• Located just underneath the fibrous capsule

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: A 45-year-old male with an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing's Disease) is expected to show significant hypertrophy in which two specific zones of the adrenal cortex?
back:
• Zona fasciculata
• Zona reticularis
• Note: The zona glomerulosa remains largely unaffected as it is controlled by Angiotensin II and Potassium.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which adrenocortical cells acquire the necessary cholesterol for steroidogenesis.
back:
• 80% is derived from plasma Low-Density Lipoproteins (LDLs)
• LDLs bind to receptors in 'coated pits'
• Internalized via endocytosis
• Cholesterol is released by lysosomes for hormonal synthesis

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Contrast the primary regulators of the zona glomerulosa with those of the zona fasciculata.
back:
• Zona Glomerulosa: Regulated by extracellular Potassium and Angiotensin II
• Zona Fasciculata: Regulated by the Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axis via ACTH

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Identify the rate-limiting step and the specific enzyme responsible for initiating steroidogenesis in all three cortical zones.
back:
• Conversion of cholesterol to Pregnenolone
• Enzyme: Cholesterol desmolase (P450scc)
• Occurs within the mitochondria

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: The middle and widest layer of the adrenal cortex, which accounts for approximately [___]% of the total cortical thickness and primarily secretes cortisol, is the zona fasciculata.
back:
• 75%
• Also secretes small amounts of androgens and estrogens

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: In a patient with severe chronic renal artery stenosis causing excessive renin-angiotensin activation, which histological change is most likely found in the adrenal gland?
back:
• Hypertrophy of the Zona Glomerulosa
• Driven by elevated Angiotensin II levels
• Leads to increased aldosterone output

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Explain why steroid hormones produced in the adrenal cortex are not stored in secretory vesicles, unlike medullary catecholamines.
back:
• Steroids are highly lipid-soluble
• Once synthesized, they immediately diffuse across the cell membrane
• Large stores of precursor cholesterol esters are kept instead of the active hormone

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
coreConcept: Hormonal Zonation of the Adrenal Cortex
front: Distinguish the hormonal output of the zona reticularis from that of the zona fasciculata.
back:
• Zona Reticularis: Primarily adrenal androgens (DHEA and androstenedione)
• Zona Fasciculata: Primarily glucocorticoids (Cortisol and corticosterone)

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Identify the three major functional categories of hormones produced by the adrenal cortex.
back:
• Mineralocorticoids (e.g., Aldosterone)
• Glucocorticoids (e.g., Cortisol)
• Androgens (e.g., DHEA)

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Aldosterone initiates its cellular action by diffusing into the principal cells of the renal tubules and binding to the [___] in the cytoplasm, which then translocates to the nucleus to stimulate mRNA synthesis.
back:
• Mineralocorticoid receptor (MR)
• Induces synthesis of apical Epithelial Sodium Channels (ENaC)
• Increases basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase pump activity
• Action is characteristically delayed (45–60 minutes) due to required protein synthesis

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
coreConcept: Functional Histology of the Adrenal Cortex
front: The adrenal cortex is histologically organized into three distinct zones, where the outermost layer, the [___], is the only zone capable of secreting significant amounts of aldosterone due to the presence of aldosterone synthase.
back:
• Zona Glomerulosa (outer): Secretes mineralocorticoids.
• Zona Fasciculata (middle): Widest zone; secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol).
• Zona Reticularis (inner): Secretes adrenal androgens (DHEA).

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Once aldosterone enters the cytoplasm of a principal cell, it binds to a specific [___] receptor to initiate its primary effects.
back:
• Mineralocorticoid Receptor (MR).
• Forms an aldosterone-receptor complex.
• The complex then translocates to the nucleus to act as a transcription factor.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: A patient with hypertension and hypokalemia is found to have a tumor in the zona glomerulosa. This condition increases the production of [___] mRNA in renal principal cells.
back:
• Messenger RNA (mRNA) related to sodium and potassium transport.
• Leads to synthesis of AIPs (Aldosterone-Induced Proteins).
• Specifically induces ENaC and Na+/K+ ATPase synthesis.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Describe the nuclear events that follow the binding of aldosterone to its cytoplasmic receptor.
back:
• Complex binds to Hormone Response Elements (HRE) on DNA.
• Activates transcription of specific genes.
• Increases formation of mRNA for transport enzymes.
• Characteristically delayed effect due to protein synthesis time-course.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Contrast the genomic effects of aldosterone with its proposed nongenomic actions regarding time-course and signaling.
back:
• Genomic: Slow (45+ minutes); involves DNA transcription and protein synthesis.
• Nongenomic: Rapid (seconds/minutes); uses second messengers like cAMP.
• Nongenomic actions occur in vascular smooth muscle and renal tubules.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Identify the three specific transport proteins/enzymes synthesized in response to aldosterone-mediated gene transcription in principal cells.
back:
• ENaC (Epithelial Sodium Channels) on the luminal membrane.
• ROMK (Potassium channels) on the luminal membrane.
• Na+/K+ ATPase pump on the basolateral membrane.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: The enzyme [___] protects the mineralocorticoid receptor from non-specific activation by cortisol by converting it to inactive cortisone.
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2).
• Localized in renal tubular epithelial cells.
• Prevents high-affinity cortisol from overwhelming the MR receptors.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: A patient consumes excessive licorice, which inhibits 11β-HSD2. Explain the resulting cellular effect on the Mineralocorticoid Receptor (MR).
back:
• Cortisol fails to convert to inactive cortisone.
• Intracellular cortisol concentration rises and activates the MR.
• Simulates aldosterone excess (sodium retention, hypertension).
• Results in Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME).

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: How does aldosterone influence the metabolic capacity of renal principal cells to support active transport?
back:
• Stimulates synthesis of mitochondrial enzymes.
• Enhances ATP production via the citric acid cycle.
• Provides the energy necessary for increased basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase activity.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Distinguish between the action of aldosterone on the luminal (apical) versus the basolateral membrane of principal cells.
back:
• Luminal: Increases sodium entry via ENaC and potassium exit via ROMK.
• Basolateral: Increases active Na+/K+ pumping (ATPase).
• Integrated effect: Net sodium reabsorption into the interstitium.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Identify the primary physiological reason for the 45-60 minute 'latent period' observed after aldosterone administration.
back:
• Dependent on de novo protein synthesis.
• Time required for mRNA transcription in the nucleus.
• Time required for translation at ribosomes and membrane insertion.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Upon entering the cytoplasm of a renal tubular cell, aldosterone binds specifically to the [___] receptor.
back:
• Mineralocorticoid Receptor (MR)
• Forms a hormone-receptor complex
• Translocates into the nucleus to act as a transcription factor

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: A patient with excessive licorice ingestion presents with hypertension and hypokalemia. Explain the failure of the 'gate-keeper' mechanism in this context.
back:
• Glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits 11β-HSD2
• Prevents conversion of cortisol to inactive cortisone
• High cortisol levels overwhelm and activate mineralocorticoid receptors

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Explain the biological sequence of the genomic effect of aldosterone after nuclear translocation occurs.
back:
• Binds to DNA hormone response elements
• Stimulates mRNA transcription
• Promotes translation of specific transport proteins and enzymes

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Contrast the physiological lag time of aldosterone action with that of vasopressin (ADH).
back:
• Aldosterone: Delayed (45–60 mins) due to required gene transcription and protein synthesis
• Vasopressin: Rapid (5–10 mins) via cAMP-mediated insertion of pre-formed aquaporins

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Identify the three primary proteins/enzymes upregulated by aldosterone to facilitate sodium reabsorption.
back:
• Na+-K+ ATPase (basolateral pump)
• Epithelial Sodium Channels (ENaC, luminal)
• Renal Outer Medullary Potassium channels (ROMK, luminal)

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: The basolateral membrane pump strengthened by aldosterone is the [___].
back:
• Sodium-Potassium Adenosine Triphosphatase (Na+-K+ ATPase)
• Pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ into the cell
• Maintains the electrochemical gradient for luminal Na+ entry

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: A patient with Conn's syndrome (Primary Aldosteronism) develops muscle paralysis. Relate the cellular mechanism of aldosterone to this finding.
back:
• Excessive K+ secretion via ROMK and Na+-K+ pump activity
• Severe extracellular hypokalemia
• Hyperpolarizes nerve/muscle membranes, preventing normal action potential transmission

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Explain how aldosterone facilitates the entry of sodium from the tubular lumen into the principal cell.
back:
• Upregulates and inserts ENaC (Epithelial Sodium Channels) into the luminal membrane
• Sodium moves down its concentration gradient into the cell via facilitated diffusion

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Distinguish between the genomic and nongenomic cellular actions of aldosterone.
back:
• Genomic: Lag phase, requires DNA transcription and protein synthesis
• Nongenomic: Seconds to minutes, involves second messengers (cAMP/PIP2), structures not yet fully defined

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Specify the lipid solubility of aldosterone and its consequence for cellular entry.
back:
• Highly lipid-soluble steroid hormone
• Readily diffuses across the phospholipid bilayer of cell membranes
• Requires no membrane-bound receptor for initial cell entry

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: The thin, outermost layer of the adrenal cortex, which constitutes approximately 15% of the gland and is the exclusive site of aldosterone production, is the [___].
back:
• Zona glomerulosa.
• Contains the enzyme aldosterone synthase.
• Regulated primarily by Angiotensin II and extracellular potassium levels.
• Relatively independent of ACTH control.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: A patient presents with hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and hypotension. Biopsy shows atrophy specific to the subcapsular cortical layer. Identify the deficient hormone and the layer involved.
back:
• Hormone: Aldosterone (mineralocorticoid).
• Layer: Zona glomerulosa.
• Pathophysiology: Loss of this zone prevents sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the renal tubules, leading to circulatory collapse.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Explain the cellular mechanism through which the adrenal cortex acquires the necessary precursor for all steroid hormone synthesis.
back:
• LDL Uptake: 80% of cholesterol is derived from plasma low-density lipoproteins.
• Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis: LDLs bind to coated pits and are internalized.
• Lysosomal Release: Enzymes liberate free cholesterol from the endosomes for mitochondrial transport.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Contrast the structural and regulatory characteristics of the Zona Glomerulosa with the Zona Fasciculata.
back:
• Zona Glomerulosa: Thin outer layer; secretes mineralocorticoids; regulated by Angiotensin II/K+.
• Zona Fasciculata: Thick middle layer (75%); secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol); regulated by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis via ACTH.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Identify the rate-limiting enzymatic step in the synthesis of all adrenocortical hormones and its intracellular location.
back:
• Conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone.
• Enzyme: Cholesterol desmolase (P450scc).
• Location: Mitochondria.
• Regulation: Step is stimulated by both ACTH and Angiotensin II.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: The innermost layer of the adrenal cortex, which secretes dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and androstenedione, is the [___].
back:
• Zona reticularis.
• Secretes adrenal androgens and small amounts of estrogens.
• Regulated by ACTH and potentially cortical androgen-stimulating hormone.
• Cells are arranged in branching cords.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: A 4-year-old boy presents with premature development of male sexual organs and rapid skeletal growth. In this 'adrenogenital syndrome,' the pathology involves hyperfunction of which specific cortical zones?
back:
• Zona reticularis and Zona fasciculata.
• These zones secrete adrenal androgens (DHEA/androstenedione).
• Overproduction causes intense masculinizing effects due to excessive protein deposition and androgenic activity.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Describe the trophic influence of ACTH on the anatomical structure of the adrenal cortex during chronic stress.
back:
• Hypertrophy and Proliferation: Causes growth of the Zona fasciculata and Zona reticularis.
• LDL Receptor Upregulation: Increases the number of receptors for cholesterol uptake.
• Steroidogenic Enzyme Activation: Enhances conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone.

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Contrast the embryological origins and functional control of the adrenal cortex versus the adrenal medulla.
back:
• Cortex: Derived from mesoderm; controlled by hormonal/ionic signals (ACTH, Ang II, K+).
• Medulla: Derived from neural crest cells (ectoderm); controlled by direct preganglionic sympathetic neural stimulation (acetylcholine).

category: Explain the physiological anatomy of adrenal cortex
front: Specify the primary enzyme found in the Zona Glomerulosa that is absent in the Zona Fasciculata, determining its unique secretory product.
back:
• Aldosterone synthase (P450c11AS).
• This enzyme catalyzes the final steps of aldosterone synthesis.
• Its absence in deeper zones prevents mineralocorticoid production outside the glomerulosa.

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: The specific cell type in the renal collecting tubules responsible for aldosterone-mediated sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion is the [___].
back:
• Principal cells
  • Aldosterone increases ENaC (sodium channels) and ROMK (potassium channels) in these cells
  • Stimulates Na+-K+ ATPase activity on the basolateral membrane

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: A 45-year-old male with a suspected adrenal tumor presents with hypertension and episodic muscle paralysis. The most likely electrolyte abnormality explaining the paralysis is [___].
back:
• Hypokalemia
  • Excess aldosterone increases renal K+ secretion
  • Low ECF potassium hyperpolarizes muscle membranes, preventing normal action potential transmission

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Explain the molecular sequence of events initiated by aldosterone binding to the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR).
back:
• Aldosterone diffuses across the cell membrane to bind cytoplasmic MR
  • The MR-hormone complex migrates to the nucleus
  • Induces DNA transcription to mRNA
  • Promotes synthesis of transport proteins (ENaC) and enzymes (Na+-K+ ATPase)

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Contrast the effect of aldosterone on the principal cells versus the intercalated cells of the cortical collecting tubule.
back:
• Principal cells: Stimulates Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion
  • Intercalated cells: Stimulates H+ secretion via H+-ATPase
  • Result: Excess aldosterone leads to hypernatremia and metabolic alkalosis

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Describe the physiological mechanism behind "aldosterone escape."
back:
• Chronic excess aldosterone causes initial ECF volume expansion
  • Rising arterial pressure triggers pressure natriuresis and diuresis
  • Sodium and water excretion return to normal despite high hormone levels
  • Hypertension remains, but edema is prevented

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: The primary enzyme responsible for converting active cortisol to inactive cortisone in renal epithelial cells to prevent illicit MR activation is [___].
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2)
  • Protects mineralocorticoid receptors from high circulating cortisol
  • Deficiency causes Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME)

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency presents with hypotension and intense salt cravings. Explain the underlying renal defect causing this presentation.
back:
• Mineralocorticoid deficiency (Addison's)
  • Failure to reabsorb Na+ leads to "sodium wasting"
  • Results in ECF dehydration, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia
  • Can progress to circulatory shock

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: How does aldosterone influence the composition of sweat and salivary gland secretions?
back:
• Stimulates Na+ and Cl- reabsorption from the excretory ducts
  • Stimulates K+ and HCO3- secretion into the ducts
  • Primary purpose: Conservation of body salt in hot environments

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Distinguish between the effects of hyperkalemia and angiotensin II on aldosterone secretion.
back:
• Both are potent direct stimulators of the zona glomerulosa
  • Hyperkalemia: Direct depolarization of cell membranes
  • Angiotensin II: Stimulates phospholipase C second messenger system
  • Both increase conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Identify the specific enzyme exclusively expressed in the zona glomerulosa that allows for the synthesis of aldosterone.
back:
• Aldosterone synthase
  • Absent in the zona fasciculata and reticularis
  • Enables the final step of mineralocorticoid production from corticosterone

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Aldosterone primarily exerts its mineralocorticoid effects on the [___] cells of the renal late distal and collecting tubules.
back:
• Principal cells
• Stimulates sodium (Na+) reabsorption
• Promotes potassium (K+) secretion into the tubular lumen

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: A 45-year-old male presents with persistent hypertension and profound muscle weakness. Lab results reveal a plasma potassium of 2.2 mEq/L and high aldosterone levels. Identify the likely diagnosis and the associated acid-base disturbance.
back:
• Conn's Syndrome (Primary Aldosteronism)
• Metabolic Alkalosis
• Caused by increased hydrogen (H+) secretion in the intercalated cells

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Explain the cellular mechanism of aldosterone action once it binds to its cytoplasmic mineralocorticoid receptor (MR).
back:
• Complex diffuses into the nucleus to induce DNA transcription
• Forms mRNA for transport proteins
• Synthesizes ENaC, ROMK, and Na+-K+ ATPase pump proteins

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Contrast the physiological state of the heart and ECF volume in a patient with untreated Addison’s disease versus a patient with an aldosterone-secreting tumor.
back:
• Addison’s: Low ECF volume, reduced cardiac output, and circulatory shock
• Tumor: Increased ECF volume and hypertension
• Both involve cardiac risk (arrhythmia) due to potassium imbalances

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Describe how Spironolactone manages the effects of excessive mineralocorticoid activity in the renal tubules.
back:
• Acts as a pharmacological antagonist
• Competes with aldosterone for the Mineralocorticoid Receptor (MR)
• Blocks the synthesis of Na+/K+ transport proteins

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: The physiological "escape" from further sodium retention and edema during chronic aldosterone excess is primarily mediated by the mechanism of [___].
back:
• Pressure Natriuresis (and Diuresis)
• Rising arterial pressure increases renal excretion of sodium/water
• Returns sodium balance to normal despite continued high aldosterone

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: An individual consumes large quantities of black licorice containing glycyrrhetinic acid. Predict the effect on renal Mineralocorticoid Receptor (MR) activation and the clinical name for this state.
back:
• Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME)
• Inhibits 11̢-HSD2 enzyme
• Prevents cortisol-to-cortisone conversion, allowing cortisol to activate MR

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Explain the role of mineralocorticoids in the function of extra-renal secretory structures like sweat and salivary glands.
back:
• Increases sodium chloride reabsorption in excretory ducts
• Increases potassium and bicarbonate secretion
• Essential for conserving body salt in hot environments

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Contrast the metabolic loop effect of aldosterone deficiency versus excess on plasma potassium levels and the associated risk to the heart.
back:
• Deficiency: Hyperkalemia; risk of cardiac toxicity and heart failure
• Excess: Hypokalemia; risk of muscle paralysis and nerve inexcitability

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Identify the two most potent physiological factors that directly stimulate the zona glomerulosa to secrete aldosterone.
back:
• Increased extracellular potassium (K+) concentration
• Increased Angiotensin II levels (via renin-angiotensin system)
• ACTH plays only a permissive role

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: The outermost layer of the adrenal cortex, which exclusively contains aldosterone synthase to produce mineralocorticoids, is the [___].
back: • Zona glomerulosa

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: A patient with an adrenal adenoma presents with hypertension, a plasma potassium of 2.2 mEq/L, and severe muscle weakness. This weakness results from [___].
back:
• Hypokalemia-induced hypernegativity of intracellular potential
• Altered electrical excitability of nerve and muscle fiber membranes

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Explain the role of the Na+-K+ ATPase pump in the cellular mechanism of aldosterone action within the renal principal cells.
back:
• Synthesized and activated at the basolateral membrane
• Pumps sodium into the interstitial fluid
• Pumps potassium into the cell to maintain the gradient for luminal secretion

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Contrast the long-term effect of aldosterone on sodium concentration versus its effect on extracellular fluid (ECF) volume.
back:
• Na+ Concentration: Minimal change (thirst and ADH balance the osmolarity)
• ECF Volume: Increases 5% to 15% (initiates pressure natriuresis)

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Identify the two factors that serve as the most potent direct stimuli for aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa.
back:
• Increased extracellular potassium ion concentration
• Increased Angiotensin II levels

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: The renal enzyme that prevents cortisol from saturating mineralocorticoid receptors by converting it to inactive cortisone is [___].
back: • 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2)

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: A patient presents with hypotension, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis following total adrenal destruction. Explain the primary cause of the acidosis in this condition.
back:
• Failure of aldosterone-mediated H+ secretion
• Reduced K+-H+ exchange in the intercalated cells of the collecting tubules

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Explain how the 'aldosterone escape' mechanism prevents the development of generalized edema in Conn's syndrome.
back:
• Volume expansion raises arterial pressure
• Triggers 'pressure natriuresis' and 'pressure diuresis'
• Returns renal Na+ and water output to normal levels despite high hormone levels

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Contrast the genomic and non-genomic actions of aldosterone regarding their signaling pathways and latency.
back:
• Genomic: Binds cytoplasmic MR; requires 45–60 minutes for protein synthesis
• Non-genomic: Uses cell membrane receptors; activates cAMP or phosphatidylinositol within seconds

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Enumerate the three major non-renal sites where aldosterone significantly enhances sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.
back:
• Sweat glands
• Salivary glands
• Intestinal epithelial cells (especially the colon)

category: Explain the effects of mineralocorticoid hormone
front: Aldosterone, the primary mineralocorticoid, regulates electrolyte balance by stimulating the renal reabsorption of sodium and the simultaneous secretion of [___] ions into the tubular lumen.
back: - Potassium (K+) and Hydrogen (H+) ions - Site: Principal and intercalated cells of the collecting tubules - Effect: Increases extracellular fluid volume and maintains arterial pressure

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: The primary electrolyte stimulus that directly triggers the release of aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex is an increase in extracellular [___] concentration.
back: • Potassium (K+) ions (most potent direct stimulus). • Angiotensin II (via renin-angiotensin system). • ACTH (essential permissive role). • Atrial Natriuretic Peptide and high sodium (inhibitory regulators).

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Cortisol stimulates the formation of carbohydrates from proteins and other substances in the liver, a metabolic process known as [___].
back:
● Gluconeogenesis
● Increases liver enzymes for glucose synthesis
● Mobilizes amino acids from extrahepatic tissues (muscle)
● Antagonizes insulin's inhibitory effects in the liver

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: A patient with Cushing’s syndrome presents with a "buffalo hump" and "moon face" despite limb muscle wasting. Identify the underlying metabolic shift.
back:
● Lipid Redistribution
● Cortisol mobilizes fatty acids from adipose tissue in extremities
● Excess fat is deposited in the thoracic and head regions
● Accompanied by increased cellular fat oxidation for energy

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Explain the primary cellular mechanism by which cortisol prevents the release of proteolytic enzymes during the early stages of inflammation.
back:
● Lysosomal Membrane Stabilization
● Toughens lysosomal membranes to prevent rupture
● Decreases release of inflammatory chemicals from damaged cells
● Reduces capillary permeability to prevent plasma leakage

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Contrast the effects of cortisol on protein stores in hepatic versus extrahepatic tissues.
back:
● Extrahepatic: Causes protein depletion (catabolism and decreased synthesis)
● Hepatic: Increases protein synthesis and plasma protein production
● Facilitates amino acid transport specifically into liver cells

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Identify the characteristic changes in circulating blood cell counts observed in a patient with excessive cortisol secretion.
back:
● Increases: Red Blood Cells (Polycythemia)
● Decreases: Lymphocytes and Eosinophils
● Atrophies lymphoid tissue
● Decreases T-cell and antibody production

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: In tissues like the liver and brain, the isoform [___] converts inactive cortisone into active cortisol to amplify glucocorticoid effects.
back:
● 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β-HSD1)
● Acts as an intracellular gatekeeper of cortisol action
● 11β-HSD2 performs the opposite (deactivation) in the kidneys

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: A 40-year-old female with an ACTH-secreting tumor presents with hyperglycemia (200 mg/dl) that is resistant to normal insulin doses. Name this clinical finding.
back:
● Adrenal Diabetes
● Caused by high rates of gluconeogenesis
● Cortisol inhibits GLUT-4 translocation in skeletal muscle
● Leads to severe insulin resistance

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Describe the mechanism by which cortisol prevents the lethal effects of anaphylactic shock.
back:
● Suppression of Allergic Response
● Blocks the inflammatory reaction triggered by antigen-antibody binding
● Reduces the release of inflammatory products
● Does not affect the basic allergic reaction itself

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Contrast how cortisol and aldosterone interact with the Mineralocorticoid Receptor (MR) in the renal tubules.
back:
● Both bind MR with high affinity
● 11β-HSD2 converts cortisol to inactive cortisone in the kidney
● This protects MR from cortisol, allowing specific aldosterone action

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: List two significant non-metabolic adverse effects of chronic high cortisol on the skeletal system and gastrointestinal tract.
back:
● Bone: Decreased osteoblastic activity and matrix formation (Osteoporosis)
● GI Tract: Increased gastric acid secretion (Risk of Peptic Ulcers)

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: The most potent direct stimulator of aldosterone secretion by the zona glomerulosa is an increase in extracellular [___] concentration.
back:
• Potassium ion ([K+]) concentration.
 • Even small increases in [K+] can cause a several-fold increase in secretion.
 • Acts directly on the adrenal cells to trigger release.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: A 45-year-old male presents with persistent hypertension, muscle weakness, and a plasma potassium of 2.1 mEq/L. A CT scan reveals a small adrenal adenoma. Identify the likely condition and the affected zone.
back:
• Conn’s Syndrome (Primary Aldosteronism).
 • Affected Zone: Zona Glomerulosa.
 • Pathophysiology: Excess aldosterone causes Na+ retention, K+ wasting, and hypertension.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Describe the physiological sequence by which a decrease in renal blood flow leads to increased aldosterone secretion.
back:
• Renin release from kidneys converts Angiotensinogen to Angiotensin I.
 • ACE converts Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II.
 • Angiotensin II stimulates zona glomerulosa receptors to secrete aldosterone.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Contrast the regulatory roles of Angiotensin II and ACTH in the secretion of aldosterone.
back:
• Angiotensin II: Primary rate-controller; responds to volume and electrolyte shifts.
 • ACTH: Permissive role; required for secretion but has little effect on the rate of output in most physiological states.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Specify the role of Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) in the regulation of aldosterone dynamics.
back:
• Inhibitory effect: ANP decreases aldosterone secretion.
 • Trigger: Released when cardiac atria are stretched by volume expansion.
 • Result: Promotes natriuresis by reducing Na+ reabsorption.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: The zona glomerulosa is the only layer of the adrenal cortex capable of producing aldosterone because it uniquely contains the enzyme [___].
back:
• Aldosterone synthase.
 • This enzyme converts corticosterone into aldosterone.
 • Controlled primarily by Angiotensin II and Potassium.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: A patient with high aldosterone levels shows initial sodium retention, yet edema is absent and sodium excretion eventually returns to normal despite high hormone levels. Name this phenomenon.
back:
• Aldosterone Escape.
 • Mechanism: Increased arterial pressure triggers pressure natriuresis and diuresis.
 • Outcome: Excess sodium and water are excreted despite continued mineralocorticoid action.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Explain the intracellular mechanism by which aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the renal principal cells.
back:
• Binds cytoplasmic mineralocorticoid receptor (MR).
 • Induces mRNA transcription and protein synthesis.
 • Synthesizes Na+/K+ ATPase (basolateral) and ENaC channels (luminal).

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Contrast the primary regulators of the Zona Glomerulosa with those of the Zona Fasciculata.
back:
• Zona Glomerulosa: Regulated by [K+] and Angiotensin II (electrolyte/volume focus).
 • Zona Fasciculata: Regulated by ACTH (metabolic/stress focus).
 • These zones operate largely independently of each other.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Identify the direct effect of plasma sodium concentration on aldosterone secretion.
back:
• Minor effect compared to K+ or Angiotensin II.
 • Low sodium ([Na+]) slightly stimulates secretion.
 • High sodium slightly inhibits secretion.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Cortisol increases the rate of [___] by the liver by 6 to 10-fold through the induction of hepatic enzymes and mobilization of substrates from extrahepatic tissues.
back:
• Gluconeogenesis
• It increases enzymes required to convert amino acids to glucose
• It antagonizes insulin's inhibitory effects on glucose production.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: A patient presents with a rounded "moon face," a buffalo-like torso, and purple striae on the abdomen. This specific pattern of fat redistribution is a hallmark of [___].
back:
• Cushing’s Syndrome (Hypercortisolism)
• Caused by excess fat deposition in the chest and head regions
• Associated with increased food intake and altered lipid mobilization.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Explain the mechanism by which cortisol prevents the release of damaging proteolytic enzymes during the early stages of tissue inflammation.
back:
• It stabilizes lysosomal membranes
• This makes it much more difficult for intracellular lysosomes to rupture
• Consequently, fewer inflammatory enzymes are released into the tissues.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Contrast the functions of the 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11̢̢-HSD) isoforms 1 and 2 regarding cortisol activity.
back:
• 11̢̢-HSD1 (Liver/Muscle): Converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol, amplifying effects.
• 11̢̢-HSD2 (Kidneys/Colon): Converts active cortisol to inactive cortisone, protecting mineralocorticoid receptors.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: How does cortisol's effect on protein stores in skeletal muscle differ from its effect on protein stores in the liver?
back:
• Skeletal Muscle: Decreases protein stores through increased catabolism and decreased synthesis.
• Liver: Increases protein synthesis and increases plasma proteins released into the blood.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: A high-yield hematological finding used to diagnose overproduction of cortisol is the significant reduction in the blood count of [___] and [___].
back:
• Eosinophils
• Lymphocytes (Lymphocytopenia)
• Cortisol also simultaneously increases red blood cell production (polycythemia).

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: A 50-year-old patient with hypercortisolism exhibits blood glucose levels 50% above normal and a poor response to insulin. This condition is termed [___].
back:
• Adrenal Diabetes
• Results from increased gluconeogenesis and decreased glucose utilization
• Characterized by insulin resistance in peripheral tissues like skeletal muscle.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Describe how cortisol facilitates the "shift" from carbohydrate to fat utilization during periods of long-term starvation or stress.
back:
• Mobilizes fatty acids from adipose tissue to increase plasma concentration
• Enhances the cellular oxidation of fatty acids
• Decreases glucose transport into fat cells by reducing alpha-glycerophosphate.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Contrast the effect of cortisol on amino acid transport in extrahepatic cells versus hepatic cells.
back:
• Extrahepatic (Muscle): Depresses amino acid transport, leading to protein wasting.
• Hepatic (Liver): Enhances amino acid transport, facilitating gluconeogenesis and protein synthesis.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Identify the primary second messenger system activated within adrenocortical cells when ACTH stimulates the production of cortisol.
back:
• Cyclic Adenosine Monophosphate (cAMP)
• cAMP activates protein kinase A
• This catalyzes the rate-limiting step: converting cholesterol to pregnenolone.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: The electrolyte [___] is the most potent direct stimulator of aldosterone secretion by the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex.
back:
Potassium ($K^+$).

*   Small percentage increases in extracellular $K^+$ can cause severalfold increases in aldosterone.
*   It acts directly on the glandular cells to stimulate secretion.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: A patient with renal artery stenosis presents with secondary hypertension and hypokalemia. The excess aldosterone in this case is primarily driven by the [___] system.
back:
Renin-Angiotensin System.

*   Decreased blood flow to kidneys triggers renin release.
*   Angiotensin II is formed, which is a major stimulator of aldosterone production.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Explain how Angiotensin II influences the biosynthetic pathway of aldosterone within the adrenal mitochondria.
back:
It stimulates the rate-limiting step.

*   Increases the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone.
*   Activates enzymes in all three zones, but aldosterone is only formed in the zona glomerulosa.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Contrast the regulatory sensitivity of aldosterone secretion to changes in extracellular potassium versus extracellular sodium.
back:
Potassium is far more potent.

*   Potassium: A small percentage increase causes a massive (several hundred percent) rise in secretion.
*   Sodium: A 10-20% decrease is required to produce a minor (50%) increase in secretion.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Which anterior pituitary hormone acts as a 'permissive' factor for aldosterone secretion rather than a primary rate-controller?
back:
Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH).

*   Necessary for any aldosterone to be secreted.
*   However, it has little effect in controlling the daily rate of secretion in most conditions.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: In response to volume expansion and atrial stretch, aldosterone secretion is inhibited by the hormone [___].
back:
Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP).

*   Secreted by specific cells in the cardiac atria.
*   Directly decreases aldosterone secretion to promote sodium and water loss (natriuresis).

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: A patient with primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s Syndrome) shows high blood pressure but undetectable renin levels. Explain this lab finding.
back:
Negative Feedback Inhibition.

*   Excessive aldosterone expands extracellular fluid volume and increases arterial pressure.
*   The elevated pressure and volume suppress the kidney's release of renin.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Explain the 'aldosterone escape' mechanism and its role in regulating renal sodium excretion during chronic hormone excess.
back:
Pressure Natriuresis Override.

*   Aldosterone initially causes sodium/water retention.
*   ECF volume expansion raises arterial pressure.
*   Increased pressure forces kidneys to excrete sodium/water, returning balance to normal despite high aldosterone.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Contrast the primary hormonal control of the zona glomerulosa with that of the zona fasciculata.
back:
Regulator Specificity.

*   Zona Glomerulosa: Controlled by Potassium and Angiotensin II (Aldosterone).
*   Zona Fasciculata: Controlled by ACTH via the hypothalamic-pituitary axis (Cortisol).

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Identify the specific enzyme, found only in the zona glomerulosa, that is essential for the final step of aldosterone synthesis.
back:
Aldosterone Synthase.

*   Located only in the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex.
*   Its presence explains why aldosterone is not produced in deeper layers.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Due to its lipid-soluble nature, aldosterone enters target cells and binds with high specificity to the cytoplasmic [___].
back:
• Mineralocorticoid Receptor (MR).
• Forms a complex that translocates into the nucleus.
• Targets renal tubular epithelial cells.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: A 40-year-old male with hypertension and severe hypokalemia is found to have a small tumor in the zona glomerulosa. Explain the cellular mechanism driving his symptoms.
back:
• Excess aldosterone over-activates Mineralocorticoid Receptors.
• Genomic induction of Na+-K+ ATPase and luminal ENaC channels.
• Causes excessive sodium reabsorption and potassium wasting.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Explain the genomic sequence initiated once the activated aldosterone-receptor complex binds to DNA.
back:
• Activation of specific DNA sequences (hormone response elements).
• Induction of mRNA transcription.
• Translation of specific transport and enzymatic proteins at the ribosomes.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: A patient has a mutation making their Mineralocorticoid Receptors (MR) unresponsive. Contrast the cellular findings in this patient with those seen in Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME).
back:
• MR Unresponsive: Failure of protein synthesis; chronic sodium wasting/hyperkalemia.
• AME: Cortisol (not inactivated by 11β-HSD2) saturates MR; causes extreme sodium retention despite low aldosterone.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Detail the primary reason for the characteristic 45-minute latent period before aldosterone increases sodium transport.
back:
• Dependence on the genomic pathway.
• Time required for nuclear transcription of mRNA.
• Lag time for translation and insertion of new proteins into the membrane.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption by inducing the synthesis of [___] at the basolateral membrane.
back:
• Na+-K+ ATPase (Sodium-Potassium Pump).
• Provides the energy/gradient for active sodium transport.
• Increases intracellular potassium concentration.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: A patient with refractory hypertension is started on Amiloride. Describe the specific molecular target of this drug in the context of aldosterone action.
back:
• Blocks Epithelial Sodium Channels (ENaC).
• Located on the luminal (apical) membrane of principal cells.
• Directly inhibits the primary sodium entry pathway induced by aldosterone.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Explain how aldosterone facilitates the movement of potassium from the renal interstitial fluid into the tubular lumen.
back:
• Basolateral: Na+-K+ ATPase actively pumps K+ into the cell.
• Luminal: Induction of ROMK (Potassium) channels.
• High intracellular [K+] drives diffusion through ROMK into the urine.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Contrast the 'aldosterone escape' mechanism with the cellular actions that occur during the first 24 hours of aldosterone excess.
back:
• First 24 Hours: Active genomic signaling; maximum protein synthesis and Na+ retention.
• Escape: Systemic pressure natriuresis overrides MR-mediated Na+ absorption; Na+ output returns to normal.

category: Explain the cellular mechanism of Aldosterone action
front: Identify the chemical nature and metabolic precursor of aldosterone.
back:
• Steroid hormone.
• Synthesized from cholesterol.
• Rate-limited by the conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Cortisol significantly enhances blood glucose levels by stimulating [___], a process that increases the rate of carbohydrate formation from proteins and other substances by 6- to 10-fold.
back:
● Gluconeogenesis
● Increases liver enzymes for amino acid conversion
● Mobilizes amino acids from extrahepatic tissues (mainly muscle)
● Antagonizes insulin's inhibitory effects on glucose production.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: A patient undergoing a kidney transplant is administered high doses of synthetic glucocorticoids to prevent graft rejection. This pharmacological effect is primarily due to cortisol's ability to suppress [___].
back:
● T-lymphocyte reproduction
● Lymphoid tissue mass (atrophy)
● Antibody production
● Inflammatory cytokine release (e.g., IL-1).

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which excessive cortisol levels produce a 'diabetogenic' effect leading to insulin resistance.
back:
● Decreases translocation of GLUT 4 transporters to the cell membrane
● Primarily affects skeletal muscle and adipose tissue
● Elevated plasma free fatty acids (from lipolysis) further impair insulin sensitivity.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Contrast the physiological roles of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11β-HSD) isoform 1 versus isoform 2.
back:
● 11β-HSD1: Converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol (amplifies action in liver/fat)
● 11β-HSD2: Converts active cortisol to inactive cortisone (protects mineralocorticoid receptors in kidneys).

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Identify the primary mechanism by which cortisol prevents the initial onset of inflammation in damaged tissues.
back:
● Lysosomal membrane stabilization
● Prevents rupture and release of proteolytic enzymes
● Decreases capillary permeability
● Inhibits phospholipase A2 (reducing prostaglandins/leukotrienes).

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: While cortisol depletes protein stores in extrahepatic tissues, it uniquely increases the synthesis and storage of proteins in the [___].
back:
● Liver
● Enhances hepatic amino acid transport
● Increases liver enzymes for protein synthesis and deamination
● Increases production of plasma proteins.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: A laboratory report for a patient with suspected Cushing’s Syndrome shows a significantly low eosinophil count. Explain the relationship between cortisol and blood cell distribution.
back:
● Causes lymphocytopenia and eosinopenia
● Increases red blood cell production (polycythemia)
● Begins within minutes to hours after cortisol elevation.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Explain why the metabolic effects of cortisol have a latent period of 45–60 minutes before they become physiologically evident.
back:
● Cortisol is lipid-soluble and binds to intracellular receptors
● Hormone-receptor complex must enter the nucleus
● Activates DNA transcription to mRNA
● Requires time for ribosomal translation and protein synthesis.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: Contrast the effects of cortisol on fat metabolism in the limbs versus the torso.
back:
● Limbs: Promotes lipolysis and mobilization of fatty acids from adipose tissue
● Torso/Face: Promotes fat deposition (mechanism unclear), leading to 'Buffalo torso' and 'Moon face'.

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
front: The precursor protein from which both ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH) are derived is [___].
back:
● Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
● Clinically explains hyperpigmentation in Addison’s disease
● Processed by tissue-specific prohormone convertases.

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: In the renal tubules, the enzyme [___] converts active cortisol into inactive cortisone to prevent inappropriate activation of mineralocorticoid receptors.
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2)
• It acts as a pre-receptor metabolic barrier
• Ensures receptor specificity for aldosterone

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: A 40-year-old male presents with hypertension and hypokalemia but low plasma aldosterone. He consumes large amounts of natural licorice. Identify the enzymatic target inhibited by glycyrrhetinic acid.
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2)
• Inhibition allows cortisol to bind mineralocorticoid receptors
• Results in Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME) syndrome

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Explain the role of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β-HSD1) in tissues like the liver and adipose tissue.
back:
• Converts inactive cortisone back to active cortisol
• Amplifies local glucocorticoid signaling
• Contributes to insulin resistance in obesity

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Contrast the physiological direction of reaction and primary tissue distribution of 11β-HSD1 versus 11β-HSD2.
back:
• 11β-HSD1: Reductase (Cortisone → Cortisol); Liver and Adipose
• 11β-HSD2: Dehydrogenase (Cortisol → Cortisone); Kidney and Colon
• 11β-HSD1 amplifies, while 11β-HSD2 inactivates

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: State why high plasma cortisol does not typically cause mineralocorticoid effects in the kidney despite its high affinity for the mineralocorticoid receptor.
back:
• Rapid inactivation by local 11β-HSD2
• Cortisol is converted to inactive cortisone
• Protects receptors from being overwhelmed by cortisol

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Besides the kidneys, 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 is also expressed in the [___], [___], and placenta.
back:
• Colon
• Salivary glands
• Sweat glands

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: A child is diagnosed with a genetic deficiency of 11β-HSD2. Describe the resulting effect on sodium balance and blood pressure.
back:
• Increased renal sodium reabsorption
• Resultant hypertension and hypokalemia
• Caused by cortisol mimicking aldosterone at the receptor level

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Describe the protective mechanism of the placental 11β-HSD2 isoform regarding fetal development.
back:
• Inactivates maternal cortisol into cortisone
• Prevents excessive glucocorticoids from reaching the fetus
• Protects against premature organ maturation and growth restriction

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Contrast the metabolic implications of 11β-HSD1 upregulation in adipose tissue with its downregulation in the brain.
back:
• Adipose upregulation: Promotes visceral obesity and diabetes
• Brain downregulation: Associated with protection against age-related cognitive decline
• Governs local tissue glucocorticoid "tone"

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Name the two specific steroid molecules whose interconversion is regulated by 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoforms.
back:
• Active Cortisol
• Inactive Cortisone

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: The interconversion of glucocorticoids is mediated by two enzymes: [___] converts inactive cortisone to active cortisol in the liver, while [___] inactivates cortisol to cortisone in the kidneys.
back:
• **11β-HSD1** and **11β-HSD2**
• 11β-HSD1: Activates cortisone into cortisol to amplify effects.
• 11β-HSD2: Inactivates cortisol to cortisone to protect mineralocorticoid receptors from cross-activation.
• 11β-HSD2 inhibition (e.g., by licorice) causes Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess.

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: The enzyme isoform responsible for converting active cortisol into inactive cortisone in renal tubular cells is [___].
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11β-HSD2)
• Function: Protects mineralocorticoid receptors from cortisol
• Location: Kidney, colon, sweat glands

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: A patient with a genetic mutation in the 11β-HSD2 enzyme presents with hypertension and hypokalemia despite low aldosterone levels. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME) syndrome
• Mechanism: Cortisol fails to be inactivated to cortisone
• Result: Cortisol binds and activates Mineralocorticoid Receptors (MR)

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
coreConcept: Pre-receptor protection of MR by 11 beta-HSD2
front: Explain why 11β-HSD2 is physiologically essential in the kidney despite cortisol and aldosterone having similar affinities for the mineralocorticoid receptor.
back:
• Cortisol plasma levels are 2000x higher than aldosterone
• 11β-HSD2 inactivates cortisol to cortisone locally
• This prevents cortisol from flooding and over-activating renal MRs

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Contrast the net physiological effect of the 11β-HSD1 and 11β-HSD2 isoforms on local glucocorticoid activity.
back:
• 11β-HSD1: Converts cortisone to cortisol; amplifies glucocorticoid action (e.g., in liver/adipose)
• 11β-HSD2: Converts cortisol to cortisone; diminishes glucocorticoid action (e.g., in kidney/placenta)

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Identify the specific chemical substance in licorice that inhibits 11β-HSD2 and leads to secondary hypertension.
back:
• Glycyrrhetinic acid
• Mechanism: Competitive inhibition of 11β-HSD2
• Clinical effect: Mimics primary hyperaldosteronism with low renin/aldosterone

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: In tissues like the liver and adipose tissue, the [___] isoform facilitates the conversion of inactive cortisone to active cortisol.
back:
• 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (11β-HSD1)
• Role: Intracellular amplification of cortisol
• Clinical link: Potentially contributes to obesity-related insulin resistance

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: A patient with Cushing’s syndrome develops severe hypokalemia and hypertension. Explain the enzymatic mechanism allowing cortisol to cause these mineralocorticoid-like effects.
back:
• Massive cortisol levels overwhelm 11β-HSD2 capacity
• Excess active cortisol escapes inactivation to cortisone
• Cortisol directly activates Mineralocorticoid Receptors in renal tubules

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: How does 11β-HSD1 expression in adipose tissue potentially contribute to the metabolic abnormalities seen in obesity?
back:
• Increases local cortisol production from inactive cortisone
• Local glucocorticoid excess promotes insulin resistance
• Associated with metabolic syndrome and abdominal fat accumulation

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Contrast the primary tissue distribution of 11β-HSD1 versus 11β-HSD2.
back:
• 11β-HSD1: Liver, brain, adipose, skeletal muscle, skin
• 11β-HSD2: Kidney, colon, sweat glands, salivary glands, placenta

category: Explain the interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone by the 2, 11 beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoform
front: Identify the primary role of the 11β-HSD enzymes that allows them to be described as "intracellular gate-keepers."
back:
• Interconversion of active cortisol and inactive cortisone
• Modulates glucocorticoid access to tissue-specific receptors
• Regulates local hormone concentration independently of plasma levels

category: Discuss the metabolic and non-metabolic functions of cortisol
coreConcept: Metabolic and Non-metabolic Actions of Cortisol
front: The hallmark metabolic function of cortisol involves the stimulation of [___] in the liver, while its non-metabolic anti-inflammatory role is centered on stabilizing lysosomal membranes.
back: • Gluconeogenesis. • Metabolic: Mobilizes peripheral amino acids and fatty acids for energy. • Non-metabolic: Decreases capillary permeability and suppresses T-lymphocytes. • Blood: Causes lymphocytopenia, eosinopenia, and polycythemia.

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: In the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, the rate-limiting step in aldosterone synthesis is the conversion of cholesterol to [___], a process stimulated by both ACTH and Angiotensin II.
back:
• The intermediate steroid is Pregnenolone
• This rate-limiting step is catalyzed by cholesterol desmolase (P450scc)
• The process occurs in the mitochondria and is the essential foundation for all adrenocortical hormone synthesis

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: A patient with congestive heart failure exhibits significantly elevated plasma aldosterone levels despite a high-salt diet. Explain the primary physiological stimulus driving this hyperaldosteronism.
back:
• Decreased renal blood flow triggers the Renin-Angiotensin System
• Elevated Angiotensin II acts directly on zona glomerulosa cells
• Stimulates aldosterone secretion to restore blood volume via sodium and water retention

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which an increase in extracellular potassium (K+) concentration stimulates aldosterone secretion.
back:
• Direct depolarization of the zona glomerulosa cell membranes occurs
• Opens voltage-gated calcium channels allowing ionic influx
• Increased intracellular calcium activates specific protein kinases that stimulate the production and release of aldosterone

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Contrast the effects of Chronic Sodium Depletion versus excess ACTH administration on the morphology and secretory capacity of the adrenal cortex layers.
back:
• Sodium Depletion: Causes hypertrophy of the zona glomerulosa and selectively increases aldosterone output
• excess ACTH: Causes hypertrophy of the zona fasciculata and reticularis, selectively increasing cortisol/androgens with minimal effect on glomerulosa size

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Identify the specific inhibitory effect of Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) on the adrenal cortex and its resulting influence on blood pressure regulation.
back:
• Directly decreases aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa
• Opposes the effects of Angiotensin II and potassium
• Results in natriuresis and diuresis, effectively reducing blood volume and lowering arterial pressure

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: In patients with Primary Aldosteronism (Conn’s Syndrome), the regulatory loop is disrupted, resulting in high aldosterone levels and a characteristically low plasma [___] concentration.
back:
• Plasma Renin concentration
• Secretion is suppressed by increased blood volume and high arterial pressure
• This negative feedback via the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) is a key diagnostic finding in Conn’s syndrome

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: A 40-year-old male with persistent hypertension is treated with an ACE inhibitor. Describe the subsequent change in aldosterone regulation and the expected electrolyte shift.
back:
• The drug blocks the conversion of Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II
• Reduced Angiotensin II leads to significantly decreased aldosterone secretion
• Results in increased renal sodium excretion and potential potassium retention (hyperkalemia)

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Describe the "permissive" role of Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) in the regulation of aldosterone secretion.
back:
• Basal ACTH levels are required for the adrenal glands to secrete aldosterone
• However, ACTH has little effect in controlling the specific daily rate of secretion
• Total absence of ACTH reduces output, but it is not a primary regulator

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Contrast the impact of a 10% change in extracellular Sodium (Na+) concentration versus a 10% change in Potassium (K+) concentration on aldosterone release.
back:
• Sodium: A slight decrease causes only a minor, weak increase in aldosterone secretion
• Potassium: A small percentage increase acts as the most potent regulator, causing a severalfold, acute increase in aldosterone output from the adrenal cortex

category: Discuss the regulation of aldosterone secretion
front: Name the specific enzyme located only in the zona glomerulosa that allows it to synthesize aldosterone, distinguishing it from other adrenal layers.
back:
• Aldosterone synthase (P450c11AS)
• Necessary for the final conversion of corticosterone to aldosterone
• Its unique expression in the outermost layer is regulated primarily by Angiotensin II and extracellular potassium

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
coreConcept: Hypothalamic Regulation of the HPA Axis
front: In the regulation of glucocorticoid secretion, the hypothalamus releases [___], which travels through the hypophysial portal vessels to stimulate the secretion of ACTH from the anterior pituitary.
back:
• Corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF or CRH)
• Synthesized in the paraventricular nucleus (PVN)
• Acts on corticotropes to activate the adenylyl cyclase–cAMP second messenger system

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: The primary hypothalamic peptide that stimulates the release of ACTH from the anterior pituitary corticotropes is [___].
back: Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) or factor (CRF).

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: A patient with chronic exogenous steroid use suddenly stops their medication and develops an 'Adrenal Crisis.' Pathophysiologically, this occurs because long-term feedback inhibited the secretion of [___] and [___].
back:
• CRH (Hypothalamus)
• ACTH (Anterior Pituitary)
• Results in disuse atrophy of the adrenal zona fasciculata.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Describe the intracellular signaling cascade used by ACTH to stimulate glucocorticoid synthesis in the adrenal cortex.
back:
• Binding to G-protein coupled receptors
• Activation of adenylyl cyclase to increase cAMP
• Activation of Protein Kinase A (PKA)
• Phosphorylation of enzymes converting cholesterol to pregnenolone.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Contrast the feedback inhibition of cortisol on the hypothalamus versus its effect on the anterior pituitary gland.
back:
• Hypothalamus: Decreases synthesis and secretion of CRH.
• Pituitary: Reduces ACTH synthesis and decreases responsiveness to CRH stimulation.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Identify the specific rate-limiting enzymatic step in cortisol synthesis that is acutely stimulated by ACTH.
back:
• Conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone.
• Catalyzed by the enzyme cholesterol desmolase (P450scc) in mitochondria.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Glucocorticoid levels typically reach their peak concentration at approximately [___] AM due to the inherent hypothalamic circadian rhythm.
back:
• 6:00 AM to 8:00 AM.
• Lowest levels occur around midnight.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: A patient subjected to severe surgical trauma shows a 20-fold rise in cortisol despite high baseline levels. Explain why the negative feedback loop fails to prevent this rise.
back:
• Physiological stress (pain/trauma) is the most potent stimulus.
• It 'breaks through' the inhibitory feedback mechanism of cortisol.
• Overrides normal homeostatic set-points via the limbic system and amygdala.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Explain the route by which Corticotropin-Releasing Factor (CRF) reaches its target cells in the pituitary.
back:
• Secreted by neurons in the paraventricular nucleus.
• Released into the primary capillary plexus in the median eminence.
• Carried via hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels to the anterior pituitary.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Contrast the 'Long-loop' and 'Short-loop' negative feedback mechanisms within the HPA axis.
back:
• Long-loop: Cortisol inhibits CRH (hypothalamus) and ACTH (pituitary).
• Short-loop: ACTH inhibits the secretion of CRH from the hypothalamus.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Name the large precursor protein synthesized in the pituitary from which ACTH is post-translationally cleaved.
back:
• Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC).
• Can also be cleaved into MSH, endorphins, and lipotropins.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: The hypothalamic peptide that serves as the primary secretagogue for adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary is [___].
back: • Corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF), also known as Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH).

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: A patient under severe surgical stress maintains high cortisol levels despite normal negative feedback mechanisms. Explain why the HPA axis remains active.
back:
• Stress signals (physical or mental) are potent enough to break through the direct inhibitory negative feedback of cortisol.
• This leads to periodic or prolonged exacerbations of secretion during chronic or acute stress.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Explain the intracellular signaling pathway through which ACTH stimulates the synthesis of adrenocortical steroids.
back:
• ACTH binds membrane receptors to activate adenylyl cyclase.
• Increased cAMP activates protein kinase A.
• Protein kinase A catalyzes the rate-limiting step: conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: A 40-year-old female presents with hyperpigmentation and low cortisol levels. Contrast the hypothalamic and pituitary response expected in this primary adrenal insufficiency.
back:
• Decreased cortisol relieves negative feedback.
• Hypothalamus: Increases CRF secretion.
• Anterior Pituitary: Increases ACTH and simultaneous MSH (melanocyte-stimulating hormone) secretion due to shared POMC precursor.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Identify the specific hypothalamic nucleus that contains the cell bodies of neurons secreting CRF.
back: • Paraventricular nucleus (PVN).

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: The large precursor protein synthesized in the anterior pituitary that is enzymatically cleaved to produce ACTH, endorphins, and MSH is [___].
back: • Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC).

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: A patient's cortisol levels are measured at 20 μg/dl at 8:00 AM and 5 μg/dl at midnight. Apply your knowledge of hormonal rhythm to explain this finding.
back:
• Reflects the 24-hour circadian rhythm of glucocorticoid secretion.
• Driven by cyclical alterations in hypothalamic signals (CRF) that follow the patient's sleep-wake cycle.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Explain the function of the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system in glucocorticoid regulation.
back:
• CRF is released into the primary capillary plexus at the median eminence.
• Portal vessels transport CRF directly to the anterior pituitary.
• This prevents dilution in systemic blood, ensuring rapid ACTH response.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Contrast the effects of acute versus chronic ACTH stimulation on the adrenal cortex.
back:
• Acute: Immediate activation of steroidogenesis (cholesterol to pregnenolone conversion).
• Chronic: Causes hypertrophy and proliferation of cells in the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: Identify the primary feedback target(s) of cortisol within the brain and endocrine system.
back:
• Hypothalamus: Decreases CRF formation.
• Anterior Pituitary: Decreases ACTH formation.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
front: The hypothalamic peptide responsible for stimulating the secretion of Adrenocorticotropic Hormone (ACTH) from the anterior pituitary is [___].
back:
* Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH).
* Produced in the paraventricular nucleus.
* Secreted into the primary capillary plexus of the median eminence.

category: Explain the mechanism for regulation of glucocorticoid secretion by hypothalamus and pituitary
